skills.name: flight-booking
skills.description: When the user asks you to find, compare, book, change, or check in for a flight, look up an itinerary, or fetch a boarding pass, before you search for flights, open an airline or travel site, or touch a checkout.
skills.instructions:
---
name: flight-booking
description: >- When the user asks you to find, compare, book, change, or check in for a flight, look up an itinerary, or fetch a boarding pass, before you search for flights, open an airline or travel site, or touch a checkout.
---
# Flight booking You find, compare, and book flights, then handle check-in and boarding passes. When `FlightSearch` is in your tools, its results are your fares and schedules. Otherwise Grok Bot has no flight index of its own: every price and schedule comes from a connector, a travel site in your browser, or a web search, and you say which one you used. ## Entry points - "Get me on a flight to Chicago next Thursday" gives a destination and a date; the home airport is the origin.
- "Cheapest nonstop LAX to JFK on the 12th" is a fixed route with a ranking rule.
- "I have to be in Lisbon sometime in May" is a flexible window; find its cheapest dates before you search fares.
- A forwarded confirmation or deal email is an itinerary to look up, check in for, or rebook, not a new search. ## Before you search - Read the Memory section for the home airport, who usually travels with the user, seat, cabin, stop, and airline preferences, loyalty programs, known traveler numbers, and passport expiry. Call RecallMemory for older trips or preferences that are not listed.
- A search needs an origin, a destination, and dates. The home airport is the origin unless the user names another. When the user has several home airports or names a metro, pass the metro as `origin` ("Bay Area", "New York", "NYC") so one search covers all of them; an airport code searches only that airport. Ask only for what is still unknown, in one short question, without saying you will search. A flexible window ("sometime in May", "a long weekend in spring") needs only a trip length to search. Take it from the user's words: "a long weekend" is 2 to 4 nights, leaving Thursday or Friday and coming back Sunday or Monday, and "a week" is 6 to 8 nights. When the length names days, only pairs on those days count, including the pairs a price calendar returns. Ask for a length only when nothing the user said implies one.
- A flexible destination is up to 3 places. Search each place the user names ("Lisbon or Porto"). For an open one ("somewhere warm", "a beach in March"), pick 2 or 3 places that fit the season and the origin instead of asking. Name them in one short line before your first search or calendar read, because those can take minutes. When the user names more than 3, ask which 3 to compare. With several places and a window that needs a price calendar, read each place's calendar at one trip length, the middle one the user allows ("a long weekend" is 3 nights, Thursday to Sunday or Friday to Monday), so a turn reads at most 3 calendars; the dates a day either side cover the other lengths.
- Search one adult in economy unless the user or the Memory section says otherwise, and say what you assumed. When the trip sounds like a group ("we", "the kids", "my team", several names) and the head count is unknown, ask how many travel, with children's ages, before you search.
- Resolve relative dates against the time zone in your prompt's Time section. A date without a year ("Jan 12", "Tue Mar 20") is its next future occurrence; when the user also gave a weekday, take the year where the weekday matches. Search that date without asking the user to confirm the year. Say the weekday and the date together ("Thursday, October 9") before you type a date into any site. ## Searching with FlightSearch When `FlightSearch` is in your tools, it runs before any connector or site. Use those only when it finds no fares or the user asks for a site; the one exception is the price calendar for flexible dates below. - Plan 2 to 4 searches from what you know about the user and run them in one `FlightSearch` call: the trip exactly as the user asked, plus 1 to 3 `variants` that could change the pick for this user. Each variant changes one thing: - the dates, a day earlier or later on either end, when they aren't tied to an event; - the stop limit, allowing one stop when the trip as asked is nonstop only. Never add a stops variant that narrows the trip as asked (nonstop only when it already allows stops), even for a user who prefers nonstop, because its flights are already in those results; - the airports, nearby ones at either end (OAK or SJC for SFO) that the trip's search doesn't already cover; - the cabin, when the user flies another one or the flight is long.
- A question about one flight ("is UA 232 on the 12th still under $300?") needs no variants.
- When the user's window allows more than 4 date pairs, one search can't cover it. First dispatch a `computerUse` subagent with the Google Flights "prices across a date window" job, giving it the route, the window, the trip lengths, the cabin, every traveler, and the stop limit. Give it at most 3 trip lengths, since each one is another calendar read: when the user allows more ("a week or two"), pick 3 typical ones (7, 10, and 14 nights) and say which you checked. Then run one `FlightSearch` with the cheapest pair it returns as the trip and the next 3 as `dates` variants. Calendar prices are estimates, so quote fares only from the card. When the calendar can't be read, search 4 pairs spread across the window and say the rest went unchecked.
- For several destinations, run the trip to the first and an `airports` variant with `to` for each other place, on the same dates. With a window that needs the calendar, read it for each destination first, then make the trip the cheapest destination and pair, give the other destinations `airports` variants on those dates, and fill any slot left with that destination's next cheapest pair as a `dates` variant. When another destination's own cheapest dates differ and come close in price, run a second `FlightSearch` for it on those dates.
- A limit the user stated (arrive before a meeting, no red-eyes, one alliance only) applies to every search. A remembered preference only adds a variant or shapes the pick; it never removes the trip as asked.
- Pick `recommended` only from flights that meet every limit the user stated for this trip ("land by 6pm", "no red-eyes"); a stated limit beats a remembered preference. Among those, prefer the user's preferences in the Memory section (airlines and loyalty programs, nonstop, time of day, cabin), then price. Order `groups` the same way, so the comparison that best fits the stated limits comes first.
- When `ArrangeFlights` is in your tools, pass it the card id from the search result, `recommended`, and `groups`, and show the card it returns instead of the search's card.
- Describe refunds, changes, and bags only from the fare rules the flight tools give. ## Searching sites Without `FlightSearch`, or when it finds no fares: 1. Run SearchPlugins for a flights or travel connector and for the airline the user names. Use a connector when one is installed, with the resolved route, dates, passengers, and cabin, and refine there. Install a missing connector with InstallPlugin without asking; its connect card is the ask. Ask in one widget first only when the user named no service and several plugins fit (Gmail or Outlook, Google or Outlook Calendar), or the plugin has no connector. Say in the user's words why it helps, without saying plugin, MCP, or plugin id, and never paste a connect link. Do not assert that any airline has a connector before the search says so.
2. Otherwise dispatch a `computerUse` subagent to Google Flights or the airline's own site with the tightest URL you can build (route, dates, passengers, and cabin in the query string). Tell it what to read back: airline and flight number, departure and arrival times, duration, stops, connecting airports, fare name, total price, and bag rules when shown.
3. Refine with the site's filters instead of asking the user again. "No connections", "leave after lunch", "not Newark", and "anything cheaper" are filter changes. Re-dispatch with the new URL or the filter to click.
4. Vague places need airports. "Washington" means DCA, IAD, and BWI. Search all of them and label the airport in each option unless the user has ruled one out.
5. Never report that a route has no service from one empty result. Run WebSearch for the route and check the airline's own site first.
6. When the user's window allows more than 4 date pairs, read its prices first with the Google Flights "prices across a date window" job, with at most 3 trip lengths as in Searching with FlightSearch. Search the cheapest pair it returns as in step 2 without asking which dates to search, and name the next 2 cheapest pairs as other dates the user can pick. Calendar prices are estimates, so quote fares only from the site's results. When the calendar can't be read, search the window's first pair and say the rest went unchecked. ## Presenting choices Keep replies short and factual: what you found and what happens next. Start with the finding. No openers or acknowledgements ("Good news", "On it", "Got it", "Sorted", "Great choice"), greetings, emoji, filler, or enthusiasm. - When you show a flights card, the card carries the flights, prices, and fare rules. Write one or two short lines at most, such as which flight fits and why, named by airline and departure time, never by an offer ref. Don't list the flights or their prices, and mention a button only when the card shows it.
- When SendToUser rejects a reply for restating the card, rewrite it shorter but keep the answer the user asked for (the saving, the yes or no, the flight that fits). Never trade it for a vague line.
- When you searched other dates, say plainly whether moving the dates saves money, with one amount worked out from the result totals: "Flying a day later saves $40." or "Other dates aren't cheaper."
- Without a card, send a compact list of three to five flights, best first, one line each: airline and flight number, departure and arrival times with airport codes, stops, duration, and the total for all travelers. Add a bag or change caveat only when it changes the choice.
- Treat every time as local wall clock at that airport. An "arrive before 23:00" rule means the local arrival date and the local clock, so check both. When a trip crosses zones, label each time with its airport ("departs SFO 08:15, arrives JFK 16:45") and convert to the user's zone only when you say you did.
- When the user gave exact criteria ("the cheapest direct flight") and one option clearly wins, you may pick it, but still show the picked itinerary and total and get a yes before payment.
- Use a question widget for the pick only when the shortlist is real and short. Otherwise send the summary and let the user reply.
- Show what you collected in the user's language, which is the language they write to you in unless they asked for another or the Memory section names one they prefer. When a page is in another language, translate the words you put in a card or a summary, such as titles, descriptions, specs and their labels, notes, review summaries, policies, delivery and status lines, and option names. Keep brand, store, seller, and venue names, model numbers, order numbers and other codes, prices with their currency, and links as the page shows them. Brief the browser subagent and type into the site in the site's own words, and match a choice the user makes in their language back to those words. ## Savings check Run this once, on the final review page's total with shipping, tax, and fees, before you ask for the approval; a total from an earlier page can still be missing some of them. When the checkout takes codes only on an earlier page, gather them as Codes and offers below says before you leave that page and enter them there; the rest of the check still runs on the final page. It is one short pass, not a new search. - Codes and offers. Apply the offers the checkout itself shows, such as a coupon to clip, an automatic cart promotion, or a member price for a membership in the Memory section. When an email connector is installed, search the user's mail for this store's promo codes, such as a welcome, newsletter, or loyalty offer, and keep only codes that have not expired. When the checkout has a promo code field and neither a tool result nor the mail gave a code, ask whether the user has one. Enter only a code the user, a tool result, or the user's mail gave, once each; never guess codes or take them from a list of codes on another site, since stores treat that as abuse. When the store rejects a code, or the total does not drop after it, carry on at the total the page shows with any code that did apply. Tell the user in one message every code you found, where each came from (the email's sender and subject, the tool result, or the user), and which one applied. Cash-back portals and rebate sites are not part of this check; leave them out.
- The merchant's own site. When you are buying through a marketplace seller, a travel site, or another reseller and the total is above 100 USD, or that amount converted to the checkout's currency at today's rate, or above an amount the user set for this check, read the same item, dates, and terms on the merchant's own site (the brand's store, the airline, the hotel). Tell the user both totals. When the merchant's is lower and the user wants it, start the purchase over on the merchant's site from the cart or booking step, so the cart summary, the review, and the approval all come from that site; never carry lines or a total from one site to the other. Keep the reseller when the user chose it for a reason, such as a perk or their account there. When `CheckSubscriptionUsage` reports that most of this cycle's included usage is used and does not say that on-demand usage is enabled, skip this part and say so in one line.
- The card. When you will pay with a card from the user's vault (see Paying and confirming), the user has not already chosen the card, as a message naming it by Vault id does, and `Vault` list shows more than one saved card, pick the one whose `When to use:` line fits this store or this kind of purchase, and give the reason in that line's words. Name only perks a `When to use:` line states, never a reward rate or protection you assume a card has. Without such a line, pick as you otherwise would and give no reason. When the user tells you a card's perk, such as extra points on groceries or a travel credit, offer to add it to that card's hint with `Vault`, and change the hint only when they say yes.
- Then say in one line what the check saved and how ("Saved $6.00 with CAMP6 from the store's welcome email", "Saved €297 by booking direct"), or that the codes you tried did not apply. Say nothing about savings when there was nothing to try.
- After the order is placed, record each saving, since the user paid the lower price: kind promo_code for a code or checkout offer, or direct_booking for buying on the merchant's own site instead of a reseller, with the reseller's total, including any code that applied there, less the merchant's total before any code you entered on the merchant's site, since that code is its own promo_code saving, dated the order date, with the order's https link as proof. Save one fact of type "journal" with UpdateMemory for each saving, in exactly this shape: `Saving YYYYMM: YYYY-MM-DD | kind | amount CURRENCY | store | proof link`. YYYYMM is the year and month of that date with no separator. amount CURRENCY is how much less the user paid, with its ISO 4217 code, such as 6.00 USD. Never start any other fact with Saving and a month. Save nothing when nothing was saved. ## Booking When the user picks a flight, in words or from a card, book it. No flight tool holds or books a fare. When `FlightDetails` gives a time for its price, say "this price is good until <time>", and that the airline confirms the price at payment. Selecting flights on a site holds nothing either: say the flights are selected. Say a fare is held or reserved only when the airline's own page says so, and never say a price is verified or locked in. A flight card's Book button sends "Book <trip>, <fare>, for <total>", an `Offer ref:` line with that flight's offer ref, and the card's link when that link is on the airline's own site. That is the user's pick of that flight and fare, so book it in the same turn without asking which flight or fare or searching again. For step 1, call `FlightDetails` with that offer ref to check the price, and when the price is gone or couldn't be checked, show its card and stop. Otherwise send no Selected trip card in this turn: say in one short line where you're starting ("Starting your booking on alaskaair.com."), then go on with step 2. The other steps all still apply, including the savings check and the confirmation before payment, and the airline confirms the final price at checkout. 1. Check the pick before the browser starts, in one message. When `FlightDetails` is in your tools, call it for the flight and show its card. From the fare rules, say which extras the user asked for the fare already includes. When you will book in the browser (step 2), say which of the rest you will add there at the airline's price (step 5); when a tool books the fare in chat, say the rest are added on the airline's site after booking. Say so when the rules leave bags to the airline, and flag anything else the fare lacks that the user mentioned, such as changes. Flag a red-eye or a long layover. When more than one fare is offered for the flight, say in one line what each adds (bags, changes, seat choice) and the price difference, and let the user pick.
2. When none of your tools books this fare in chat, book it in the browser on the airline's own site, or on the site the user prefers. Dispatch a `computerUse` subagent with the flight numbers, dates, fare, cabin, and travelers. When the airline playbook's booking snippet has a `<CHECKOUT LINK>` slot, fill it with the link in the user's Book ask; the snippet falls back to its search link when the checkout link doesn't open the trip. With no booking snippet for the airline, start the subagent at that link, or on the airline's own site when there is none. Use the ask's link only when it's on the airline site `FlightDetails` names for that offer; otherwise leave it out and start on the airline's own site. If a travel site shows the fare but hands payment to the airline, say so before you start, because the airline page is a new sign-in.
3. Enter passenger details. Never ask for them in chat, not even one field. - Legal names, dates of birth, and contact details come from memory when you have them. Collect the rest with `RequestUserForm`. - Ask for the fields the subagent reported on the passenger page, in the same shape, because form values reach the page exactly as entered and can't be split or joined: one name box gets one field, separate first, middle, and last name boxes get three. Before that page is open, use separate first, middle, and last name fields and separate birth month, day, and year fields, the shape most airline pages use. - Use the fewest forms the tool's field limit allows: fit as many whole travelers in a form as the limit holds, and split a traveler across forms only when their fields alone exceed it. Ask for each field once; the contact phone and email go in the first form. Mark middle name optional (`required: false`). - Passport numbers and expiry dates go into the form as secret fields. Loyalty and known traveler numbers come from memory or from a saved vault key listed in the `RequestUserForm` description (the key `ktn` names one fact on every site; a frequent flyer key carries the airline in its name). - When a later page asks for something new, send a form with only the new fields.
4. When the site wants a sign-in, a one-time code, or a verify-you-are-human check, follow the Cursor-managed `sign-in` skill in its order, which ends with the Secure Form (`RequestUserForm`) and then handing over the screen with `request_box_help` and one instruction ("Sign in to your <service> account"). Never send a question widget before these; the tool is the ask. After a receipt or a hand-back, dispatch the subagent again; the session persists across turns.
5. When booking in the browser, buy the extras the user asked for in this conversation, such as "two checked bags", "a carry-on each", "seats together", or "an aisle seat", and nothing else. A seat or bag preference in the Memory section is not a request to pay; follow it only where it costs nothing. In the booking snippet's `<EXTRAS>` slot, or in the subagent's task when there is no snippet, list each extra with how many and which travelers and flights it is for, with "the lowest-priced seats that" before a seat ask ("the lowest-priced seats that sit all 3 travelers together on both flights"), or write "none". Every other offer stays declined, such as a fare upgrade or bundle the user didn't pick, priority boarding, lounge access, insurance, a hotel, or a car. When the site sells an extra only with a higher fare or bundle, that's a fare change: say what it costs and let the user pick. When the subagent reports `extra_unavailable`, or the review page lacks an extra the user asked for, say in the message before the approval which extra is missing and what the site said, and that the total doesn't include it.
6. Run the savings check (see Savings check). Then confirm the itinerary, the extras, and the total with a question widget and pay (see Paying and confirming).
7. Report the booking reference, the itinerary, and the total from the confirmation page. Save a stated preference (a new loyalty number, a favorite airline) with `UpdateMemory` only when the user confirmed it.
8. Whenever the booking stops before confirmation, for any reason (a captcha or other wall the sign-in order can't clear, a site error, a fare the site no longer sells, or the user skipping or declining a help request), end your reply with a link for the chosen flight so the user can finish. Send the first of these that exists: the `checkoutUrl` in the user's Book request, unless the subagent reported `checkout_link_failed`; the link the flight tools gave for those exact flights; the airline playbook's booking search link filled in for the flight; a Google Flights results link for the route, dates, cabin, and every traveler, built as the Google Flights playbook says. Send the airline's homepage only when none of those exists. Say in one line what stopped the booking. Never tell the user to finish on the airline's site without the link. ## Paying and confirming - Before payment, send one question widget that restates the full itinerary, passenger names, fare, each extra added with its price, and the total. When you send an order card instead, its items are the fare for all travelers and then one line per extra with the price the review page shows, such as title "Checked bags" with detail "2 travelers, both flights"; taxes and fees are charges, and together they add up to the page's total. Nothing ships, so set `requiresShipping` false and leave out `shipTo`.
- When the site wants payment, a deposit, or a card to hold the booking, work it in this order and stop at the first step that pays. First, a payment method already saved on the site's own account, not a card in the user's vault. Have the subagent select it, and when that account has several, ask which one in the confirmation widget. Next, when the account has none and the `purchases` skill lists a card saved in the user's vault, use that card as its Credit cards section says. When that skill has you send an `order` card, read every line, the total, and the ship-to address from the checkout's review page before you send it, and charge only after the user taps Pay. When neither has one and the site charges an exact total now (tax, fees, tip, and shipping included), Stripe Link is the preferred way to pay: with `RequestVirtualCard` among your tools this turn, raise a one-time card with the site as merchant and type it only into the merchant's checkout; a denial is final. Without that tool, offer Stripe Link once as the `purchases` skill says, when that skill is listed. A card kept on file for a hold or a no-show fee is not charged now, so it never gets a one-time card. Next, and right away whenever the user turns Link down, ignores the offer, or asks to use their own card, send the Secure Form (`RequestUserForm`, reason "checkout", the site's domain) for the card inputs the live checkout shows, such as card number, expiry, CVC, name, and billing ZIP; never tell them you can't take their card, and never predict that the form can't reach card inputs embedded from a payment provider. Last, when the host refuses the form or its receipt says a card field failed, or the user would rather type on the page, hand the box to the user with `request_box_help` and one instruction ("Add your card and confirm the payment on <service>"); the same handoff covers a CVC re-entry and any 2FA, 3DS, or bank prompt. The user finishes the payment inside that handoff, so when the box comes back, skip any later confirm or place-order click and read the confirmation page. When the user already typed their card into chat, use it as given for that checkout instead of sending the form. Card numbers, CVCs, and expiries stay in the merchant's checkout, never in chat or logs.
- Once the payment method is selected or entered, and unless the user already finished the payment in a handoff, the final click is yours. Give the subagent what the widget the user approved named (the itinerary or stay, the travelers, any extras, and the total), have it re-read the review or checkout page, and when nothing material changed, have it click the site's confirm, pay, book, or request-to-book control once and read the confirmation page. A material change is a total more than 1% or 5 units of its currency above the approved one, whichever is larger; a different currency; for a flight, different flights, dates, times, cabin or fare class, passenger names or count, or extras; and for a stay, a different hotel or listing, room type, number of nights, or guest count. On a material change, click nothing: show the user what changed and send a fresh question widget, whose yes is the only one that books. Nothing else stops the click. A lower total, the same total with its fees and taxes labeled or split differently, a different layout, reworded or reordered fields, and banners all go ahead, and the subagent turns down seat, upgrade, insurance, and other offers the user did not choose, then continues. In the confirmation message, give the total the confirmation page says was charged, and say so when it differs from the approved one. ## Check-in and boarding passes - Check in on the airline's own check-in page with the booking reference and passenger name through a `computerUse` subagent. Look for the reference in the itinerary, memory, and the confirmation email before asking.
- Find the confirmation and boarding-pass emails through the user's mail connector (Gmail or Outlook) when one is connected. If none is, run SearchPlugins for one. Install a missing connector with InstallPlugin without asking; its connect card is the ask. Ask in one widget first only when the user named no service and several plugins fit (Gmail or Outlook, Google or Outlook Calendar), or the plugin has no connector. Say in the user's words why it helps, without saying plugin, MCP, or plugin id, and never paste a connect link. If the user doesn't connect one, open their webmail in the browser subagent instead.
- Download the boarding pass from the airline's page or email to `/workspace` with the browser subagent, then attach the file with SendToUser. A PDF is fine. Name the file by flight and route so several legs stay apart.
- Seat changes, bag purchases, and upgrades offered at check-in are the user's choices. List them with their prices, and buy one only when the user asks for it and then approves its price in a question widget, paying as Paying and confirming says. ## Pitfalls - Prices move between search and checkout. Flag any jump before the payment step.
- Basic economy and light fares often exclude carry-on or checked bags and forbid changes. Say so when the fare name suggests it, unless the flight tools gave the fare rules; then state only those.
- International trips need passport details and sometimes visa answers. Ask early, through a form, so the booking does not stall at the passenger page.
- Travel sites that redirect to the airline for payment change the sign-in context. Expect a second sign-in, worked in the same order.
- Multi-leg and open-jaw itineraries deserve a segment-by-segment review before the widget.
- Changes, cancellations, refunds, and credits depend on the fare, the booking channel, the time to departure, and current airline policy. Look up the current policy on the airline's site before you tell the user what to click or whom to call.
- Never invent a fare, a seat map, or a confirmation number. If the page did not show it, say so. ## Site playbooks Before you dispatch the browser subagent, Read the `site-playbooks-google-flights`, `site-playbooks-united`, `site-playbooks-southwest`, `site-playbooks-delta`, `site-playbooks-american-airlines`, `site-playbooks-alaska`, `site-playbooks-jetblue`, `site-playbooks-frontier`, `site-playbooks-air-canada`, or `site-playbooks-expedia` skill in this catalog, whichever names the site you are about to use, and paste the Dispatch snippet of the job that matches your step (a read-only lookup, or a cart and checkout) into the Task text. It carries the deep link or endpoint that lands on results instead of clicking through the home page, and the stop rules for that site.

skills.name: food-ordering
skills.description: When the user asks you to order food for delivery or pickup, reorder a usual meal, get a specific dish brought to them, or says they are hungry and wants you to handle dinner, before you open a delivery app.
skills.instructions:
---
name: food-ordering
description: >- When the user asks you to order food for delivery or pickup, reorder a usual meal, get a specific dish brought to them, or says they are hungry and wants you to handle dinner, before you open a delivery app.
---
# Food ordering Order delivery or pickup through DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, the regional equivalent (Deliveroo, Wolt, iFood, Just Eat), or the restaurant's own online ordering page, using your browser. The user's account on the platform holds their past orders, saved addresses, and payment method; your memory holds their preferences. Two rules hold on every order. For delivery, the address is confirmed with the user before you place it, even when the site already has one saved; for pickup, the store and the pickup time are confirmed instead. The cart summary is confirmed with a question widget before you place it, and the yes places exactly the cart that widget read back. ## Entry points - "Sort out dinner for me" or "I'm starving, handle it" leaves the meal to you.
- "Get me the same thing I ordered last Friday" points at the platform's order history.
- "Two margherita pizzas from Roberta's for pickup at 7" gives items, restaurant, and timing.
- "Order lunch for me and my vegan boss" is an open-ended order for two: pick restaurants with a vegan main for the boss and something the user likes from memory, and build one cart with both meals.
- A pasted restaurant or menu link: open that exact URL. ## Before you start - Find the preferred app. Check the Memory section of your prompt and `RecallMemory` for a stated delivery app, then this conversation. An app the user named or memory records is the one you use. If none is, or they ask for the cheapest way, compare channels once the restaurant is picked (see Comparing channels). When only one channel is eligible to compare, order through it without comparing. When none is, because the restaurant has no online ordering page of its own and the user is signed into none of the apps that list it, in the browser or through a connector, pick the platform with the best coverage for their area, say which one you chose, and sign in there (step 2) before building a cart. Do not ask the user which app to use or which one they have an account on, and do not build carts on the others.
- When you compare channels, run `SearchPlugins` for each delivery app that lists the restaurant only to learn which are already connected. Install nothing, show no connect card, and dispatch no helper for an app until Comparing channels finds it eligible.
- Once the platform you will order through is settled (the preferred app, the only eligible channel, the platform you picked when none is eligible, or, after a comparison, the channel the widget's yes chose), run `SearchPlugins` for it. Use a connector if one is installed. Install a missing connector with InstallPlugin without asking; its connect card is the ask. Ask in one widget first only when the user named no service and several plugins fit (Gmail or Outlook, Google or Outlook Calendar), or the plugin has no connector. Say in the user's words why it helps, without saying plugin, MCP, or plugin id, and never paste a connect link. If the search finds nothing, dispatch a `computerUse` subagent. Do not claim a connector exists without a search hit.
- The DoorDash connector builds the cart in its own tools: `preview_order` quotes it with fees, tax, and tip included, which is the checkout read-back step 5 asks for, and `submit_order` places it after the widget's yes, without the browser. Never send its checkout link (`get_checkout_url`) or a cart render in place of placing the order the user asked for; send the link only when its quote shows no way to pay.
- Pull preferences from memory: dietary rules, dislikes, spice tolerance, favorite places, a tipping rule. Past orders live on the platform, not in memory; the subagent reads them there.
- Resolve delivery versus pickup and timing (now or scheduled). Scheduled times follow the Time section of your prompt: state them in the user's zone.
- Treat a stated budget as a hard constraint. Without one, size the order to what their history shows for a similar meal.
- When the ask is open-ended and quality matters ("somewhere good", "the best Thai that delivers"), use the Cursor-managed `restaurant-recommendations` skill to pick candidates, then verify on the delivery app that each is open, delivers to the address, and what the ETA and fee are. ## Flow 1. Dispatch the browser subagent read-only in your first round, in the same round as any `WebSearch`, with every menu source you know in priority order: the exact URL the user linked or the restaurant's page on the preferred platform (on DoorDash, its `/store/` URL), then the restaurant's own online ordering page. Tell it to report the first source that gives categories and prices and to skip the rest. Do not run a curl, a `WebFetch`, or a shell pipeline first and dispatch after they fail; on 2026-09-12 that order cost 49 seconds before the helper started, and the helper then had the menu about 75 seconds later from a source the parent had found in a search. Have it report the URL it ended on and which source that was. When that is the restaurant's page on the preferred platform, have it also report whether the restaurant is open and delivers to the saved address, the ETA, the delivery fee, and, for a reorder, the recent orders on the account, and every later Task text carries that URL. When the menu came from any other host, each cart step still needs the restaurant's page on the channel it orders through: resolve that URL before the cart Task, the way the site playbook's order section says when the platform has one, and never carry the other host's URL into it.
2. When the site wants a sign-in, a one-time code, or a verify-you-are-human check, follow the Cursor-managed `sign-in` skill in its order, which ends with the Secure Form (`RequestUserForm`) and then handing over the screen with `request_box_help` and one instruction ("Sign in to your <service> account"). Never send a question widget before these; the tool is the ask. After a receipt or a hand-back, dispatch the subagent again; the session persists across turns.
3. Pick the restaurant, presenting options first when the request was open-ended (see Presenting choices).
4. Build the cart: exact items, sizes, modifiers, quantities, and the user's instructions in the item notes. Only what the user asked for goes in. Carry the restaurant's URL on the channel you order through, resolved first if the menu came from another host, and the item names as the menu spelled them into the Task text, and paste the site playbook's order section snippet when the site has one, never its place section snippet. A change to the same cart goes back to the same helper, with `MessageSubagent` while it runs or `Task` with `resume` after it reports, not to a fresh dispatch. A one-item ask is a one-item cart, and when a later message narrows the order ("just the pizza", "skip the sides"), the latest message wins. Dismiss upsells ("add a drink?", "round up for charity", a subscription trial) unless the user asked for them.
5. Open checkout and have the subagent report every line: items, subtotal, delivery and service fees, tax, the tip the site preselected, the total, and, for delivery, the ETA and the delivery address shown on the page, or, for pickup, the store address and the pickup time shown on the page. Leave the site's default tip in place unless the user or memory gives a rule, and name it in the summary.
6. Send the summary with `SendToUser`, with the address written out, then one question widget whose prompt names the address and the total ("Place the $34.20 order to 512 Valencia St, ETA 35 to 45 min?") with options to place it, change the address, or edit the cart, and allowCustom on so they can paste a promo code or name a change. The saved address may be stale; the user may be somewhere else tonight. For pickup the prompt names the store and the pickup time instead ("Place the $31.50 pickup at Roberta's, 261 Moore St, ready at 7:00 PM?") with options to place it, change the time, or edit the cart. The widget ends your turn.
7. If they give a promo code or a change, apply it and re-confirm with a fresh widget when the total moved by more than the discount. Ask about a promo code before finalizing only when the checkout shows a promo field.
8. When the site wants payment, a deposit, or a card to hold the booking, work it in this order and stop at the first step that pays. First, a payment method already saved on the site's own account, not a card in the user's vault. Have the subagent select it, and when that account has several, ask which one in the confirmation widget. Next, when the account has none and the `purchases` skill lists a card saved in the user's vault, use that card as its Credit cards section says. When that skill has you send an `order` card, read every line, the total, and the ship-to address from the checkout's review page before you send it, and charge only after the user taps Pay. When neither has one and the site charges an exact total now (tax, fees, tip, and shipping included), Stripe Link is the preferred way to pay: with `RequestVirtualCard` among your tools this turn, raise a one-time card with the site as merchant and type it only into the merchant's checkout; a denial is final. Without that tool, offer Stripe Link once as the `purchases` skill says, when that skill is listed. A card kept on file for a hold or a no-show fee is not charged now, so it never gets a one-time card. Next, and right away whenever the user turns Link down, ignores the offer, or asks to use their own card, send the Secure Form (`RequestUserForm`, reason "checkout", the site's domain) for the card inputs the live checkout shows, such as card number, expiry, CVC, name, and billing ZIP; never tell them you can't take their card, and never predict that the form can't reach card inputs embedded from a payment provider. Last, when the host refuses the form or its receipt says a card field failed, or the user would rather type on the page, hand the box to the user with `request_box_help` and one instruction ("Add your card and confirm the payment on <service>"); the same handoff covers a CVC re-entry and any 2FA, 3DS, or bank prompt. The user finishes the payment inside that handoff, so when the box comes back, skip any later confirm or place-order click and read the confirmation page. When the user already typed their card into chat, use it as given for that checkout instead of sending the form. Card numbers, CVCs, and expiries stay in the merchant's checkout, never in chat or logs.
9. Place the order only after the widget's yes, and only the cart that widget read back. A correction that arrives after the widget went out ("skip the sides", "make it two") is a no for that cart: rebuild, send a fresh widget with the new lines, and wait for its yes. For the place dispatch, resume the helper that read checkout back and paste the site playbook's place section snippet when the site has one. Otherwise have the subagent click the place-order control, dismiss the post-order prompts (rate, tip more, share, add items), and read the confirmation page.
10. For a delivery order, send a shipment card at stage `placed` from the confirmation page (see Shipment card), with the restaurant as its store and the restaurant's page on the channel the order went through as its URL, and the ETA, the total charged, and the address in `content`. For pickup, or when no card goes out, report the order number, the ETA, the total charged, and the address, and attach the confirmation screenshot at its exact saved path. Save a preference the user stated or confirmed ("always DoorDash", "extra spicy") with `UpdateMemory`. If they ask to make it recurring, create a routine with `UpdateRoutine`. ## Comparing channels Delivery apps add delivery and service fees and often price the menu higher than the restaurant does, and they show those fees only at checkout, so the restaurant's own online ordering page is often the cheaper way to order the same food. When you compare channels (see Before you start): - In step 1, have the helper read every menu source instead of stopping at the first, and report the restaurant's page on each delivery app it is listed on and whether the user is signed in there. In the browser, an app counts as signed in only when its page shows the user's account; a sign-in link or a signed-out notice means it is not. An app with a connected connector counts as signed in through that connector, whatever the browser shows. Decide eligibility from that report and the `SearchPlugins` results, before any cart.
- Quote every eligible channel, even when one looks cheaper from its menu prices: a membership or promo on a delivery app can erase its fees. Quote up to three channels for the same cart: the restaurant's own online ordering page when it has one, and at most two delivery apps the user is already signed into, in the browser or through a connected connector. Do not compare an app that would need a new account or sign-in; with no eligible channel at all, build no carts and follow Before you start, which says which app to sign into. Only one browser helper runs at a time, so dispatch one helper for all the browser channels: it builds the same cart through step 5 on each channel in turn, in the same tab, and reports for every channel the checkout lines step 5 lists and the checkout page's URL. Each channel keeps its cart when the helper moves on. Tell it to stop at a sign-in, one-time code, or verify-you-are-human wall on a channel, note it, and move on to the next rather than hand it to the user; step 2 runs only for the channel the user picks. A connected connector's quote or preview tool gives its channel's checkout total, and you call it while the helper works. The same connector's order tool places that order in step 9.
- Compare the checkout totals as each page would charge them, with fees, tax, and tip included, then the ETA or pickup time. A menu price is not a quote, so never ask the user to pick a channel, or pickup versus delivery when they said either is fine, from menu prices: go from the menu straight to the carts, and let the step 6 widget be the only question. When the preselected tips differ, name each channel's tip beside its total. Leave out a channel that stopped at a wall or shows no total before payment, and name it with the reason.
- In step 6, name the cheapest channel in the widget's prompt with its total, and give each other channel's total and ETA in the summary ("$31.20 on Roberta's own site, ready at 12:40; $38.90 on DoorDash, ETA 12:35"). Add an option for another channel only when it is meaningfully faster.
- The yes places the order on the channel it chose, by resuming the helper that built the carts for step 9 with that channel's checkout URL: it opens that URL, confirms the items and total match what the widget read back, and only then places it, stopping to report if they differ. Or, for a connector's quote, through that connector's order tool. A connector order skips step 8: it pays only with a way to pay that the connector's quote lists, never a one-time card or the Secure Form, since it has no web checkout to type a card into. Leave the other carts unplaced. ## Shipment card When `SendToUser` has a `shipment` field, report an order's status as a shipment card in it, one card per order. Take its facts from the store's order or confirmation page, the carrier's tracking page, or the shipping email. The card takes the store's name in plain words and its site URL, its logo image URL when the page shows one, the order number, and each item's title, quantity, and image URL; the accessibility snapshot carries no image URLs, so the subagent reads them from the page's images with a page script. The card needs the store, the order number, and at least one item. Without that field or any of those, report in text instead. Set `stage` from the page's status: `placed` until it ships or a courier picks it up, even when it is due today, `in_transit` once it ships, `arriving_today` when it is on its way and out for delivery or due today, `delivered`, `delayed` when the page says it is late or shows a delivery exception, or `cancelled`. Put the page's own status headline in `status`, translated into the user's language when the page is in another, since a translation still keeps the store's words, and the expected or actual delivery date in `expectedDeliveryDate` as YYYY-MM-DD. For a range, use its last day. Fill `tracking` only with a tracking link a page showed or the URL of the carrier page the subagent opened, and the carrier's name; never build one from a tracking number. Leave out any value no page showed. In `content`, write one sentence on what changed, without the tracking link. The card's message takes no images, links, other cards, or voice memo, so send a screenshot or photo in its own `SendToUser` after the card. ## Presenting choices - Open-ended meal: three to five restaurants with cuisine, one quality signal, ETA, delivery fee, and any fit from memory ("you reordered from here twice"). Attach the saved screenshot of the results when the cards show photos, ratings, or delivery times worth seeing; a text summary is enough when they do not. Ask which one with a question widget before opening a menu or building a cart.
- Specific dish, no restaurant ("any chance of pad thai tonight?"): the top restaurant and item pairs with price and ETA, then ask. Do not take the first result because it is the highest rated or the fastest.
- Exact restaurant or a reorder: skip the restaurant options, but still confirm the cart, the address or pickup time, and the total before placing.
- "Same as last time" with several recent orders in the history: show the last two or three and ask which. Do not guess.
- Refinement ("something lighter", "under $25", "not pizza again"): apply it, present the new set, and ask again. Never swap in a different restaurant on your own.
- The place-order confirmation is the one widget every order needs. Decide the small things yourself (a default side, a sauce) and state them in the summary.
- Show what you collected in the user's language, which is the language they write to you in unless they asked for another or the Memory section names one they prefer. When a page is in another language, translate the words you put in a card or a summary, such as titles, descriptions, specs and their labels, notes, review summaries, policies, delivery and status lines, and option names. Keep brand, store, seller, and venue names, model numbers, order numbers and other codes, prices with their currency, and links as the page shows them. Brief the browser subagent and type into the site in the site's own words, and match a choice the user makes in their language back to those words. ## Pitfalls - Dispatching the cart build without the store URL, or with a past order to copy. The helper heads for order history and spends a minute there before the first item.
- Sending the helper to the restaurant's own site for a menu when your `WebFetch` of it showed hours and no prices. On 2026-09-12 the helper's navigates there failed twice (a name that did not resolve, then an SSL name alert) and it spent three rounds and a DNS check on them. A site that gave you no menu gives the helper none either; leave it off the source list. The restaurant's online ordering page is a different page, often on another host, and stays on the list.
- Treating a saved address as the right address. Confirm it every time, and look harder when the conversation suggests they are traveling or at work.
- Asking for a delivery address on a pickup order. The pickup widget names the store and the time; the address question is a round trip the user does not need.
- Placing a cart the user did not approve. A yes covers one specific cart. When the items changed after the widget went out, that yes is spent; re-confirm before placing.
- Building a cart before checking that the restaurant is open and delivers to the address.
- Confirming the menu subtotal instead of the checkout total. Fees, tax, and tip land at checkout; the number in the widget is the one the card will be charged. If the total changes after the yes (a substitution, a surge fee), stop and re-confirm.
- Accepting an upsell, a round-up prompt, or a subscription trial that the user did not ask for.
- A companion's item in a group order says nothing about the user's taste.
- Inventing an ETA or an order number. Report only what the confirmation page shows, and if it shows no number, say so.
- Saving an address or a dietary rule to memory that the user did not state or confirm.
- Spending on your own initiative. The user must have asked for this specific order, and the widget's yes is what places it. ## Site playbooks Before you dispatch the browser subagent, Read the `site-playbooks-doordash` skill in this catalog, if it names the site you are about to use, and paste the Dispatch snippet of the job that matches your step (a read-only lookup, or a cart and checkout) into the Task text. It carries the deep link or endpoint that lands on results instead of clicking through the home page, and the stop rules for that site.

skills.name: frc-progressions-and-prescriptions
skills.description: Use when choosing, progressing, or regressing Functional Range Conditioning (FRC) work: CARs for maintaining mobility, PAILs/RAILs for increasing mobility, and PRH → PRLO → Hovers → ERR for end-range strength and control.
skills.instructions:
# FRC progressions and prescriptions [REDACTED paragraph: person_with_client_athlete_context] Ryne overlay: methods generally go **in order**. **CARs** maintain mobility / maximize available space. **PAILs/RAILs** increase mobility. **PRH → PRLO → Hover → ERR** build strength and control at end range. Swimmer dryland context: [Swim dryland programming](sand-workflow:swim-dryland-programming) (swimmer hovers / HA for fly and catch ownership). PRI pathomechanics: [PRI Swimming An In-Depth Look](sand-workflow:pri-swimming-in-depth). ## Session placement
- CARs: after PRI techniques, before dynamic warm-up.
- PAILs/RAILs and end-range work: mobility / prep or dedicated end-range block - not competing with high-CNS primary lifts in the same slot. ## Ladder (order)
1. **CARs** - maintain / express available ROM
2. **PAILs/RAILs** - expand usable ROM + tissue adaptation
3. **PRH** → **PRLO** → **Hover** → **ERR** - teach the nervous system to own the new range PAILs/RAILs gain the range; end-range loading solidifies control. CARs help keep what you own. Cramping at end range usually means the tissue is unused to the request - regress volume/angle, don't force. --- ## 1. Controlled Articular Rotations (CARs) **Why:** Joint-only rotation on a stable body. Stress the capsule through its available envelope. Not a ROM-gaining tool ("CARs are not going to fix CARs"). **Cue:** Inhale, trap air low abs, shallow breath. Stabilize everything else. Outer limit of the circle; expand each rep. Dense air (honey/molasses). **Rx:** 1 set × 2-3 reps per direction. **Movement pool:**
- Spine: All Fours segmented cat/camel; tall kneeling T/L; standing T/L
- GH: tall kneeling; standing
- Scapula: tall kneeling or standing, arm @ scapular plane & 90° abduction
- Hip: all fours (knee on pad); half kneeling supported; standing supported --- ## 2. PAILs & RAILs (Progressive / Regressive Angular Isometric Loading) **Why:** Stretch + isometric at progressive (PAILs) and regressive (RAILs) angles to expand ROM and strengthen newly acquired and shorter angles. **Procedure (condensed):** Stretch position → active into stretch → passive hold → build irradiated isometric (PAILs) with low-ab brace → on relax, active RAILs deeper → hold new range → re-establish passive. **Achieve Rx (overrides course 2-min passive):**
- Passive stretch **45-60s** (not 2 min)
- **1 set of 3** progressive holds, **5-7s** each, for both progressive and regressive angles **Movement pool:**
- Spine: All Fours flexion/extension PAILs/RAILs
- Shoulder: All Fours Swiss ball flexion + dowel; ER + dowel; horizontal abduction; Bar hang scapular elevation
- Hip capsule: Seated 90/90 ER; Seated 90/90 IR; Seated sleeper (IR) --- ## 3. End-range strength / control (PALs/RALs ladder) ### Passive Range Holds (PRH)
- Find end range passively → remove assist → hold.
- Rep fails when joint drifts ~**15°** past the hold.
- Progress: short holds / more reps → longer holds / fewer reps `5s×6 → 10s×3 → 15s×2 → 30s×1` **Pool:** Seated 90/90 hip IR/ER; All Fours Swiss ball shoulder flex/habd; Swiss ball shoulder ER; Kneeling wrist extension (hang-clean catch); Prone shoulder IR (small prop OK). ### Passive Range Lift-Offs (PRLO)
- Leave room near PROM - don't start at absolute end.
- Progress closer to PROM while dropping reps; controlled eccentric failure, no cheat. `20°×12-15 → 10°×8-10 → 5°×6-8 → at PROM (sticky)×3-5` **Pool:** Seated 90/90 hip IR/ER; Sidelying hip ER; All Fours Swiss ball shoulder flex/habd; Swiss ball shoulder ER; Prone GH IR. ### Hovers
- Dynamic PRLO over barely-achievable targets.
- Progress zone divisions + reps: `6 → 8 → 10 → 12`. Controlled ecc failure. **Pool:** Seated 90/90 hip IR or ER hover; Prone / tall kneeling / ½ kneeling swimmer hover (swimmers ~135° before elbow flex); Prone infinity swimmer hover; Prone shoulder flex or habd hover; Prone shoulder IR hover. ### End-Range Rotational Training (ERR)
- Small circles (~tennis ball) at end range (hips / GH / scap / spine as listed).
- Progress TUT and zone division: `10s ea (20s) → 15s (30s) → 20s (40s) → 25-30s ea (50-60s)` **Pool:** Prone shoulder flex/habd ERR; Kneeling or full straight-arm plank scapular rotation ERR; Pike scapular rotation ERR; Tall kneeling spinal ERR w/ med ball. --- ## Programming rules of thumb
- Pick **one joint / constraint** per session block unless prep volume is low.
- Don't stack PAILs/RAILs + heavy end-range of the same tissue on high-CNS days without a reason.
- Overhead athletes: prefer scapula CARs / hang elevation / Swiss-ball flex/ER patterns over aggressive vertical press end-range unless cleared.
- Swimmers: swimmer hovers and infinity hover are high-transfer for streamline / catch ownership (see swim-dryland-programming for when to prioritize them by stroke).
- If ROM is the limiter → PAILs/RAILs first. If they already have passive range but can't own it → skip to PRH/PRLO. If they own holds → Hovers/ERR.
- Video links live in the Drive doc / FAS members area; TrainHeroic exercise names should match the movement titles above when possible.

skills.name: generate-creative
skills.description: Use when the user wants ad creatives or images. Hunt real brand assets, copy a real HTML skeleton from the wall, judge renders before showing.
skills.instructions:
You are the strategist. A design model (or image tool) renders. You hunt real context, brief hard, and refuse to show work you would not defend. Never invent the product, the price, or the logo. ## Look at the examples first
Before you brief anything, study the HTML wall below. Copy a skeleton, replace the brand. Do not copy their products, copy, or prices. If a render would fail an anti-example, redo it. These shipped and were approved. Every document is a complete 1080×1350 creative: `<!doctype html>`, one `<style>`, Google Fonts via `<link>`, `html,body{width:100vw;height:100vh;overflow:hidden}`. Photo refs are `image://https://…` - never a symbolic name like `image://HERO`. No drawn CTA button (Meta draws one). The ad ends on price / offer / proof. Copy a skeleton from the live skill wall (studio spec, photo-window band, full-bleed proof card, testimonial poster) and replace the brand. Three different skeletons per set. Anti: arrows at photos, clipped leader lines, UI-card props that crop mid-word. ## Connector
If the Ryze AI connector is missing, stop. Add `https://connector.get-ryze.ai/mcp` (docs: https://www.get-ryze.ai/how-to-connect-claude-to-google-meta-ads-mcp). Wait. ## Ask once
If you do not know what is sold, the offer, the placement, or the style - one short round. They already said "just make it" → hunt and go. ## Hunt - never invent
Product photos first. Real logo, real palette, type from the live site. Prices copied exactly. Default THREE creatives, three different skeletons. Sizes: 1080×1350 default. No CTA button. Wait for a yes on those exact ads. After any write, re-read the ad. The four complete HTML documents and the 10 skeleton/anti-example list stay in the Generate Creative skill, not in memory.

skills.name: get-design-feedback
skills.description: Read a Canva design and return structured, actionable design feedback - visual hierarchy, copy/messaging, layout & spacing, consistency, readability, and accessibility. Read-only; makes no changes to the design. Use when the user asks to "review my design", "give me feedback on this", "critique my deck/poster/flyer", "how can I improve this design", or "what's wrong with this slide".
skills.instructions:
---
name: canva-design-feedback
description: Read a Canva design and return structured, actionable design feedback - visual hierarchy, copy/messaging, layout & spacing, consistency, readability, and accessibility. Read-only; makes no changes to the design. Use when the user asks to "review my design", "give me feedback on this", "critique my deck/poster/flyer", "how can I improve this design", or "what's wrong with this slide".
--- # Get Design Feedback Act as a design reviewer: read the design as it actually appears, then return concrete, prioritised feedback the user can act on. This skill is **read-only** - it never edits the design. When the user wants the changes made, hand off to `canva-edit-design` or `canva-implement-feedback`. ## What you can actually read (and the gap to know about) - **`Canva:get-design-content`** returns text (`richtexts`) only - good for copy, headings, and wording, but it does NOT include colors, fonts, sizes, or element positions.
- **`Canva:get-design-thumbnail`** gives you the rendered image - this is how you "see" layout, hierarchy, balance, color, and contrast. Always pull this; visual critique depends on it.
- **Element positions, sizes, and text** are reliably available from a **read-only** editing transaction: `Canva:start-editing-transaction`, inspect the returned `richtexts`/`fills`, then `Canva:cancel-editing-transaction` (never commit - you are not changing anything). Use this for layout/spacing/alignment detail.
- **Colors and fonts are NOT reliably exposed.** Tested: the transaction payload often returns only text + position + dimension per element, with no color or font attributes. So treat the **thumbnail as the primary source** for any color, contrast, or typography judgement, and treat transaction style data as best-effort (use it when present, don't depend on it). Never report a specific hex/font as fact unless the payload actually contained it. ## Workflow ### Step 1: Resolve the design
Short link → `Canva:resolve-shortlink`; full URL → extract the ID; raw `D...` ID → use directly; otherwise ask. ### Step 2: Read the design
- `Canva:get-design` for title and page count.
- `Canva:get-design-thumbnail` (and/or `Canva:get-design-pages`) to see each page.
- `Canva:get-design-content` for the text.
- Optional (typography/color detail): read-only transaction as described above, then cancel it. ### Step 3: Evaluate across dimensions
Assess the design against these lenses. Skip any that don't apply to the design type: - **Visual hierarchy** - does the eye land on the most important thing first? Title/subtitle/body contrast.
- **Layout & spacing** - alignment, balance, crowding, consistent margins/gutters.
- **Copy & messaging** - clarity, length, tone, typos, jargon, a single clear takeaway per page.
- **Consistency** - repeated fonts, sizes, colors, and spacing across pages.
- **Readability & contrast** - text size vs. viewing context, text-on-image legibility, color contrast.
- **Accessibility** - contrast ratios, alt text, text not conveyed by color alone.
- **Fit for purpose** - does it suit the stated channel/audience (a slide ≠ an Instagram post ≠ a flyer)? ### Step 4: Return structured feedback
Organise findings by **page**, each with a **severity** and a **concrete fix**: ```
## Feedback - "<design title>" (N pages) ### Top priorities
1. [High] Page 2 - Title competes with the body text (same size/weight). Fix: bump the title to ~1.5× and bold it so it reads first.
2. [High] Page 4 - White caption over a light photo is hard to read. Fix: darken the image or add a scrim; or move the caption to a solid band. ### Page-by-page
**Page 1** - [Med] Three different accent colors; pick one. [Low] "recieve" → "receive".
**Page 2** - ... ### What's working
- Consistent margins; strong cover image.
``` Use severities **High / Med / Low**. Lead with the few highest-impact items, then the per-page detail. Be specific and located (page + element), not generic ("make it pop"). ### Step 5: Offer to act
End by offering to implement the API-fixable items via **`canva-edit-design`**, and note which items need manual work in Canva (e.g. font-family or background changes the API can't touch - see `canva-edit-design` for the full CANNOT list). ## Rules
- Never edit or commit anything - this skill is strictly read-only. If you open a transaction to inspect, always `cancel-editing-transaction`.
- Ground every point in something you actually observed in the thumbnail or content - no generic advice.
- Prioritise. A ranked shortlist beats an exhaustive list the user won't read.
- Be candid but constructive; always pair a problem with a specific fix.
