skills.name: gmail-waiting-vs-follow-up
skills.description: Use when filing or triaging Gmail for Ryne (including Penny's daily morning inbox triage) or drafting Achieve email: star only critical deadline items, lead forms marked Important then archived, newsletters archived, one-line triage report; Waiting only if last send asked a question; quiet ~3+ days → Follow-Up; archive wins; no website URL in connector signatures.
skills.instructions:
# Gmail Waiting vs Follow-Up Use these labels correctly. They are not the same folder. ## Meanings - **Waiting** - ball is on them. Ryne’s last send **asked a question** (or he is waiting to hear back before anything further).
- **Follow-Up** - chase pile. Quiet ~3+ days after a question send. Keep Follow-Up until he clears them or says otherwise.
- **Inbox** - reply pile (needs him this week). Do not recreate Action.
- **Later** - real but not this week, with a named future date.
- **Reference** - keep forever, no next step. ## Morning inbox triage (Ryne's rules, locked 2026-10-19) Penny runs this every morning on all four inboxes: work, contact@, personal, IronBlueprint. **Star (rare).** Star ONLY critical items with real consequences or a deadline in the next 1 to 2 weeks: e.g. Wealthfront "payment will fail", Tesla lease steps, real security alerts (new sign-in, Takeout). Never pin. Never star program generations, receipts, lead forms, or routine mail. Client AutoPay failures: mark Important and list them in the report; star only if Ryne says. **Mark Important (no star).** Every lead form, form submission, and new inquiry ("lead forms are always VERY important"), plus mail from a real person that needs Ryne. Then archive lead forms (Tally searches archived mail). Keep human threads that need a reply in Inbox. **Archive.** Newsletters, promos, marketing, notifications, receipts, plugin alerts, Numa/Zapier/Meta noise, WordPress "update plugins failed", password-reset requests. Ryne likes the tea newsletters (Sugimoto Tea); never list them for unsubscribe. **Never** send, reply, or unsubscribe on your own. Suggest unsubscribes as a list; act only on the names Ryne approves. **Report every run.** Post one line to Ryne: `Triage ran: X archived, Y starred, Z need you.` Name the Z people. If the run fails, say so in that line. Never stay silent, so Ryne never has to ask whether it ran. ## After send (locked 2026-09-19) 1. **Asked a question** → apply **Waiting**, remove **Inbox**.
2. Quiet ~3+ days on that question send → apply **Follow-Up** (chase), restore Inbox if needed for the chase list.
3. **Confirm / answer / FYI / close with no ask** → do **not** apply Waiting. Archive or leave labeled done.
4. Do **not** auto-strip **Follow-Up** from chase threads.
5. Do **not** dual-file Follow-Up on every send.
6. Do **not** sweep Follow-Up off Sent or Waiting just to clear a folder. Supersedes the old blunt rule “after any send apply Waiting.” ## Chase threads / follow-up list [REDACTED paragraph: parent_child_or_family_with_person] ## Signature Never type a signature into a draft body. Gmail adds it when the draft is sent, so a typed one appears twice. End the body with "Thanks," only. (Connector/API sends that bypass Gmail's signature: plain text only, no URLs, since Gmail wraps any URL into `google.com/url?…`.) ## Ownership PA / CoS / CRM all follow this. CRM owns Lead Form sheet filing; Penny marks Lead Form emails Important, then archives them. Never auto-strip Follow-Up.

skills.name: google-docs
skills.description: Author and edit Google Docs with the google-docs tools - structured writing, character and paragraph styling, lists, tables, images, headers/footers. Use when creating a formatted document, editing document content, or applying styles.
skills.instructions:
---
name: google-docs
description: Author and edit Google Docs with the google-docs tools - structured writing, character and paragraph styling, lists, tables, images, headers/footers. Use when creating a formatted document, editing document content, or applying styles.
--- # Google Docs authoring ## Locate text, never compute indexes (the #1 source of bugs) Docs edits address zero-based UTF-16 index ranges within one tab, and every
write SHIFTS later indexes. Guessed or stale indexes silently hit the wrong
paragraphs - the classic symptom is two lists merging into one continued
numbering. The tools remove the need for index math: - `find_text` returns FRESH `{start, end}` ranges for exact text - the direct source of indexes for `apply_text_style`, `apply_paragraph_style`, `delete_content`, and `set_paragraph_format`. Locate, then edit, in back-to-back calls.
- `create_list` takes `firstItemText`/`lastItemText` anchors and resolves the range itself: name the first and last item paragraphs and no index ever touches your hands. Use one `create_list` per list with the right preset (BULLET_* for bullets, NUMBERED_* for numbers); never stretch one call across two visually separate lists. When a range must come from structure instead of a phrase (styling a whole
paragraph, addressing a table), read it from `read_document` elements: a
paragraph's `{start, end}` is the range for paragraph-level tools. END IS
EXCLUSIVE: one short misses the last character, one long styles the
character after the phrase (the classic italic-or-link off-by-one). When raw indexes are unavoidable: `read_document` first, compute ONE edit,
pass `requiredRevisionId`, apply, and re-read before the next positional
edit. Order multi-part positional work BACK-TO-FRONT (highest index first)
when re-reading between steps is too expensive; earlier ranges stay valid. ## Creating a document `create_document` makes a BLANK doc (its API ignores content), so plan: - Content known up front: prefer google-drive `google_drive_create_file` with Markdown (`target_mime_type: ...document`), which imports headings, lists, and tables in one call and can target a folder.
- Building incrementally: `create_document`, then `insert_text` with `index` omitted to APPEND each paragraph; append mode reads the tail itself and is revision-guarded automatically. `paragraphStyle` styles the new paragraphs and `bold`/`italic` style the inserted text in the same call, so a well-structured document is a sequence of appends with no styling pass.
- Doc creates cannot set a parent folder. When placement matters, create and then google-drive `google_drive_move_or_rename` with `destination_folder_id`. ## Structure is not optional A document without hierarchy reads as a text dump. Default shape for any
report/memo/notes request: a TITLE paragraph, an italic byline or date line,
HEADING_2 per section, short body paragraphs with bold on the phrases that
matter, and bulleted lists for enumerations. Use `insert_text`'s
paragraphStyle/bold/italic arguments as you write rather than styling
afterwards. ## Styling - Character styling (`apply_text_style`): bold/italic/underline/strike, fontSize, fontFamily, textColor/backgroundColor as `#RRGGBB`, linkUrl. Exclusive END index: to style one paragraph without its trailing newline, use `end - 1` from the read.
- Paragraph styling: `apply_paragraph_style` for named styles (TITLE/HEADING_1..6), `set_paragraph_format` for alignment, indents, and line spacing (percent, 100 = single).
- Lists: `create_list` over the paragraphs' range; each newline-separated paragraph becomes one item. Insert the plain lines first, then bullet them.
- The preset is part of correctness: enumerations get a BULLET_* preset by default; NUMBERED_* only when the content is ordered (steps, rankings) or the request says numbered.
- Before bulleting, check the read for paragraphs that ALREADY show a leading bullet - text appended directly after a list inherits its membership, and `create_list` over such paragraphs restyles the ORIGINAL list, continuing its numbering (a second list showing 4, 5, 6). Strip first: `create_list` with `remove: true` over exactly the new paragraphs, then apply the wanted preset. ## Tables and images - `insert_table` inserts an EMPTY grid. To fill it: re-read (cells appear with their own index ranges) and `insert_text` into cells from the LAST cell to the first, so earlier cell indexes stay valid.
- Style a table AFTER filling it, addressing it by the table element's `start` from `read_document`: `set_table_cell_shading` the header row (pick the row's text color against that fill), `merge_table_cells` for a title cell spanning columns (top-left content survives, the rest is dropped), `set_table_column_width` for fixed widths in points. Structural edits (merge) shift indexes: re-read before further text edits.
- `insert_image` needs a PUBLICLY fetchable URL (Google fetches it; auth walls and private hosts fail), PNG/JPEG/GIF. Size with width/height in points (aspect kept when only one is set).
- `insert_page_break` starts a new page at an index. ## Headers and footers `set_header_footer` sets the default header or footer in one call: it
creates the segment when the doc has none, replaces the text otherwise,
and empty text clears it. The text is static (no page-number fields exist
in the API); it applies to the first tab. Never `insert_text` a fake header
into the body - it scrolls away with the content. ## Bulk text ops `replace_text` replaces literal strings everywhere (or in named tabs) with
no index math; prefer it for renames and corrections. `delete_content`
rejects ranges that split table structure or surrogate pairs; deleting a
paragraph's final newline merges it with the next. ## Verify your work Re-read with `read_document` for structure and styles, or google-drive
`google_drive_read_file` for the whole doc as Markdown, or
`google_drive_export_file` (pdf) when the visual result matters. After any
styling call, confirm the styled span covers exactly the intended text
before moving on.

skills.name: google-drive
skills.description: Work with Google Drive through its MCP tools - search, read, create, organize, share, comment, and export files. Use when creating files in specific folders, moving or renaming, converting Markdown/CSV into Docs/Sheets, managing comments, or exporting a rendered PDF.
skills.instructions:
---
name: google-drive
description: Work with Google Drive through its MCP tools - search, read, create, organize, share, comment, and export files. Use when creating files in specific folders, moving or renaming, converting Markdown/CSV into Docs/Sheets, managing comments, or exporting a rendered PDF.
--- # Google Drive files ## Ids come from search, never guesses Every tool takes Drive file ids. Get them from `search` (or
`list_folder` for a known folder,
`list_recent_files` for "what was I just working on"), or from
the id in a URL the user pasted. `exact_name` beats `query` for a known
filename; add `mime_type_filter` to cut noise. Never invent an id or reuse
one from a stale conversation - re-search first. ## Folder targeting - `create_folder` takes `parent_folder_id`; without it the folder lands in My Drive root. When the user names a destination folder, resolve its id and pass it - a file created in root when a folder was specified is a wrong result even if the content is perfect.
- `create_file` also takes `parent_folder_id`, so create files directly where they belong instead of creating then moving.
- The Docs/Sheets/Slides providers' own create tools CANNOT target a folder (their APIs have no parent parameter). When placement matters, either create the artifact there with `create_file` (Markdown to Doc, CSV to Sheet), or create it and then `move_or_rename` with `destination_folder_id`.
- `move_or_rename` does either or both in one call; renaming does not change the id.
- `update_file` is the same rename/move with the hosted Drive tool's argument names (`fileId`; `title` renames, `parentId` moves by replacing the current parent); it exists on both the translator and hosted surfaces, so prefer it in guidance that must work on either.
- Grant limits: this app's grant is `drive.file`, so moving into or writing files/folders this app never created (and the user never picked) can 403. That 403 is a permission fact, not a transient error; do not retry it. ## Markdown and CSV conversion `create_file` with `target_mime_type:
application/vnd.google-apps.document` converts Markdown (headings, lists,
tables) into a real Google Doc in one call; `...spreadsheet` converts CSV
into a Sheet. This is the fastest correct way to produce a formatted Doc:
prefer it over create-then-insert when the content is known up front.
`update_file_content` converts in place the same way. ## Copying, metadata, and sharing - `copy_file` duplicates a file (optionally into a folder) - the right way to instantiate a template without touching the original.
- `get_file_metadata` returns the full record (mime type, parents, size, owners, modified time); use it to confirm a move landed.
- `get_file_permissions` lists who has access; `share_file` grants a role to an email. Share only when the user asked; report the link rather than widening access speculatively.
- `download_file` returns the raw bytes base64-encoded for non-Google files (images, PDFs, plain text). ## Reading and exporting - `read_file` returns text: Docs as Markdown, Sheets as CSV per tab, Slides as plain text. Use it to verify content after writes.
- `export_file` returns rendered bytes base64-encoded: `pdf` for Docs/Sheets/Slides (Sheets PDF renders every tab, charts included), `png`/`svg` for Drawings, plus office formats (docx/xlsx/pptx). Use PDF when the user wants to see the final look; exports cap at 10 MB.
- For one slide as PNG use the google-slides `get_slide_thumbnail` tool, not Drive export. ## Comments Comments live on the Drive file, so one tool set covers Docs, Sheets, and
Slides alike: - `list_comments` returns each comment's text, quoted document text, resolved state, and replies; it pages, so follow `nextPageToken` before concluding a thread does not exist.
- `add_comment` adds a file-level comment (no text anchor).
- `reply_to_comment` replies by comment id, and its `action: "resolve"` (content optional) is the ONLY way to resolve a thread; editing document text near a comment never resolves it. Leave already-resolved threads alone. ## Deleting `trash_file` is recoverable (~30 days) and works on files and
folders (a trashed folder takes its contents). Permanent deletion is
deliberately not available; never promise it. ## Verify your work After creates and moves, confirm placement with `list_folder`
on the destination or `get_file_metadata` (check `parents`).
After content writes, `read_file` is the ground truth for text
and `export_file` (pdf) for the rendered result.

skills.name: google-sheets
skills.description: Build and edit Google Sheets with the google-sheets tools - values, formatting, charts, conditional formatting, structure, validation, named and protected ranges. Use when creating a spreadsheet or dashboard, formatting cells, adding or fixing charts, or reorganizing tabs and rows.
skills.instructions:
---
name: google-sheets
description: Build and edit Google Sheets with the google-sheets tools - values, formatting, charts, conditional formatting, structure, validation, named and protected ranges. Use when creating a spreadsheet or dashboard, formatting cells, adding or fixing charts, or reorganizing tabs and rows.
--- # Google Sheets authoring ## Two coordinate systems, on purpose - VALUE tools (`read_range`, `write_range`, `append_rows`, `clear_range`) address a TAB TITLE plus A1 cells: `{sheet: "Data", cells: "A1:B4"}`.
- STRUCTURE/FORMAT tools (`format_cells`, `set_borders`, `merge_cells`, `add_chart`, `add_conditional_formatting`, `insert_rows_or_columns`, `delete_rows_or_columns`, `freeze_rows_or_columns`, `sort_range`, `set_data_validation`, `set_basic_filter`, `add_banding`, `set_column_width`, `rename_sheet_tab`, `delete_sheet_tab`) address the numeric `sheetId`. `get_spreadsheet` returns both (each tab's title AND sheetId) with no cell
data - call it first and keep the mapping. A new tab's sheetId is in
`add_sheet_tab`'s reply (`replies[0].addSheet.properties.sheetId`). ## Sequencing a styled sheet: values first, then format, chart last 1. `create_spreadsheet` (optionally with named tabs; it cannot target a folder - move it after with google-drive `google_drive_move_or_rename`).
2. `write_range` the data with `parseInput: true` when values include numbers, dates, or formulas (default false stores everything as literal text - a top source of "chart is empty" bugs).
3. Format like a real dashboard, not a bare grid: - `format_cells` bold header with a fill color and white text; number patterns on value columns (`$#,##0`, `0.0%`). - `freeze_rows_or_columns` the header row. - `set_basic_filter` over the table range - filter dropdowns are what make it read as a data table. - `set_borders` (outer heavier than inner) or `add_banding` for alternating row colors; `set_column_width` so nothing clips. - `add_conditional_formatting` for thresholds worth seeing at a glance.
4. `add_chart` LAST, after the data exists. ## Charts - In `add_chart`, the FIRST range is the domain (x axis / pie labels) and later ranges are the series, one column each; anchoring a chart to the wrong or reversed ranges is the most common chart bug. All ranges live on the same tab as the chart. `headerCount: 1` uses the first cells as series labels - include the header row in each range when you set it.
- Place the chart over empty cells beside or below the table, not on top of the data it plots.
- A wrong chart is fixed in place, not worked around: `get_spreadsheet` lists every tab's charts (chartId, title), `update_chart` replaces a chart's spec keeping its position, `delete_chart` removes one. Never add a second chart to paper over a bad first one. ## Named and protected ranges - `add_named_range` makes formulas self-documenting (`=SUM(Budget)` instead of `=SUM(B2:B13)`); write the formula with `parseInput: true`. Names cannot look like cell references.
- `protect_range` guards headers and formula cells (`warningOnly: true` by default warns editors; `false` locks them). Protect AFTER the last write to that range, or your own writes fight the protection.
- `get_spreadsheet` lists both, with the ids `delete_named_range` and `unprotect_range` need. ## Pitfalls - No revision guard anywhere: last write wins. Read before writing when a collaborator may be editing.
- `merge_cells` keeps only the top-left value; write the text after merging.
- `sort_range` rewrites cell positions; sort before adding formulas that reference the range, and exclude the header row from the sorted range.
- `insert_rows_or_columns` / `delete_rows_or_columns` positions are 1-based (A=1); deletes are immediate and not undoable through the API.
- `find_replace_sheet` is literal (never regex here) and can search inside formulas with `searchFormulas: true`.
- Whole-tab reads can blow the byte cap; bound `cells` (e.g. "1:2000") on tabs you have not sized and follow `nextCells` when truncated. ## Verify your work `read_range` for values (FORMATTED_VALUE shows what the user sees;
UNFORMATTED_VALUE the raw numbers - use it to confirm numbers are numbers,
not text). `get_spreadsheet` for structure: tabs, charts, named ranges,
protections. google-drive `google_drive_export_file` (pdf renders every tab
including charts and formatting) when the visual result matters.

skills.name: google-slides
skills.description: Build and edit Google Slides through the google-slides MCP tools - slides, grids of cards and columns, text boxes, shapes, images, tables, styling, layout inspection, and per-slide PNG rendering. Use when creating a deck, laying out slide elements, matching a template, or verifying how a slide looks.
skills.instructions:
--- name: google-slides description: Build and edit Google Slides through the google-slides MCP tools - slides, grids of cards and columns, text boxes, shapes, images, tables, styling, layout inspection, and per-slide PNG rendering. Use when creating a deck, laying out slide elements, matching a template, or verifying how a slide looks. --- # Google Slides authoring Coordinates are POINTS from the slide's top-left; a standard slide is 720x405 (read_slide_layout reports the real size). Everything is addressed by objectId from `read_presentation`. Pass `requiredRevisionId` from the latest read or write so a concurrent edit fails the write instead of corrupting it. ## Building a new deck: compose, then look Write each slide as a layout, not as coordinates. `compose_slide` takes a tree (stacks, grids, cards, text, images) or an HTML/CSS subset and lays the whole slide out in one call: equal peer sizes, even gutters, vertical centering, and contrast pairs hold by construction, text can `fit: "shrink"`, and the reply carries every element's box plus lints on the plan. Per slide: 1. `add_slide` layout BLANK (or the deck's first slide with `clear: true`), then `compose_slide` with the SAME `theme` every time (palette roles background/surface/primary/textSecondary and the font family). Colors in the tree are roles, not hexes, so one theme change restyles a deck. 2. Read the reply's `issues`. `text_overflow` means shorten, `fit: "shrink"`, or give the node more `size`; an `overlap` means two nodes share a box (usually a row that needs `gap`). 3. `get_slide_thumbnail` (LARGE) once per slide and LOOK at it: crowding, dead corners, a title that reads as body text, an image fighting the palette. Fix by re-composing the slide (delete the old elements first, or compose onto a fresh BLANK slide and `delete_object` the old one). Tree recipes (column root; the root box is the slide minus a 48 pt margin): - Title slide: `stack column justify:center` with a `display` text and an `h2` subtitle in `textSecondary`, both `align:center`. - KPI cards: `h1`, then a `stack row size:150 gap:24` of `card`s, each with a `caption` label (`textSecondary`) over a `kpi` value. - Text + image: `stack row gap:32` of a `body` text (`bullets:true`, `size:{flex:1}`) and an `image` (`size:{flex:1}`); the image aspect-fits. - Agenda: one `body` text with newline-separated items and `bullets:true`. HTML form, same result: `
` with `

`, `
` of `
……
`, `
  • ` bullets, ``. Only the documented tags and properties compile; anything else is refused by name, never dropped. ## Editing an existing deck: place, inspect, fix, look For decks that already have content, or elements the tree does not model: 1. `insert_grid` for any row, column, or grid of cards/text/images (one call, aligned, equal sizes); `insert_text_box` / `insert_shape` / `insert_image` for singletons. 2. `read_slide_layout`: every element's box, z-order, text style, estimated wrapped height (`textFit.fits`), and `issues`. Fix every `error` and `warn` (`text_overflow`, `overlap`, `off_slide`, `low_contrast` with the fill actually behind the text named) and the `info` items when cheap (`near_miss_alignment`, `unequal_peers`, `tight_margin`, `empty_placeholder`). 3. `get_slide_thumbnail` once the lints are clean, and look. ## Grid conventions (when placing by hand) Title at x 40, y 32, 640 wide, height 60-70 for one line of 28-34 pt (two lines need ~110); subtitle under it at 16-18 pt. Content region x 40, y 130, 640 x 235 (insert_grid's default). Footer at y 370, 12 pt. Keep 40 pt side margins unless an element is deliberately full-bleed. Process flows: `insert_grid` the step shapes (columns = steps), then `connect_shapes` between neighbors; connectors follow shapes when moved. A 34 pt bold title wraps past ~32 characters in a 600 pt box and spills over whatever sits below (the API does not grow boxes). `textFit` in the layout read and `issues` in the compose reply predict this; long titles go to 24-28 pt, `fit: "shrink"`, or two lines with the subtitle pushed down. ## Palette and contrast Pick a palette FIRST and reuse it on every slide (as `compose_slide`'s `theme.palette`): background, one card/surface color, one accent, and a secondary text color; on-colors derive automatically. When the user names a template or brand, take its colors; otherwise these pairs pass WCAG AA as-is: - Dark: background #0B2A4A, cards #1E4976, accent #4FC3F7, titles/text #FFFFFF, secondary #B8CCE0. - Light: background #FFFFFF, cards #F1F3F4, accent #0B57D0 (white text on it), text #202124, secondary #444746. Text color never defaults sensibly on a colored fill: every text-bearing call picks its color against the fill BEHIND the text (the card's, not the slide's). No mid-gray on mid-anything; on white, secondary text is #444746 or darker (#5F6368 is borderline, lighter fails). For a template or brand palette, run `check_contrast` on every text/fill pair you intend to use before writing (it returns a passing tint or shade for each failing pair); `low_contrast` in the layout read is the check afterwards. Tables on colored slides render dark-on-dark from theme fills: `set_table_cell_fill` every cell (light fill + dark text, or accent + white) and restyle with `set_text_style` (cellRow/cellColumn). Prefer stat cards over a grid of numbers on title and summary slides; a table only for genuinely tabular data, with the header row filled in the accent and kept to a handful of rows. ## Slides and repetition - `create_presentation` starts with one blank slide (delete its placeholders, or fill them with `set_shape_text`); it cannot target a folder, so move it after with google-drive `google_drive_move_or_rename`. - `add_slide` with a predefined layout fills title/body placeholders in the same call (fastest theme-consistent slide); `move_slide` reorders. - Repeated layouts (one template, N variants): build the first slide fully, then per variant `duplicate_object` on the slide id (the copy lands right after) and `replace_text` scoped by `pageObjectIds` to the copy; distinct placeholders like {{TITLE}} keep the replaces unambiguous. - `set_shape_text` REPLACES a shape's or cell's whole text (cell = {rowIndex, columnIndex}); `set_text_style` restyles all of one shape or cell, not a range. `update_element_position` moves but does not resize: delete and re-create at the right size instead. - Speaker notes: `set_shape_text` with pageObjectId = the slide's notesPageId and objectId = speakerNotesObjectId from `read_presentation`. - Whole-deck render: google-drive `google_drive_export_file` (pdf).

skills.name: grocery-shopping
skills.description: When the user asks you to buy groceries or household staples, do, repeat, or schedule a weekly grocery order, save or change their usual grocery list, fill a grocery cart they will check out themselves, turn a recipe or meal plan into a shopping list, or order from Instacart, Costco Same-Day, or another grocery delivery site, before you open the store, add anything to a cart, save a usual list to memory, or create a routine that reorders one.
skills.instructions:
---
name: grocery-shopping
description: >- When the user asks you to buy groceries or household staples, do, repeat, or schedule a weekly grocery order, save or change their usual grocery list, fill a grocery cart they will check out themselves, turn a recipe or meal plan into a shopping list, or order from Instacart, Costco Same-Day, or another grocery delivery site, before you open the store, add anything to a cart, save a usual list to memory, or create a routine that reorders one.
---
# Grocery shopping You build grocery carts for the user on Instacart, Costco Same-Day, and other grocery delivery sites. A grocery order is many small choices, so it goes smoothly when you remember the user's usual products and rules and ask only about what is truly unclear. The user approves the cart and the total, and you place the order only after that yes. ## Entry points - "Do my weekly Safeway order" or "restock the usual" is a repeat cart. Start from the user's usual list in memory and the store's buy-again page. With no usual list saved for that store, build one from the buy-again page and confirm it with the user before you fill the cart.
- "Get everything for tacos for six" is a recipe. Turn it into a list, scale it to the servings, and leave out what the user said they have.
- A pasted list, or a photo of a handwritten list, is the list itself.
- "We're out of milk and paper towels" is a small top-up to the store they usually use.
- "Do a Costco run" goes to Costco Same-Day, the grocery storefront, not the costco.com retail site.
- "Fill my cart, I'll check out" is cart only (see Cart only). ## Before you start - Pick the store: the one the user named, then their usual grocer from the Memory section, then ask. On Instacart, also pick the retailer, because prices and stock differ by store.
- Read the Memory section for the usual list at that store, brands and sizes they buy, dietary rules and allergies, brands to avoid, organic or other preferences, substitution rules, household size, and whether they always check out themselves (see Cart only). The usual list is saved in parts and the Memory section can leave some out, so for a repeat cart always call `RecallMemory` with the store's name before you build the list, and build it from every part that comes back.
- Run SearchPlugins for the grocer. Use a connector when one is installed. Install a missing connector with InstallPlugin without asking; its connect card is the ask. Ask in one widget first only when the user named no service and several plugins fit (Gmail or Outlook, Google or Outlook Calendar), or the plugin has no connector. Say in the user's words why it helps, without saying plugin, MCP, or plugin id, and never paste a connect link.
- Confirm the delivery address with the user before checkout, even when the site has one saved. ## Flow Every message in this flow, from the questions about close matches to the cart summary, substitutions, delivery windows, and confirmation, follows one rule. Show what you collected in the user's language, which is the language they write to you in unless they asked for another or the Memory section names one they prefer. When a page is in another language, translate the words you put in a card or a summary, such as titles, descriptions, specs and their labels, notes, review summaries, policies, delivery and status lines, and option names. Keep brand, store, seller, and venue names, model numbers, order numbers and other codes, prices with their currency, and links as the page shows them. Brief the browser subagent and type into the site in the site's own words, and match a choice the user makes in their language back to those words. 1. Build the list before you open the store: each item with its quantity, and the brand and size from memory when one is saved. For a recipe, name the pantry staples you left off (salt, oil, spices) so the user can add them back.
2. Dispatch the browser subagent once with the whole list, using the site playbook's cart job. That job stops at the cart, and its "never check out" line holds for this dispatch only. Ask it to report, for each list item, the product it chose (name, brand, size), its product page URL and image URL, the unit price, any deal, whether it came from past purchases, and which items it could not find or found out of stock. Only the list goes in the cart; have it dismiss suggested items, membership or delivery subscription trials, and round-up prompts.
3. When the site wants a sign-in, a one-time code, or a verify-you-are-human check, follow the Cursor-managed `sign-in` skill in its order, which ends with the Secure Form (`RequestUserForm`) and then handing over the screen with `request_box_help` and one instruction ("Sign in to your <service> account"). Never send a question widget before these; the tool is the ask. After a receipt or a hand-back, dispatch the subagent again; the session persists across turns.
4. Sort the results. A line is a usual product when it matches memory or past purchases, a close match when the brand or size differs, out of stock, or not found. For a repeat cart, When you rebuild a usual order, compare each line with the saved list: an item out of stock or not found, a price at least 10% above or below the saved one in the same currency, or another size or pack. Open your first message about the rebuilt cart with one line that counts them and names each changed item ("2 items out of stock: oat milk and eggs. Coffee up 12%"), or that says nothing changed since the last order. A product tile shows no note, so that line is where the user sees what changed, and it is the first line of the message's `content` even when a card carries the products. When `SendToUser` has a `shopping` field, show each changed line as a product with no `badge`, a `note` that names its change ("Out of stock", "Up 12% since your last order", "New size"), and one `caution` reason with the saved and the new value, and give an out-of-stock line's offer `availability` `out_of_stock`. The user's yes to the rebuilt cart covers its prices only: when a line's price at checkout differs from the cart they approved, stop before you place the order and ask again, and name each such line with both prices in that message ("Greek yogurt: $7.49 in the cart, $7.99 at checkout"), since a new total alone does not say which line moved.
5. Ask once about everything uncertain, except on a routine's wake, where your picks go out with the step 9 widget as Remembering the usual order says. Send one message that lists every close match and missing item with your proposed pick, so the user can approve them all or correct a few, instead of one question per item. An item the store sells in several sizes or pack counts is one line with the size you picked and the other sizes with their prices, not one line per size.
6. Send the cart summary: one line per item with product, size, quantity, and price, then the subtotal, delivery and service fees, the preselected tip, and the estimated total as far as the site shows them, with the cart screenshot attached at its saved path. When the subtotal is under a free delivery threshold or an order minimum, say how far under, and add nothing to close the gap unless the user picks it. Unless Cart only applies, this summary leads on to step 9's widget, never to an offer to hand over the screen so they check out themselves.
7. Set substitutions. When the site asks what to do if an item is out of stock, apply the user's saved rule for that item. With no rule, choose no replacement for anything tied to an allergy or dietary rule and the site's closest match for the rest, and tell the user which you chose.
8. Delivery window and tip. Show the windows the site offers and let the user pick. Leave the site's default tip unless the user or memory gives a rule, and name it in the summary.
9. Confirm before you place it. The grocery playbooks have no checkout job, so write that step yourself: resume the helper that built the cart, so it keeps the same session and cart, and have it open checkout and read back every line (items, subtotal, delivery and service fees, tax, the preselected tip, the estimated total, the address, and the window), entering no payment and placing nothing. Then send one question widget whose prompt names the item count, the delivery address, the window, and the estimated total from the checkout page with fees, tax, and tip included ("Place the $86.40 Safeway order, 23 items, to 512 Valencia St, Saturday 10 to 11 AM?") with options to place it, change the window or address, or edit the cart. A dismissed widget is a no, and a change after the widget went out needs a fresh widget. The widget ends your turn.
10. When the site wants payment, a deposit, or a card to hold the booking, work it in this order and stop at the first step that pays. First, a payment method already saved on the site's own account, not a card in the user's vault. Have the subagent select it, and when that account has several, ask which one in the confirmation widget. Next, when the account has none and the `purchases` skill lists a card saved in the user's vault, use that card as its Credit cards section says. When that skill has you send an `order` card, read every line, the total, and the ship-to address from the checkout's review page before you send it, and charge only after the user taps Pay. When neither has one and the site charges an exact total now (tax, fees, tip, and shipping included), Stripe Link is the preferred way to pay: with `RequestVirtualCard` among your tools this turn, raise a one-time card with the site as merchant and type it only into the merchant's checkout; a denial is final. Without that tool, offer Stripe Link once as the `purchases` skill says, when that skill is listed. A card kept on file for a hold or a no-show fee is not charged now, so it never gets a one-time card. Next, and right away whenever the user turns Link down, ignores the offer, or asks to use their own card, send the Secure Form (`RequestUserForm`, reason "checkout", the site's domain) for the card inputs the live checkout shows, such as card number, expiry, CVC, name, and billing ZIP; never tell them you can't take their card, and never predict that the form can't reach card inputs embedded from a payment provider. Last, when the host refuses the form or its receipt says a card field failed, or the user would rather type on the page, hand the box to the user with `request_box_help` and one instruction ("Add your card and confirm the payment on <service>"); the same handoff covers a CVC re-entry and any 2FA, 3DS, or bank prompt. The user finishes the payment inside that handoff, so when the box comes back, skip any later confirm or place-order click and read the confirmation page. When the user already typed their card into chat, use it as given for that checkout instead of sending the form. Card numbers, CVCs, and expiries stay in the merchant's checkout, never in chat or logs. A grocery order is not an exact total now: the final charge can settle above the checkout total once items are weighed or substituted, so a one-time card does not fit it. Do not raise one or offer Stripe Link here; when neither the account nor the user's vault has a card saved, go to the Secure Form.
11. Check the final checkout page against the widget before you place it. A change is material when the total is higher than the widget's by more than the larger of 1% and 5 units of its currency, the currency differs, or an item, its size or quantity, the store, the delivery address, or the window differs from what the widget named. A lower total, a rise within that margin, the same total under other fee, tax, or tip labels, lines in another order or other words, and a substitution the user already approved are not material. A material change spends that yes: place nothing, show both numbers, and send a fresh widget with the new total, and only its yes lets you place the order. Anything else goes ahead on the yes you have.
12. Place the order only after the widget's yes, only the cart that widget read back, and only with no material change since (step 11). When the user already confirmed payment in a `request_box_help` handoff, that confirmation placed the order: dispatch no place click, and only have the helper read the confirmation page. Otherwise, for the place dispatch, resume the helper that read checkout back. Give it the store, lines, address, and window the widget named, any substitution the user approved, and the highest total it may place: the widget's total plus the larger of 1% and 5 units of its currency. Have it stop and report without placing if the cart is empty, the store differs, an item, size, or quantity differs other than an approved substitution, the address, window, or currency differs, or the total is above that ceiling. Only then does it select the payment method from the payment step, click the place-order control, dismiss the post-order prompts (rate, tip more, add items, a membership offer), and read the confirmation page. Once the site confirms the order, send a shipment card at stage `placed` from the confirmation page (see Shipment card), with the item count, the delivery window, and the total charged in `content`. When no card goes out, report the order number, the delivery window, and the total charged, and attach the confirmation screenshot. Either way, when the total charged differs from the widget's, say so and give both totals. ## Shipment card When `SendToUser` has a `shipment` field, report an order's status as a shipment card in it, one card per order. Take its facts from the store's order or confirmation page, the carrier's tracking page, or the shipping email. The card takes the store's name in plain words and its site URL, its logo image URL when the page shows one, the order number, and each item's title, quantity, and image URL; the accessibility snapshot carries no image URLs, so the subagent reads them from the page's images with a page script. The card needs the store, the order number, and at least one item. Without that field or any of those, report in text instead. Set `stage` from the page's status: `placed` until it ships or a courier picks it up, even when it is due today, `in_transit` once it ships, `arriving_today` when it is on its way and out for delivery or due today, `delivered`, `delayed` when the page says it is late or shows a delivery exception, or `cancelled`. Put the page's own status headline in `status`, translated into the user's language when the page is in another, since a translation still keeps the store's words, and the expected or actual delivery date in `expectedDeliveryDate` as YYYY-MM-DD. For a range, use its last day. Fill `tracking` only with a tracking link a page showed or the URL of the carrier page the subagent opened, and the carrier's name; never build one from a tracking number. Leave out any value no page showed. In `content`, write one sentence on what changed, without the tracking link. The card's message takes no images, links, other cards, or voice memo, so send a screenshot or photo in its own `SendToUser` after the card. ## Cart only Follow this when the user wants a filled cart and will check out themselves, or when memory says they always do. - A guest cart in your browser does not show on the user's phone or computer. Before step 2, ask once whether they have an account at this store. With one, sign in the way step 3 says (credentials through the Secure Form, or a hand-off so they sign in on the box). When that sign-in hand-off comes back, dispatch step 2 in the signed-in session. With no account, or when they would rather not sign in, dispatch step 2 as a guest.
- Follow the Flow through step 6, then stop. Never set a delivery window, open checkout, enter payment, or place the order in this mode.
- Send the step 6 cart summary. For a signed-in cart, add the store's cart page link and one line that the cart is waiting in their account. For a guest cart, say it stays in your browser and send each item as its product link with the size and quantity instead of the cart link, as product cards when `SendToUser` has a `shopping` field (see Product cards).
- In the same message, offer to hand over the screen with `request_box_help` and one instruction ("Check out your cart on <store>"), so they check out in your browser themselves. When that checkout hand-off comes back, read the page. Report an order as step 12 says only when the page is the store's order confirmation. Otherwise say the cart is still waiting. ## Product cards - When `SendToUser` has a `shopping` field, show the products you name in it instead of a text list: the matches the helper reported when it could not add to the cart, the close matches and proposed picks in step 5, the changed lines of a repeat cart, and a guest cart's items. Write each product from the helper's report: its name and size as `title`, its image URL as the one entry in `images`, and one variant with `options` `{}` and one offer whose `seller` is the store, `url` is its product page, and `price` is the unit price as `{ amount, currency }`, such as `{ "amount": 12.99, "currency": "USD" }`. A changed line of a repeat cart also gets the `note`, the `caution` reason, and, when it is out of stock, the offer `availability` that step 4 names.
- Keep quantities, the subtotal, fees, and what you need from the user in `content`, and send any question widget as its own message after the card.
- A product the helper reported with no image URL or no product page stays a text line. ## Remembering the usual order - After the first order at a store, offer once to remember it as their usual list there, along with any substitution rules they stated ("no substitutes for oat milk", "any brand of bananas is fine"). Save with `UpdateMemory` (action "write") only after they agree.
- A usual list is kept per store, in facts of about 5 items each, and every fact starts with the store and its part ("Fresh Basket usual list, part 2: ..."). Each item has its brand, size, usual quantity, and the price and date of its last order. Save these facts with type "shared_journal", so every one of the user's bots reads the same list. Where UpdateMemory does not offer that type, or refuses a write to it, save them with type "journal". When UpdateMemory also takes an audience, as on a Team Bot or in a shared conversation, give audience "user", so only this person sees them, and never "team" or no audience, which teammates would read. When audience "user" is refused, save nothing and tell the user this chat cannot remember the list. When two facts hold the same part, use the newer one. Build a list from the last 3 months of orders, and when you rewrite a part, drop any item last ordered more than 3 months ago. A fact longer than 500 characters is cut at the end with no error, so keep each part under 450 characters. After each write, check that the saved text UpdateMemory returns still ends with that part's last item; when it does not, save the cut items as a new part before you forget any old text. One memory fact holds at most 500 characters, which is why a list takes several, and the store's substitution rules get one fact of their own.
- Keep one usual list per store. When they add, drop, or swap an item, change a quantity, or an order charges a new price for an item, rewrite only the part of that list that holds it instead of saving a second list for the same store: write the new text first, and forget the old text only after that write is saved, so a failed write never loses the part. When a part grows past about 5 items, move the extra items into a new part. Name the change in one short line. An item that was out of stock this time stays on the list.
- For a usual order on a schedule ("reorder my usual every Sunday"), offer a routine, and read the Cursor-managed `routines` skill before you create it. Write into its instructions only the run's part: the store, and that each run recalls the store's usual list, rebuilds the cart in the user's signed-in account there without opening checkout, compares each line with the list (an item out of stock or not found, a price at least 10% above or below the saved one in the same currency, or another size or pack), and calls WakeParent with what changed, the item count, and the subtotal. Write that the run wakes you even when nothing changed and says so, because the order still needs the user's approval. That wake is for you, not the user, so the run adds no replacement and asks the user nothing, because you pick the replacements and send the one approval. Also write that a run cannot sign in, so when the store asks it to sign in or shows the account signed out, it stops and calls WakeParent saying sign-in is needed. A run never opens checkout or places the order. The rest is what you do when a wake reaches you, so leave it out of the instructions, which never tell the run to pick a replacement, message the user, ask for approval, or place the order. The user asked for each order the routine builds when they set it up, so a wake's order counts as one they asked for, and it is spent only after their yes to the approval you send. When a wake says sign-in is needed, ask the user to sign in, then rebuild the cart yourself and go on as below. Lines the run added at a new price or in another size are already in the cart, so put your pick in the cart only for each item the run could not add, except one tied to an allergy or dietary rule, which stays out. Then open checkout and read it back yourself, even when nothing changed, because the run's subtotal leaves out shipping, fees, and tax. Before the approval, send one message with the changes line or that nothing changed, your picks, each item left out for an allergy or dietary rule, and what checkout shows: each line with its quantity and price, then shipping, fees, tax, the total, the address, the delivery date or window, and the payment method. Then send the one approval the order needs, naming that total and never the run's subtotal, so a single yes covers the picks and the order without those items. Adding one of them afterwards changes the cart, so read checkout again and send a fresh approval. When that yes comes after the approval expired, or checkout then shows a price that differs from the one the approval named, read checkout again and ask again. For groceries, that approval is the step 9 widget, and steps 11 and 12 still hold, except that a line price that differs from the one the approval named asks again even when the total stays within the larger of 1% and 5 units of its currency. ## Pitfalls - Items sold by weight (produce, meat, deli) and substitutions can change the final charge after delivery, so call the total an estimate.
- A deal that needs a loyalty card or a minimum quantity only applies when the cart meets it. Say so instead of counting the sale price.
- Turn down a membership or delivery subscription trial (Instacart+ and the like), priority delivery, a round-up prompt, and suggested items unless the user asked for them.
- Spend only on an order the user asked for, and only after the widget's yes. A routine's order counts as asked for only after the user's yes to the widget you send when its run wakes you.
- Never invent a product, a price, a deal, or a delivery window. If the page did not show it, say so. ## Site playbooks Before you dispatch the browser subagent, Read the `site-playbooks-instacart` or `site-playbooks-costco` skill in this catalog, whichever names the site you are about to use, and paste the Dispatch snippet of the job that matches your step (a read-only lookup, or a cart and checkout) into the Task text. It carries the deep link or endpoint that lands on results instead of clicking through the home page, and the stop rules for that site.

skills.name: group-chat-turns
skills.description: When a user message starts with a [Group chat: "…"] tag: you are taking a turn in a group chat room, not your private chat, so read this before replying.
skills.instructions:
---
name: group-chat-turns
description: >- When a user message starts with a [Group chat: "…"] tag: you are taking a turn in a group chat room, not your private chat, so read this before replying.
---
# Group chat turns A user message that begins with a [Group chat: "..."] tag is a turn in that group chat room, not your private chat (an untagged user message is your private 1:1 chat with your user). Your one conversation carries your private chat and your turns in every room you're in, each room turn tagged this way. For the whole of a room turn, SendToUser delivers to that room instead of your user. Text, attachments, widgets, and cards alike are rendered in the room for everyone there, just as they would be in your private chat. To say something privately to your own user during a room turn, send it with to:"dm". It lands in your 1:1 chat and the room never sees it.
- Reply-first does not apply in a room turn: your tool calls and plain assistant text are private scratch space the room never sees, so when the conversation calls for real work, do the work first, then deliver the result with SendToUser. A room turn with no SendToUser means you stayed silent.
- You have your full toolkit in rooms, with the same tools as your private chat and no reduced limits. Never claim you lack a tool in a room that you have in your private chat. The one exception is your computer: you can use it, but in a room you never hand it over or have anyone sign in on it. Answering the room from your unified history, including what you learned in your private chat, is expected; the only exceptions are things your user explicitly asked you to keep out of a room. Never go looking for a teammate's private chats, memory, or files.
- Several distinct participants share a room. Speak only as yourself: never write as another participant or as the user, and never narrate the conversation from the outside.
- Keep each message short and conversational, usually one to three sentences, the way people actually chat. Send at most 3 messages in one room turn. Do not monologue or summarize the whole thread.
- React to what was just said: build on it, agree, disagree, or ask a pointed question. Address others by name when it helps. Do not repeat points already made, and do not restate other people's messages back to them.
- Mentions: write @Name to direct your message at a specific teammate, or @everyone for the whole room. If you are @-mentioned you are being asked to weigh in, so respond; to pull a teammate into the conversation, @-mention them.
- If you have nothing new worth adding right now, simply end your turn without calling SendToUser. In a room, staying silent is a first-class move, never a failure. It lets the conversation settle instead of spinning forever. Say your piece in one turn, then stop.

skills.name: guide-to-tapering
skills.description: Use this when building or checking an Achieve competition taper (volume cut, intensity held, last lift timing).
skills.instructions:
---
name: Guide to tapering
description: Use this when building or checking an Achieve competition taper (volume cut, intensity held, last lift timing).
---
# Guide to tapering Full source: `/home/box/agent-data/shared/sc-reference/guide-to-tapering.txt` ## Rules
- Build strength ≥4 weeks before tapering.
- Start taper ~2-3 weeks before first competition day; ~2-week taper ending ~5 days before first event.
- Cut total volume (sets × reps × load) **gradually** by **40-60%** (heavier athletes closer to 60%). Don’t dump it all at once.
- Keep intensity the same or ≤5-10% lower.
- Power: usually keep 3-4 sets; advanced heavy power can cut volume too.
- More rest (often +1-2 min). No new exercises. No high-eccentric / long-TUT work.
- Keep core and shoulder-health work.
- Track volume: sets × reps × weight (each limb separate for unilateral).
- Final lift (~5 days out): primary 2-3×2-4; secondary 1-2×3-5.
- Stop S&C ~5 days before first event. Pair with [Athlete phase focus breakdown](sand-workflow:athlete-phase-focus-breakdown).

skills.name: hawkin-athlete-plate-brief
skills.description: Use when writing an Achieve athlete force-plate brief or handoff to Coach from Hawkin CMJ/SJ data - Mundy strategy, curve shape, trend as higher/lower/plateau (never soft/hard), swimmer SJ priority; paste-ready for Coach's Force Plates wrap.
skills.instructions:
# Hawkin athlete plate brief Default template for every Achieve athlete plate brief / Strength Coach handoff. Curve shape stays king. Never invent a metric that is not on the test. Document jump-height method continuity (Hawkin `Jump Height(m)` to Hawkin is fine; do not mix ForceDecks FT without labeling). ## Always include (analysis) 1. **Session-best** of recent trials (not a noisy mean), test date(s), n, body mass if used for relative metrics.
2. **Trend first (locked 2026-10-02):** Lead every brief with jump-height **direction**. Use only **higher / lower / plateau** (with dates) - never “soft,” “hard,” “soft day,” or “hard day” for jump output. Compare latest session-best to recent days and own peak (~4-6 week window when available).
3. **Swimmers (locked 2026-10-02):** Treat **SJ as at least as important as CMJ** - usually more so (starts/turns = concentric). Always report both when both exist; call SJ trend separately with higher/lower/plateau + dates; EUR when same-day both. Do not CMJ-only a free/fly/back/breast athlete.
4. **Curve shape** (propulsive) from the force-time skill - Early/Late Peak, Unimodal/Bimodal/Plateau, or Inconsistent.
5. **Core numbers** with units: Jump Height(m) [note Hawkin CMJ height], EUR if SJ exists that day (best CMJ / best SJ), phase times that matter (unweight / brake / propulsive or TTT/contraction time), L/R only when available and decision-relevant.
6. **Mundy strategy block (locked)** - four lines, short: - **Strategy:** deep-slow vs shallow-fast vs mixed - from countermovement depth + propulsive force and time. Same height can need opposite work. - **Height × TTT:** jump height + time to takeoff (or contraction time). Say long-TTT vs short-TTT vs their own baseline. - **Relative propulsive force × propulsive time:** when both exist on the test. Prefer this over impulse alone for “more force vs more speed through the push.” - **Braking and/or P1:P2 only when they change the week:** peak relative braking (or brake quality from curve + brake time) if the stop is the limiter; P1:P2 Propulsive Impulse Index if propulsion is front-loaded vs back-loaded. **Omit** if nothing actionable.
7. **Limiter → this-week interventions** (plate-driven, Achieve exercise language). Hand full programs to Coach (`5d64c948-3315-41b3-b9a6-196b4d1e2072`), who writes them in chat with Ryne. Strength Coach is deleted; never send to it.
8. **Asymmetry** as its own flag when real - never bury it inside the strategy line. ## Private handoff shape (locked 2026-10-02) Strength Coach’s room wrap uses a **Force Plates** section. Private DM to SC must be paste-ready under that header - plain bullets, not a long report dump: ```
Force Plates
- Trend: CMJ higher|lower|plateau (date → date, inches); SJ higher|lower|plateau (date → date, inches)
- Main finding
- Main finding
- … (flex count)
- Programming recommendations based on findings: - … - …
``` For swimmers, put **SJ trend and latest SJ** in the findings (not a footnote under CMJ). **Main findings** = decision-relevant plate facts (date, session-best CMJ/SJ/EUR/RSI as needed, curve tag, strategy/height×TTT or force×time that changes the week, asymmetry only if it flags). Plain English; numbers with units.
**Programming recommendations** = plate-driven only (unload vs load, ISO→jump, get-down vs brake work, contact dose, what *not* to program from the curve). Do not write the full program. Jump-dose language: “quality / fewer contacts / unload” - never “soft day” / “hard day.” Optional detail (curve landmarks, trend table) can sit below the paste block for SC if useful - the paste block comes first. ## Do not put on the default brief - Full FTO metric dump / seven-determinants list
- Universal fatigue % thresholds (population-specific; only when a readiness call is asked)
- Invented IMTP/DSI without both tests
- Fixed exercise mandates from Mundy (he did not give them)
- Framing jump-dose gates as “new lifter” when training age is known - dose from plates + quality limits
- Latest-only reports with no trend line
- Soft/hard jump-day language (use higher / lower / plateau + dates) ## Delivery - Normal athlete ask: Send the Force Plates paste block (+ short limiter note if needed) privately to Coach (`5d64c948-3315-41b3-b9a6-196b4d1e2072`) (priority true). Strength Coach is deleted. The handoff counts as delivered only when Coach confirms. Do not post the plate report into a shared room unless Ryne @-mentions Hawkin.
- Numbers with units and dates. Physics first, then prescription.

skills.name: hawkin-first-athlete-programming-report
skills.description: Use when deciding how to program an athlete from force-plate data - trend first (higher/lower/plateau), SJ primary for swimmers, especially for a default 2-day week.
skills.instructions:
# Hawkin-first athlete programming report 1. Before recommending programming, request the athlete’s bounded Hawkin data from the Hawkin specialist. Do not pull the Hawkin API directly. Ask for: **trend** (higher / lower / plateau vs recent dates - never “soft”); curve-shape notes; session-best jump of the most recent trials (not means); EUR = best CMJ / best SJ that day; and the locked Mundy strategy block (strategy deep-slow vs shallow-fast; height × TTT; relative propulsive force × propulsive time when available; braking and/or P1:P2 only when they change the week). **Swimmers:** treat SJ as primary alongside CMJ (SJ often more important); always report both with trend.
2. Report the tested data first in short bullets. Lead with trend. Use higher / lower / plateau + dates. Never invent metrics or a curve shape that was not reported. Never say soft/hard for jump output.
3. Explain the mechanical reason for the overall direction before listing exercises. Use strategy + curve shape together - same jump height does not mean the same program.
4. Unless the user specifies 1 or 3 days, use the default 2-day shape (lower power, upper power, primary lower, primary upper each day). For 1×60 + 4×25 weeks, post that shape instead.
5. For every exercise, give a short rationale that cites the athlete’s actual plate numbers or curve features. Off-plate gaps stay labeled off-plate.
6. Post drafts in Coach's chat with Ryne only. Do not write or assign TrainHeroic programs unless Ryne explicitly says to.
7. Place high-CNS/high-force work first. Non-competing pairings. Overhead athletes: landmine/horizontal over true vertical press.
8. High/low: 25-min days are two pairs, 3× each, one stressor. Lows stay restore. Don’t clone the 60.

skills.name: hf-cli
skills.description: Hugging Face Hub CLI (`hf`) for downloading, uploading, and managing models, datasets, spaces, buckets, repos, papers, jobs, and more on the Hugging Face Hub. Use when: handling authentication; managing local cache; managing Hugging Face Buckets; running or scheduling jobs on Hugging Face infrastructure; managing Hugging Face repos; discussions and pull requests; browsing models, datasets and spaces; reading, searching, or browsing academic papers; managing collections; querying datasets; configuring spaces; setting up webhooks; or deploying and managing HF Inference Endpoints. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions 'hf', 'huggingface', 'Hugging Face', 'huggingface-cli', or 'hugging face cli', or wants to do anything related to the Hugging Face ecosystem and to AI and ML in general. Also use for cloud storage needs like training checkpoints, data pipelines, or agent traces. Use even if the user doesn't explicitly ask for a CLI command. Replaces the deprecated `huggingface-cli`.
skills.instructions:
---
name: hf-cli
description: "Hugging Face Hub CLI (`hf`) for downloading, uploading, and managing models, datasets, spaces, buckets, repos, papers, jobs, and more on the Hugging Face Hub. Use when: handling authentication; managing local cache; managing Hugging Face Buckets; running or scheduling jobs on Hugging Face infrastructure; managing Hugging Face repos; discussions and pull requests; browsing models, datasets and spaces; reading, searching, or browsing academic papers; managing collections; querying datasets; configuring spaces; setting up webhooks; or deploying and managing HF Inference Endpoints. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions 'hf', 'huggingface', 'Hugging Face', 'huggingface-cli', or 'hugging face cli', or wants to do anything related to the Hugging Face ecosystem and to AI and ML in general. Also use for cloud storage needs like training checkpoints, data pipelines, or agent traces. Use even if the user doesn't explicitly ask for a CLI command. Replaces the deprecated `huggingface-cli`."
--- Install: `curl -LsSf https://hf.co/cli/install.sh | bash -s`. The Hugging Face Hub CLI tool `hf` is available. IMPORTANT: The `hf` command replaces the deprecated `huggingface-cli` command. Use `hf --help` to view available functions. Note that auth commands are now all under `hf auth` e.g. `hf auth whoami`. Generated with `huggingface_hub v1.18.0`. Run `hf skills add --force` to regenerate. ## Commands - `hf cp SRC` - Copy files between local paths, repositories, and buckets. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf download REPO_ID` - Download files from the Hub. `[--type [model|dataset|space] --revision TEXT --include TEXT --exclude TEXT --cache-dir TEXT --local-dir TEXT --force-download --dry-run --max-workers INTEGER --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf env` - Print information about the environment. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf sync` - Sync files between local directory and a bucket. `[--delete --ignore-times --ignore-sizes --plan TEXT --apply TEXT --dry-run --include TEXT --exclude TEXT --filter-from TEXT --existing --ignore-existing --verbose --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf update` - Update the `hf` CLI to the latest version. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf upload REPO_ID` - Upload a file or a folder to the Hub. Recommended for single-commit uploads. `[--type [model|dataset|space] --revision TEXT --private --include TEXT --exclude TEXT --delete TEXT --commit-message TEXT --commit-description TEXT --create-pr --every FLOAT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf upload-large-folder REPO_ID LOCAL_PATH` - Upload a large folder to the Hub. Recommended for resumable uploads. `[--type [model|dataset|space] --revision TEXT --private --include TEXT --exclude TEXT --num-workers INTEGER --no-report --no-bars --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf version` - Print information about the hf version. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]` ### `hf auth` - Manage authentication (login, logout, etc.). - `hf auth list` - List all stored access tokens. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf auth login` - Login using a token from huggingface.co/settings/tokens. `[--add-to-git-credential --force --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf auth logout` - Logout from a specific token. `[--token-name TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf auth switch` - Switch between access tokens. `[--token-name TEXT --add-to-git-credential --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf auth token` - Print the current access token to stdout. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf auth whoami` - Find out which huggingface.co account you are logged in as. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]` ### `hf buckets` - Commands to interact with buckets. - `hf buckets cp SRC` - Copy files between local paths, repositories, and buckets. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf buckets create BUCKET_ID` - Create a new bucket. `[--private --region [us|eu] --exist-ok --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf buckets delete BUCKET_ID` - Delete a bucket. `[--yes --missing-ok --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf buckets info BUCKET_ID` - Get info about a bucket. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf buckets list` - List buckets or files in a bucket. `[--human-readable --tree --recursive --search TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf buckets move FROM_ID TO_ID` - Move (rename) a bucket to a new name or namespace. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf buckets remove ARGUMENT` - Remove files from a bucket. `[--recursive --yes --dry-run --include TEXT --exclude TEXT --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf buckets sync` - Sync files between local directory and a bucket. `[--delete --ignore-times --ignore-sizes --plan TEXT --apply TEXT --dry-run --include TEXT --exclude TEXT --filter-from TEXT --existing --ignore-existing --verbose --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]` ### `hf cache` - Manage local cache directory. - `hf cache list` - List cached repositories or revisions. `[--cache-dir TEXT --revisions --filter TEXT --sort [accessed|accessed:asc|accessed:desc|modified|modified:asc|modified:desc|name|name:asc|name:desc|size|size:asc|size:desc] --limit INTEGER --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf cache prune` - Remove detached revisions from the cache. `[--cache-dir TEXT --yes --dry-run --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf cache rm TARGETS` - Remove cached repositories or revisions. `[--cache-dir TEXT --yes --dry-run --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf cache verify REPO_ID` - Verify checksums for a single repo revision from cache or a local directory. `[--type [model|dataset|space] --revision TEXT --cache-dir TEXT --local-dir TEXT --fail-on-missing-files --fail-on-extra-files --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]` ### `hf collections` - Interact with collections on the Hub. - `hf collections add-item COLLECTION_SLUG ITEM_ID ITEM_TYPE` - Add an item to a collection. `[--note TEXT --exists-ok --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf collections create TITLE` - Create a new collection on the Hub. `[--namespace TEXT --description TEXT --private --exists-ok --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf collections delete COLLECTION_SLUG` - Delete a collection from the Hub. `[--missing-ok --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf collections delete-item COLLECTION_SLUG ITEM_OBJECT_ID` - Delete an item from a collection. `[--missing-ok --format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`
- `hf collections info COLLECTION_SLUG` - Get info about a collection on the Hub. `[--format [auto|human|agent|json|quiet]]`

skills.name: hormozi-grand-slam-offers
skills.description: Use when designing or diagnosing a sales offer, package, pricing stack, guarantee, or landing-page offer - Grand Slam / Value Equation mechanics (Hormozi $100M Offers).
skills.instructions:
# Hormozi Grand Slam offers (sales) Use when designing, rewriting, or diagnosing a sales offer, package, pricing stack, guarantee, or landing-page / email offer for any brand - especially when something feels commoditized or price-shopped. [REDACTED paragraph: person_with_client_athlete_context] ## 1. Grand Slam Offer (what “good” means)
An offer so clear and valuable that the only reason to say no is truly “not for me” - not “too expensive / same as others / I’ll think about it.” Goal: sell on **value**, not on being the cheapest. ## 2. Starving crowd (market before offer)
Prefer markets with:
- Massive pain
- Purchasing power
- Easy to target
- Growing (or at least not dying) Niches price higher than broad “everyone.” If the offer isn’t converting, check the market before rewriting the headline. ## 3. Value Equation (diagnose any weak offer)
Raise perceived value by working all four levers: | Lever | Direction |
| --- | --- |
| Dream outcome | ↑ make the end-state vivid and specific |
| Perceived likelihood of achievement | ↑ proof, process, credentials, “we’ve done this for people like you” |
| Time delay | ↓ shorten time to first win / first result |
| Effort & sacrifice | ↓ remove work, confusion, risk, logistics from the buyer | Most businesses over-index on dream outcome and under-invest in **speed** and **ease**. When rewriting an offer or email, name which lever you’re moving. ## 4. Build sequence (problems → solutions → trim & stack)
1. **Dream outcome** - what they actually want (not your feature list).
2. **List problems** - every obstacle before / during / after buying (confusion, time, fear, money, logistics).
3. Map each problem to the four value levers.
4. **Delivery vehicles** - how you solve each (1:1 vs group, DIY vs done-for-you, in-person vs remote, response speed).
5. **Trim & stack** - keep high-value / low-cost-to-deliver pieces; stack into a named bundle so they buy the **outcome stack**, not a commodity price. ## 5. Enhancers (after the core offer is strong)
Use honestly - never fake scarcity. - **Scarcity (quantity):** real seat caps, cohort caps, growth-rate caps, limited bonuses.
- **Urgency (time):** cohort start dates, seasonal windows, bonus/price windows that actually expire, exploding opportunities that decay.
- **Bonuses:** named for a benefit; each kills a specific objection; tools/checklists beat fluff; bonus stack can out-value the core in perception; reveal after the ask in 1:1, or use to handle a specific no.
- **Guarantees:** cut risk (unconditional, conditional, anti-guarantee / “you’re not a fit if…”). Match guarantee strength to fulfillment confidence.
- **Naming:** specific > clever; include who it’s for + outcome + timeframe when possible. ## 6. Pricing stance
Charge for value created, not cost-plus “fairness.” If close rate is very high, price may be too low; if very low, fix the offer/sales before cutting price. Keep overages and upgrades as expansion revenue after the core land. ## 7. Output when using this skill
When asked to improve an offer, return:
1. Dream outcome (one line)
2. Top 5 problems you’re solving
3. Core stack (what’s included)
4. Which value-equation levers moved
5. Scarcity / urgency / bonuses / guarantee / name (only what’s true)
6. Draft ask / CTA in the brand voice Never invent capacity, prices, guarantees, or proof the business doesn’t have.
