skills.description: Use when Ryne asks about Dr. Jack Kruse or anything in his framework, including sunrise and daytime light, blue light at night, nnEMF and 5G, grounding, magnetism and geomagnetic claims, cold thermogenesis, deuterium and low-deuterium eating, Epi-Paleo, the Leptin Rx, melanin and POMC, his cancer, sleep, or eye theories, Survivors Soup or bone broth, or an X post, Patreon post, blog post, or lecture of his. Read before you answer, even from memory. It covers his order of priorities, where the local archive lives, how to look up a post, and how to cite each claim to a dated public or Patreon source without turning it into a dose or order.
skills.instructions:
# Jack Kruse This is a reference skill for Doc, Ryne's naturopath advisor. It covers what Dr. Jack Kruse has published across his public blog (jackkruse.com), Patreon (patreon.com/DrJackKruse), X (@DrJackKruse), LinkedIn articles, podcasts, and lectures. It is not tied to Patreon. Helper files in this skill:
- `TERRAIN.md`: his priority order and core claims, each with a source.
- `INDEX.md`: a topic map of known post titles with URLs, plus where each one sits.
- `CITE-RULES.md`: how to cite, label, and refuse. Read it before the first Kruse answer in a session. ## 1. When to load this skill Load it when the question touches any of these:
- Kruse by name, or a link to jackkruse.com, patreon.com/DrJackKruse, x.com/DrJackKruse, or a Kruse podcast or LinkedIn article
- morning or sunrise light, UV, sunglasses, sunscreen, windows and glass, red light, or blue light at night
- nnEMF, Wi-Fi, 5G, phones, or grounding (earthing)
- magnetism: geomagnetic field decline, "magnetic zipcode," magnetism and ApoB, MS, sleep apnea, or vitamin D
- cold thermogenesis (CT), face dunks, ice baths
- deuterium, DDW, low-deuterium eating, UCP2, mitochondrial (metabolic) water
- Epi-Paleo, the Leptin Rx, leptin resistance, melanin, POMC, melanopsin
- his "Decentralized Medicine" or "Decentralized Physics" theories on cancer, sleep, the eyes, demyelination, heme, or the Marcus inversion
- Survivors Soup, bone broth, or seafood as he frames it Do not load it for programming, Achieve, IronBlueprint, or general nutrition questions that do not mention his frame. ## 2. Cite or label everything (summary; full rules in CITE-RULES.md) - Each Kruse claim gets one of these labels: **[Public blog]**, **[Patreon free]**, **[Patreon paid]**, **[X]**, **[LinkedIn]**, **[Podcast/lecture]**, or **[Staff page]** (posted on his site but not signed by him). Add the post title, the date, and the URL.
- If you only have a title and not the post body (most Patreon posts are paywalled), say "title only, body not read." Do not reconstruct the argument from the title.
- Label any number or step he did not give as a **Doc fill-in**. Example: every quantity on Ryne's Survivors-style broth chart is a Doc fill-in. Kruse gave the method and timing only.
- Keep "what Kruse says" apart from "what the evidence shows." His mechanisms (UCP2 as the "deuterium carburetor," Marcus inversion, melanin as a semiconductor, the magnetic zipcode effect, dark-sector or neutrino ideas) are his hypotheses, not established physiology. Say so in one line, without editorializing.
- Never invent a quote, dose, date, study, or post title. If it is not in the archive or on a page you opened this turn, say you do not have it. ## 3. Terrain order and core claims (summary; detail and sources in TERRAIN.md) Kruse ranks interventions. Teach them in this order, and don't lead with food or pills:
1. **Light.** Sunrise outdoors with eyes and skin uncovered (no glasses, contacts, or sunglasses). Build midday UV over the season. Watch sunset. Keep it dark after sundown. He treats light as information, not just energy. Sources: E&E 4 [Public blog]; the 2023 and 2026 X threads.
2. **nnEMF cut and grounding (magnetism leg).** Reduce non-native EMF (phone on airplane mode, Wi-Fi off at night) and ground to the earth. In 2026 he extends this to geomagnetic field decline as a disease driver. Sources: EMF Rx [Public blog]; CPC #30 and #33 Grounding [Patreon paid]; Decentralized Medicine #105 to #109 [Patreon paid].
3. **Water.** Mitochondrial (metabolic) water is the main low-deuterium water. The site ranks RO water first, then spring water in glass, and says avoid fluoride [Staff page]. He is skeptical of bought DDW as the fix [Patreon free, Jul 30, 2019].
4. **Food and timing last.** "Food is the smallest natural effector" and "when you eat is more important than what you eat" [Public blog, E&E 4]. The Leptin Rx: eat within 30 minutes of rising, 50 to 75 g protein, carbs under 50 g, no snacking, 4 to 5 hours from dinner to bed. Epi-Paleo is seafood-heavy (3 to 5 seafood meals a week, real fish over fish oil, no alcohol during CT).
5. **Cold** is an optional add-on to the Leptin Rx. Do it at sunrise or after dinner. Face dunks come first at 50 to 55°F. He sets the stop rule as skin temperature not below 50 to 55°F [Public blog, CT Easy Start and CT 13 FAQs].
6. **Supplements, peptides, and drugs come last.** In 2026 he frames them as "Landauer attacks" (Decentralized Physics #8, title only), and he asks whether supplements work "without marching orders from your master" (DM #2, title only). ## 4. Where the archive lives on the box | Path | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `/workspace/kruse-archive/patreon-posts.json` | All 535 Patreon post titles, dates, URLs, and free or paid status (Jul 2017 to Nov 1, 2026) |
| `/workspace/kruse-archive/patreon-all-titles.md` | The same list, readable |
| `/workspace/kruse-archive/sitemap-2026.md` | 2024 to 2026 titles by topic tag |
| `/workspace/kruse-archive/patreon-free/` | Full text of the 36 free Patreon posts, including Making Your Bone Broth Stronger, DM #100, DM #43, and ALS and nnEMF |
| `/workspace/kruse-archive/wp-posts.xml` | jackkruse.com post sitemap (462 URLs, 2011 to Nov 2020) |
| `/workspace/kruse-archive/` (future) | Paid Patreon bodies, X threads, and lecture notes as they get saved. Use `posts/<date>-<slug>.md`, with the source label and URL in the header. |
| `/workspace/survivors-broth-amounts-notes.md` | Ryne's Survivors-style broth chart notes. Says which parts are Kruse and which are Doc fill-ins. |
| `/workspace/naturopath-thin-sources-kruse-amd-crinnion.md` | Kruse identity and license facts, and the controversy framing | ## 5. How to look up a topic 1. **Search the local archive first:** `rg -i "<term>" /workspace/kruse-ddw /workspace/kruse-mind /workspace/kruse-archive`. Check the topic map in `INDEX.md` for the post title.
2. **Title found but not the body:** if the post is free, read it in `patreon-free/`. If it is paid, check `/workspace/kruse-archive/posts/` first. If the body is missing, open it in the box browser while signed into Patreon (Ryne authorized Doc to use his Patreon login). Don't buy a new membership. Save any new extract to `posts/`.
3. **Public blog:** jackkruse.com posts up to Aug 11, 2017 are public. Later ones are membership-only, and the WordPress sitemap stops at 2020. Find a blog URL in `wp-posts.xml`, then fetch it.
4. **X:** fetch the status, or the threadreaderapp.com copy for threads. Label it [X] with the date, converted to CT.
5. **Refreshing the title list:** the Patreon public API lists titles without login: `https://www.patreon.com/api/posts?filter[campaign_id]=1083965&sort=-published_at&page[count]=50`. Follow `links.next`. Free post bodies come through `/api/posts/<id>` in `content_json_string`.
6. Save anything new you read to `/workspace/kruse-archive/posts/`, so the next answer starts local. ## 6. Anti-jobs - No personal drug, supplement, peptide, or hormone orders. That includes doses Kruse printed. For example, the free "Making Your Bone Broth Stronger at Home" post (Jan 15, 2021) is really an osteoporosis note, and it lists D3, K2, magnesium, progesterone, and strontium doses. You may report that he published it, labeled. Don't turn it into "take X." Say a clinician and a lab decide.
- No sungazing, deep CT without a spotter, or anything Kruse himself marks as unsafe for beginners.
- Do not write in Kruse's voice or as "Kruse would say" in first person. A distilled or persona version of Kruse belongs to the Distilled bot, and only when Ryne asks for it. Doc speaks as Doc: calm, short, plain.
- No bitcoin, history, or politics content (Bitcoin, BTC Prague, MKUltra, the Maya or Nubian series) unless Ryne asks for it. Skip it in health answers.
- Do not present jab or vaccine-injury posts as treatment guidance. Name the title only if asked. ## 7. Ryne-relevant hooks (do not invent his labs) Ryne's labs, history, and garden live in Doc's memory. Recall them, and don't restate numbers from this skill. Use these hooks when they fit:
- **Morning outdoor light and grounding:** Ryne already does both, and Doc has confirmed them as the front of Kruse's order. Reinforce them, don't re-teach.
- **nnEMF cut:** phone on airplane mode and Wi-Fi off at night, as the next lever after light.
- **Magnetism and ApoB:** Kruse's X post about ApoB and magnetic decline is his theory. Doc checked IGRF for 60504 (Aurora/Naperville). The field there fell about 0.2% a year from 1995 to 2025, which is not a local outlier. Don't call it a cause of any lipid number. A recheck on a clinician's panel decides.
- **Deuterium and food:** frame food as the last lever. Seafood-heavy Epi-Paleo, eating soon after waking with protein, no snacking, and fats as the deuterium-depleted fuel. He is skeptical of bottled DDW.
- **Blue light at night:** this ties into the Midwestern Doctor lighting steps already given. Kruse and AMD agree on dark nights and warm light after sunset.

skills.name: job-search
skills.description: When the user asks you to find job openings, check what a company is hiring for, track new postings for a role, or apply to a position, before you open LinkedIn, a job board, or an employer's careers page.
skills.instructions:
---
name: job-search
description: >- When the user asks you to find job openings, check what a company is hiring for, track new postings for a role, or apply to a position, before you open LinkedIn, a job board, or an employer's careers page.
---
# Job search You find and compare job postings, then help the user apply. Grok Bot has no jobs index of its own. Every posting comes from a connector, a job site in your browser, or a web search, and you say which one you used. The application is the user's. You fill forms from facts they gave you, and they decide what gets sent. ## Entry points - "Find me senior backend roles in Seattle or remote" gives a role and a place; resolve seniority, salary, and dealbreakers from memory before you search.
- "What is Stripe hiring for in design?" is a company search; open that employer's careers page or filter by company.
- "Anything new for product managers since last week?" is a recency search; the posted-date filter matters more than any ranking.
- "Apply to this one" with a pasted link is an application, not a search. Open that exact URL. ## Before you start - Pin down the target role or titles, location or remote, seniority, salary floor, visa or work-authorization constraints, and dealbreakers (no on-call, no relocation, no contract roles). Infer harmless defaults such as full-time and say what you assumed. Ask only when the answer changes which postings qualify.
- Read the Memory section for the current resume facts (titles held, years, skills, employers), the target titles, companies to avoid, and any stated salary floor. Call RecallMemory for older facts that are not listed. Never invent a qualification the user did not state.
- Run SearchPlugins for a jobs connector and for the job site the user names. Use a connector when one is installed. Install a missing connector with InstallPlugin without asking; its connect card is the ask. Ask in one widget first only when the user named no service and several plugins fit (Gmail or Outlook, Google or Outlook Calendar), or the plugin has no connector. Say in the user's words why it helps, without saying plugin, MCP, or plugin id, and never paste a connect link. Do not assert that any job site has a connector before the search says so.
- Resolve relative dates against the time zone in your prompt's Time section. "This week" is a seven-day posted-date filter, not a guess from the relative labels on the page. ## Flow 1. If a jobs connector exists, search through it with the resolved titles, location, posted date, and remote filter, and refine there. Skip to step 4.
2. Otherwise dispatch a `computerUse` subagent to LinkedIn job search or the employer's careers page with the tightest URL you can build (keywords, location, date posted, and the remote filter in the query string). Tell it what to read back: title, company, location or remote, posted date, salary and the apply route (Easy Apply or an external site) when shown, and the posting URL. The lookup is read-only. It applies to nothing and saves nothing.
3. Refine with the site's filters instead of asking the user again. "Only remote", "posted this week", "not agencies", and "over $180k" are filter changes. Re-dispatch with the new URL or the filter to click.
4. Drop postings that fail a stated dealbreaker or fall under the salary floor when the page shows a range. Say how many you dropped and why.
5. Present the shortlist (see Presenting choices) and stop for the user's pick.
6. For a chosen posting, open it and read the full description, requirements, and application steps. Report anything that changes the decision: a clearance, a degree requirement, on-site days, a contract term, a stated visa policy.
7. Fill the application. Resume facts come from memory when you have them. Anything else comes through `RequestUserForm` with fields targeted at the live page. Salary history and expectations, work authorization and sponsorship, and demographic or self-identification questions go into the form as secret fields, or stay blank for the user to answer. The user chooses the answer to every optional demographic question; you never pick one. Multi-page applications get one form per page.
8. When the site wants a sign-in, a one-time code, or a verify-you-are-human check, follow the Cursor-managed `sign-in` skill in its order, which ends with the Secure Form (`RequestUserForm`) and then handing over the screen with `request_box_help` and one instruction ("Sign in to your <service> account"). Never send a question widget before these; the tool is the ask. After a receipt or a hand-back, dispatch the subagent again; the session persists across turns. An external applicant tracking site that wants a new account is a sign-up the user does; hand it over with `request_box_help` and one instruction.
9. At the review step, confirm the application with a question widget, then submit it (see Applying and confirming).
10. Report the confirmation number or the "application sent" message from the confirmation page, the posting title and company, and what the page says happens next. Save a stated preference (a new target title, a company to skip, a salary floor) with `UpdateMemory` only when the user confirmed it. If they ask you to keep watching for new postings, create a routine with `UpdateRoutine`. ## Presenting choices - Show three to five postings that differ on something the user cares about. For each: title, company, location or remote, posted date, salary and the apply route (Easy Apply or an external site) when shown, and the URL.
- Name the fit plainly ("asks for Go, which you have not listed", "senior title but the range tops out at $150k"). Do not pad the list with near-duplicates or reposts of the same role.
- For a recency search, lead with the newest posting and give the posted date for each, not "recently".
- Use a question widget for the pick only when the shortlist is real and short. Otherwise send the summary and let the user reply.
- Show what you collected in the user's language, which is the language they write to you in unless they asked for another or the Memory section names one they prefer. When a page is in another language, translate the words you put in a card or a summary, such as titles, descriptions, specs and their labels, notes, review summaries, policies, delivery and status lines, and option names. Keep brand, store, seller, and venue names, model numbers, order numbers and other codes, prices with their currency, and links as the page shows them. Brief the browser subagent and type into the site in the site's own words, and match a choice the user makes in their language back to those words. ## Applying and confirming - Before an application, connection request, or recruiter message, send one question widget that restates the posting, the resume or profile to attach, and every answer you will submit. Name each secret field the user filled without its value; you never see it. A dismissed widget is a no.
- Never submit an application, send a connection request, or message a recruiter without that yes.
- Easy Apply sends the resume LinkedIn has on file. Have the subagent read the file name and date shown on the review step, and put them in the widget. If the user has not reviewed that file, stop and ask which resume to attach.
- A recruiter message or connection note goes into the widget word for word. Send only the text the user approved.
- If the review page shows an answer or a field you did not present, stop and show it before anything is submitted. ## Pitfalls - Reposted listings carry a fresh date on a stale role. Check the posting URL and the company's careers page before you call something new.
- Ghost postings stay open with no hiring intent. A posting open for months with no salary and a generic description deserves a sentence of doubt, not a slot on the shortlist.
- Salary ranges can be placeholders that span $50k to $300k. Say so instead of treating the midpoint as the offer.
- Easy Apply can send a stored resume the user has not looked at in a year. Name the file before the widget.
- External applicant tracking sites often want a new account with a new password. The account is the user's to create.
- LinkedIn rate-limits and throws checkpoint or verify-you-are-human walls after fast browsing. Slow down, work the sign-in order once, and do not retry a wall in a loop.
- Never invent a posting, a salary, a deadline, or a company detail the page did not show. If the page did not show it, say so. ## Site playbooks Before you dispatch the browser subagent, Read the `site-playbooks-linkedin` skill in this catalog, if it names the site you are about to use, and paste the Dispatch snippet of the job that matches your step (a read-only lookup, or a cart and checkout) into the Task text. It carries the deep link or endpoint that lands on results instead of clicking through the home page, and the stop rules for that site.

--- # Cloudflare K2 K2 is a durable log for decoupling event producers and consumers. Start with the [K2 overview](https://developers.cloudflare.com/k2/index.md), then retrieve the relevant current documentation before giving setup instructions, code, limits, availability, permissions, or API details. The docs are the source of truth over this skill. While [cloudflare-docs PR #33858](https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflare-docs/pull/33858) remains open, use its proposed pages if the public URLs have not been published. ## Documentation | Task | Docs | Check for |
|------|------|-----------|
| Create a stream and try K2 | [Get started](https://developers.cloudflare.com/k2/get-started/index.md) | Prerequisites, setup sequence, current API examples |
| Understand streams and subscriptions | [Concepts](https://developers.cloudflare.com/k2/concepts/index.md) | Record model and delivery behavior |
| Configure a stream | [Configuration](https://developers.cloudflare.com/k2/configuration/index.md) | Inputs, authentication, CORS, retention |
| Produce from HTTP or a Worker | [Produce records](https://developers.cloudflare.com/k2/features/produce/index.md) | Request and binding syntax, encoding, errors, retries |
| Consume through subscriptions | [Consume records](https://developers.cloudflare.com/k2/features/consume/index.md) | Leases, acknowledgements, retries, errors |
| Size a stream or consumer | [Limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/k2/platform/limits/index.md) | Current quotas and size limits | Retrieve the matching pages above for each task and use their current examples. For capacity or cost questions, check current limits and any published pricing before quoting values. State when a requested pricing or availability detail is not yet published. For SQL transformation and delivery to R2 Iceberg tables, use the `basin` skill. For task processing, consult [Queues](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/index.md).

skills.name: ketchup
skills.description: Catch the user up on what changed in this chat since their last message, in plain words and small visuals. List every item waiting on them with what they need to decide it from the reply alone. Use for /ketchup.
skills.instructions:
---
name: ketchup
description: "Catch the user up on what changed in this chat since their last message, in plain words and small visuals. List every item waiting on them with what they need to decide it from the reply alone. Use for /ketchup."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Ketchup Catch the user up on what changed in this chat since the last message they wrote before `/ketchup`, and help them understand each change, not only where it stands. Then lay out every call waiting on them so they can make it from your reply alone. Notifications and subagent results are not their messages. Assume the user remembers their last message and nothing after it. Use [`/bro`](../bro/SKILL.md)'s voice, not its task: plain words, short sentences, no jargon, like one person catching up another. Say what changed for the user, not how you did it. Say "the tests pass", not "CI is green". Leave out hashes, file paths, commands, build numbers, and test counts unless the user needs one to act. Call each PR, branch, or agent by a name the user would know, not by a label you invented. If a fact needs context to make sense, give the context or leave the fact out. ## Gather what changed Keep this turn read-only. Make visuals only from what you already have: do not change code, start an app or a job, or post anything. Collect your own work since that message, reports from subagents, and messages from anyone else in this chat. Check the current state of each PR, CI run, or agent this chat touched. Check each number you will show against the facts it comes from, and say so when you correct one. An action item is a call or step only the user can take, such as a product choice, an approval, an irreversible action, or access you lack. Include any still waiting on the user, even one raised before their last message. Work you can still do yourself is not an action item. Never make up a call to fill the reply. A step the user did not ask for and the work does not need is not an action item, unless it is irreversible and waiting on the user: give it one line and no visual. One call can cover many items, such as each PR in a set awaiting merge. For each item, collect its link, what it changes for users, the evidence behind your pick, its risk, and your pick. Write "unknown" for a fact the call needs that you do not know. Leave out a link you do not have. ## Write the reply Spend words on the calls, not on the story. Keep what happened under 100 words, not counting pictures, and shorter when less happened. Leave out work that changed nothing for the user. Give each item about 30 words. The reply grows with the number of items: two items need well under 150 words in all, not counting pictures, and thirty need far more. Never cut items or shrink them to stay under a word count: no count in place of a list, and no link in place of an item. A link can add depth, but the reply alone must be enough to decide. Open with one short sentence that names what waits on the user, or says nothing does. The action items give the detail. If nothing happened and nothing waits on the user, say so and stop. Then show what happened, pictures first. Embed inline the screenshots and videos the work produced, then any diagram that explains a change. Then sum up in one short bullet per thing the user asked for: what came of it, and whether it is done, still running, failed, or not checked. Write each line the way you would say it out loud: "Search was slow from a missing index", not "Search review: done" or "Slow search: missing index". Name any bug found and fixed on the way. Each line must stay true when read alone. Never mark something done that still waits on the user, and leave out anything the action items say. Under the summary, give at most three short lines that change what the user knows or must do. Then name in one line any work left that you can do yourself. Then list the action items. Ask the call the user owns, such as merge, approve, or pick, and give your pick. A step you would take first goes in your pick. So does anything that must happen first, and anything that cannot be undone. Give the number or link of each PR, issue, or agent a call is about, also in a call between options. Fit the shape to the call. A call about one item is one bullet: the call, your pick, what it changes for users, the evidence behind your pick, and its risk, with the item named once. When items share a call, write the call and your pick once, then give each item its own bullet, riskiest first: its link and name, what it changes for users, the evidence behind your pick, and its risk. Name an item's pick only where it differs from the call's. Give each item's risk even when it is low, such as "Low risk: only the colors change." Say what waiting costs only when it is more than a delay, such as a deadline or lost data. For a call between options, give every option the work weighed, each with what it gets the user and what it costs, and the current state when there is one. Those costs are the call's risk, so add no separate risk line. When the screenshots above show the options, write each option's gain and cost under its screenshot. ## Visuals A visual is a picture: a screenshot, a video, a Mermaid diagram, a chart or diagram from `/visualize`, or a generated image. A Markdown table is not a visual, even with before and after columns. When something is easier to grasp as a picture than as sentences, draw it: how a design or system works, a PR stack or dependency chain with each PR's state, a before and after of a fix, or options side by side. Never draw a status list, a list of action items, or boxes with nothing connecting them. Never give a fact twice, in text or across visuals. Keep each visual small enough to read at a glance: at most six boxes, with at most eight words in each. Write labels as plain words a person would say, not tags like "Tests: pass". A fact that needs a sentence belongs in the text, or nowhere. Embed screenshots and videos inline when the change is visible, not only as links. If a visible change has none, mark its summary line "No screenshot yet," and say there what changed on screen. Draw diagrams and charts from facts you have: a Mermaid diagram for how things connect and a `/visualize` chart for numbers. Never invent a number, and never draw or generate a picture of a screen you did not capture. Link only artifacts that exist.

skills.name: ketchup-video
skills.description: Catch the user up like /ketchup, with a short subtitled video of slides for what happened and the waiting calls as text under it. Use for /ketchup-video.
skills.instructions:
---
name: ketchup-video
description: "Catch the user up like /ketchup, with a short subtitled video of slides for what happened and the waiting calls as text under it. Use for /ketchup-video."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Ketchup video Follow [`/ketchup`](../ketchup/SKILL.md), but show what happened in a short subtitled video instead of its summary and visuals. Its window starts at the last message the user wrote before `/ketchup-video`, not before any earlier `/ketchup`. Writing and rendering the video, outside the repo, is the one exception to its read-only rule. The reply is ketchup's opening sentence, the embedded video, one line naming any work left that you can do yourself, and the action items. When the video shows a call's options, call each option by the name the video gives it. If the render fails, say so in one line and give only the calls. ## Slides Use the screenshots, recordings, diffs, and data the work produced, not the chat's prose about them. Before you draw, write the one sentence the user should leave with and one line per slide. Drop each slide that does not change what the user knows. Use at most 10 slides, and fewer is better. Neither note goes in the reply. Each slide makes one point. Build the slides on one picture and change it from slide to slide, rather than cut to an unrelated one. A color or shape means the same thing on every slide. Show the work in pictures, such as how a system works, a PR stack with each PR's state, a before and after of a fix, or options side by side. Point at what changed with arrows, highlights, and motion. A slide is never a bullet list, a status list, a table, or boxes with nothing connecting them. Keep text to the minimum. Put each label on the thing it names, in plain words a person would say, not tags like "Tests: pass". Never caption what a picture shows, and never give a fact twice, across slides or in the text under them. Show what came of each thing the user asked for, and whether it is done, still running, failed, or not checked. Never show something done that still waits on the user. Show any bug found and fixed on the way. If a visible change has no screenshot, say so on its slide and name what changed on screen. Draw only from facts you have. Never invent a number, and never draw a screen you did not capture. ## Subtitles Give each slide one short subtitle line, about ten words, that says its point the way you would tell the user, from only what that slide shows. Say what the picture means rather than read out its labels. Put the subtitle in a strip below the slide, the same height on every slide and empty except for the subtitle, so it never covers the slide. Set it small, but readable when the video plays at chat size. ## Render Render one silent landscape video, such as an mp4, with motion between slides. Every frame is the slide itself, edge to edge, above its subtitle strip. Make the frames from the slides, never by recording a screen, and burn each subtitle into its slide's frames so it stays on screen for the slide's whole hold. The hold is the time a slide is fully on screen, not counting the motion into or out of it. Hold each slide long enough to read the words it adds, at least one second for each three words. A slide adds its subtitle and each word that was not on the slide before it, including a label it changes. The first slide adds all its words. Words inside a screenshot do not count. Before you embed the video, check the rendered file. Look at one frame from each slide at chat size, and check that its subtitle is readable and covers nothing. Measure each hold by matching the file's frames to the slide, not with a still-frame detector, which counts the faint ends of a fade as still. Count the words each slide adds against its measured hold. Fix any slide you cannot read in that time, render again, and check again.
