### Opening a PR Invoked at the end of every other playbook. **Worktree.** Work from a git worktree off main. Subagents inherit it. Multiple `Task` calls on the same branch each get their own worktree, or `git fetch && git reset --hard origin/<branch>` between them. Dirty branch with unrelated work: patch out, fresh worktree, apply. Snarled worktree: reset from main, redo minimally. **Commits.** Commit liberally. Rebase into small, ordered commits before opening PRs. Each commit is a future PR: landable, ordered to tell the story. Amend when the fix belongs in a just-made commit. New commit when separable. Commit bodies don't restate the subject. **PRs.** Run `/deslop` from `cursor-team-kit` over the diff before commit and `/no-comments` before review. Write every PR title, description, and commit body with `/technical-writing` (every layer except Diátaxis, and apply the STE vocabulary rules: one word per action, keep articles, a plain verb over `-ing` where one works), then apply `/unslop`. **Titles.** Conventional Commits `type(scope): subject`, no trailing period. Type such as `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`, or `perf`. Scope is the area, such as `pstack` or `poteto-mode`. Subject is short, imperative, and names a real symbol when one carries the change, for example `fix(pstack): retarget opening-a-pr babysit trigger`. **Descriptions.** The PR body is a one-minute briefing, not a lab notebook, for a reviewer who has the diff. It says why the change exists, what it leaves out, what it could break, and how you proved it works. Write short, simple sentences with few identifiers, no walls of text. The body becomes the squash commit body, so keep that commit under about 40 lines. Use `##` headings, not bold lead-ins, in this order, and drop a section with nothing to say: - `## Why`: the problem and approach, 1-3 short sentences. No SHAs, rebase genealogy, or "based on main" preamble.
- `## What changed`: 1-3 short bullets. Name a real symbol or path only when it carries the change. Name both sides of a rename or retarget.
- `## Scope`: always. 1-3 short items on what it covers and what it deliberately leaves out (a follow-up, a known gap). No symbols, paths, or file-by-file essay.
- `## Tradeoffs`: only rejected alternatives a reviewer would otherwise ask about. Skip when there was no real choice.
- `## Blast Radius`: 1-2 sentences on who or what it touches and why that is safe or risky. If main is red, state the cost of leaving it red.
- `## Verification`: 1-3 bullets, each a real run path and its outcome. Perf: one primary number with its unit, `before → after`, and a link to the arena or swarm directory for the rest. No sample-size methodology, swarm recitals, or metric tables. After the sections, attach videos or screenshots when they prove a claim. Full SHAs, swarm or arena lane recitals, lever-correction essays, file-by-file checklists, and "CLEAN" verdicts go in a linked artifact, not the body. **Forge.** Resolve the forge before the first PR operation and keep that choice for create, edit, view, watch, and merge. GitHub CLI (`gh`) is the default. If `command -v origin` succeeds and Origin can resolve the repository, prefer `origin pr ...`. If Origin is absent or cannot resolve the repository, stay on `gh` and record the fallback. Do not require Graphite (`gt`). **Built-in PR tool.** When the run provides a built-in PR tool, create, edit, retarget, and mark ready through it, never through a forge CLI. A CLI-made PR misses what the tool tracks. Use the resolved forge for everything the tool does not cover, and for every PR operation when the run has no such tool. **Size and stacks.** Prefer five narrow PRs to one large PR. A stack is a base-branch chain. The root PR targets trunk. Each child branch rebases onto its parent's exact tip and its PR targets the parent branch. As a parent merges, move its child onto trunk per `playbooks/shipping.md` step 4. Without a built-in PR tool, per the resolved forge, create a child with `origin pr create --status open --base <parent-branch>` or `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`, and retarget one with `origin pr edit <pr> --base <parent-branch>` or `gh pr edit <pr> --base <parent-branch>`. Branch from trunk only for independent work. Rebase on trunk before substantial stack work. **Readiness.** Open every PR ready, never as a draft. A built-in PR tool can default to draft, so set `draft: false` on every creation call through it. With Origin, pass `--status open`. With `gh`, omit `--draft`. If a PR still opens as a draft, mark it ready through the PR tool, or run `origin pr ready <number>` or `gh pr ready <number>` according to the resolved forge. Run `origin pr view <number>` or `gh pr view <number>` before you refer to PR status. **Babysit.** Opening a PR does not start a babysit. Post the URL and keep building. Finish the phase or stack first. Run a separate babysit pass only when the user asks for one after the whole stack exists. A babysit for each new PR stalls the build and spends checks on commits later waves restart. Push back when feedback drifts from intent. A subagent that opens a PR runs `/deslop` and `/no-comments`, and posts the URL. It returns to the parent without babysitting, unless it is an Autopilot-full or Autopilot-stack owner. That owner's brief assigns the babysit loop and is the ask `playbooks/babysit.md` waits for. The owner starts the loop after its code-ready report, reports merge-ready, and is exempt from the rules here and in `playbooks/babysit.md` that hold babysitting until a whole stack is built. --- file: playbooks/orchestrate.md ---
### Orchestrate **You run the program, never the code. Decide which agent does each piece of work, then check what each one produces.** For a standing project handed to one coordinator chat: multi-day, many stacked PRs, dozens to hundreds of subagents, few human turns. One task driven to a predicate is Autonomous run. One ambitious run that needs a bespoke workflow is figure-it-out. Work that one agent could finish inside the session's budget is not a program. Run it with your own tools. Spawn workers with `Task`. Keep the program's state in the Project tracker (`notes.md`) and the Project store. Watch each PR with PR and CI event subscriptions when your harness has them. Call no scripts, run no polling loops, and never relay messages or status between agents. #### Topology - **One owner per PR.** The owner is the only writer of its branch and carries the PR from build to merge. Only the owner pushes, rebases, or retargets it. Closing or retargeting a base PR orphans every PR above it, so the owner does that only on your call. You never author or edit code. Conflicted merges, chain rebases, and fixes go to owners.
- **A fresh worker for each independent task.** Its kickoff carries everything it needs, including each upstream report it depends on, pasted in full. Workers can't see their siblings. Run workers on a new cloud VM (`environment: "cloud"`) unless the work needs this machine: a `control-ui` or `control-cli` runtime check (from `cursor-team-kit`), local transcripts, a simulator, or auth that exists only here. Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section.
- **A sub-coordinator only when one area has many parallel workers.** It owns that area's workers and kickoffs and sends you one rollup, never raw worker reports. Stop at three levels: you, sub-coordinators, and workers. Keep about ten workers in flight per coordinator, and start the next one as each finishes instead of waiting on a whole batch.
- **Fork when new work needs a worker's built state,** such as its checkout, uncommitted changes, or a running process. Message a worker only for a follow-up on the same work. Never message one to check on it, because a message restarts an idle agent.
- **Each PR gets a verifier that isn't its author,** on a different model family. The owner merges only on that verifier's pass at the current head.
- **Start with one unit.** Take it through kickoff, owner, verifier, and merge before you fan out, so a flaw in the kickoff costs one agent instead of fifty. On near-identical cheap units, the first unit is that test. #### Supervision - **Each kickoff names the evidence that proves the work is done,** such as a command and its expected output, a control-skill check, or an artifact. It also names the goal, the paths the worker may and may not write, and the actions it must not take. If you can't name the evidence, the unit isn't scoped yet.
- **Read the diff or the artifact, not only the worker's summary.** Green CI is an input to a verdict, not a verdict. Behavioral work needs more than a type check. A verdict covers one head SHA, so a new push needs a new verdict. Read a sample of each sub-coordinator's kickoffs while its workers run, and fix its instructions when one fails.
- **Send back work that drifts from scope or grows past what was asked.** Keep only the fixes that block the program, and park the rest as follow-ups.
- **Check a PR's live state before you report on it,** with `gh pr view` and `gh pr checks` or your forge's equivalents, not the worker's last report. Account for every worker you spawned as done, replaced, or absorbed into another worker's scope.
- **Stop or replace a worker that stalls or loops.** Judge it by its pushes and PR activity, not its status text. Retry by cause: a smaller scope after a context or memory limit, the same kickoff after a dropped connection, and a different model after a tool error. After two retries, drop the unit and replan around it. When a stopped worker returns late, check its result against the PR's current state, and hand any unique findings to a fresh worker.
- **Ask the user only for a real decision or a blocker,** such as an irreversible action, a product or preference call that no experiment settles, or a dead end that survived a replan. Rebase mechanics, retries, CI flakes, review triage, and "should I keep going" never reach the user. **Reply:** what landed against the goal, each PR's live state and verdict with its link, what was dropped and why, and the decisions waiting on the user. --- file: playbooks/pause-safely.md ---
### Pause safely **You own a clean stop. Leave a checkpoint a cold-start agent can resume from.** This is explicit only. On "keep going", "going to bed, keep going", or "don't stop", do not pause. 1. Stop at a safe boundary. Finish the current atomic step or back out of it. Start nothing new, and cancel any nested subagents.
2. Take no irreversible action to pause. No PR and no push unless you already had one out.
3. Make the work durable. Commit uncommitted edits as one clear `wip:` commit on the current branch so nothing is lost. If the tree is broken, say so in the commit body in one line.
4. Write the resume note off-context. Capture intent, what you were doing, progress and what's verified, current state, next steps, key files, and gotchas. For the compaction trigger write it to a file like `/tmp/<slug>-resume.md`. If a show-me-your-work trail exists, point at it instead of duplicating it. **Reply:** where you are in the loop, what's on disk versus still in your head (paths, no diff dumps), the commits you made and whether the tree is clean, and the first action on resume. This is a pause, not a final report. --- file: playbooks/perf-issue.md ---
### Perf issue **You own the measurement story. Plan, review, verify the numbers.** Tie every fix to a measurement, don't read source instead of measuring. 1. Capture a baseline trace via the matching control skill. Vet the baseline, and each later number, with the **benchmark-checklist** skill.
2. `how` to ground hypotheses. Don't claim a perf ceiling without running it first. Try the performance mantras in order, cheapest first: 1. Don't do it. Stop work whose result nothing uses rather than cheapening it. 2. Do it, but don't do it again. 3. Do it less. 4. Do it later. 5. Do it when they're not looking. 6. Do it concurrently. 7. Do it cheaper. When an earlier mantra meets the target, stop.
3. Plan the fix from the trace. If it crosses a function boundary, `architect` first. Delegate implementation to a subagent using your configured perf-issue model (default `grok-4.7-xhigh-fast`). Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section. Review the diff. Capture a post-fix trace. Apply the **sequence-verifiable-units** principle skill, verifying each attempt before trying the next.
4. Parse and compare the artifacts (JSON to sqlite, diff). "Inconclusive" or wrong-surface is not a pass. Flag it.
5. Cite the measurement in the PR.
6. Run **Opening a PR**. For sustained improvement against a metric rather than a one-off fix, use the Hillclimb playbook (`playbooks/hillclimb.md`). **Reply:** baseline number, post-fix number, delta, artifact path. --- file: playbooks/prototype.md ---
### Prototype **You own the design decision, not the code. The prototype is a throwaway instrument. The real build follows Feature.** The one playbook where the Laziness Protocol's "smallest change" and the verification bar invert. Speed over polish, code quality does not matter, no planning. The rigor is in picking the right design cheaply. Propose variations the user didn't ask for, throw an approach away and try another. 1. Scope the decision the prototype exists to make: which layout, which interaction, which density, or for an empirical fork which behavior, timing, or approach. No decision means no prototype. Route to Feature.
2. Gather references when the design space is open. Search for prior art, summarize a moodboard of themes, palettes, and layouts, let the user pick directions before building. Skip when the direction is set.
3. Build throwaway in an isolated scratch dir, separate from production source. For a visual decision, vanilla HTML/CSS/JS or the lightest stack that renders the idea, CDN deps, a dev server with hot reload. For a behavioral or timing decision, the smallest script that exercises the question. No production framework, no tests, no abstractions.
4. When comparing alternatives, build them behind one switcher (buttons or a keypress), each variant labeled. This is the **exhaust-the-design-space** principle skill made cheap.
5. Verify on the matching surface. For a visual decision, screenshot each variant via the control skill and drive the interaction. For a behavioral or timing decision, observe the thing you are deciding by logging the timing, printing the output, or watching the render. The observation is the test here, not an assertion.
6. Present alternatives, tradeoffs, and a recommendation. The output is the decision plus the throwaway artifact, not shippable code. Hand the chosen direction to **Feature** (or `architect` for the shape) for the real build. **Reply:** the variants explored, the evidence (screenshots for a visual decision, the observed output or timing for a behavioral one), tradeoffs, your recommendation, and the scratch path. Say plainly that the prototype is throwaway. --- file: playbooks/refactoring.md ---
### Refactoring **You own the contract. The structure changes. The behavior does not.** Distinct from Feature, which adds behavior, and Bug fix, which corrects it. If the cleanup reveals a missing feature or a real bug, split it out and ship the structural change first against the pinned contract. A redesign is allowed, but name it and route to Feature. Large or cross-cutting structural work belongs to the **figure-it-out** skill. This playbook is the focused-to-medium change. 1. Pin the behavior contract first. Run the **how** skill over the affected subsystem to learn the contract, then write a characterization test, snapshot, or equivalence harness that captures current behavior before any structure moves. If the area has no coverage, write the pin before touching structure. Type check and lint are not a pin.
2. Name the structure the code is missing per **principle-model-the-domain**. Boring code stays when the shape is already clear and local. The reshape must delete branches or invalid states, not add indirection.
3. Name the target shape. State what the module layout, types, and call graph should be if built today (**principle-foundational-thinking**, **principle-redesign-from-first-principles**). If the target crosses a function boundary, run the **architect** skill for parallel design exploration of the shape before the move.
4. Subtract before you add. Delete dead code, collapse one-caller wrappers, drop redundant validators, and remove orphan references before introducing the new shape (**principle-subtract-before-you-add**). The smallest change that reaches the target shape ships (**principle-laziness-protocol**). A speculative cleanup that "might help" gets reverted.
5. Move in small behavior-preserving steps, each keeping the pin green. For API reshapes, migrate every caller and delete the old API in the same wave (**principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis**). No compatibility shims, no parallel old-and-new paths. Spot-check every rename against the actual files. Renames silently miss usages in strings, prose, and back-references. Delegate the mechanical edits to a subagent using your configured refactoring model (default `grok-4.7-xhigh-fast`) with a specific scope (file paths, the names being moved, the behavior to hold). Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section.
6. Prove behavior is unchanged on the real artifact, not "it compiles" (**principle-prove-it-works**). For larger reshapes, run an equivalence check: a script that diffs old-vs-new outputs, a recorded baseline replayed against the new code, or a smoke run on the matching surface via the relevant control skill.
7. Confirm the change is worth keeping. The success measure is reduced reader load (**principle-minimize-reader-load**). If the diff does not lower reader load somewhere, revert it.
8. Rebase into small ordered commits. A subtraction commit, then the reshape, then any follow-on cleanup. Shape them with the **sequence-verifiable-units** principle skill, so each behavior-preserving slice stays green before the next. Run **Opening a PR**. **Reply:** the structure that changed, the pin you held it against, the equivalence proof, the reader-load delta, what shipped and what got reverted. No new behavior. --- file: playbooks/runtime-forensics.md ---
### Runtime forensics **You own the diagnosis. Instrument the live process, don't theorize from source.** The deliverable is a cited diagnosis, not a fix. 1. Capture the live signal on the matching surface via the control skill: a CPU profile for a spinning process, a heap snapshot for a leak, a CDP trace for a visual glitch. A real artifact, not a guess.
2. Reduce the artifact to the smoking gun: the function on the hot path, the retainer chain from the leaked object to a GC root, the loop firing without input. Parse large artifacts in a subagent (the **guard-the-context-window** principle skill), keep the reduced finding in the main thread. Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section.
3. Prove the mechanism before believing it. Inject instrumentation via CDP eval on the running process, or hotfix the live code without reloading, to confirm the hypothesis cheaply.
4. Map the finding back to source: file, symbol, the line that allocates or schedules.
5. Throughput checkpoint stays one line: `throughput checkpoint: n/a, read-only forensics`. **Reply:** the signal captured, the reduced finding, how you proved the mechanism, the source location, artifact paths. No fix unless asked. Hand back to Bug fix or Perf once the cause is known. --- file: playbooks/session-pickup.md ---
### Session pickup **You own the resume point. Read the prior trail, don't redo it.** 1. Locate the prior trail. A local transcript under the active workspace's `agent-transcripts/` directory (the system prompt names the path. Do not glob across `~/.cursor/projects/*/`, that crosses workspace boundaries and reads private chats from unrelated projects), a cloud-agent URL, or a pushed branch. Read the metadata overview and last messages first, then scan back for the decision points. Parse a long transcript in a subagent and keep the reduced timeline in the main thread (the **principle-guard-the-context-window** skill). Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section.
2. Reconstruct operational state. The branch and worktree, what already landed (`git log`, `git diff` against the base), the open todos, the decisions made. The prior trail is authoritative input. Resist the bias to re-derive it.
3. Diff done vs pending. Compare what shipped against what was planned, name the resume point, do not re-run the prior repro or redo completed work. A "let me verify from scratch" pass means you're treating the trail as untrustworthy when it's authoritative.
4. Route the remaining work to the matching playbook and pick the verdict: continue the execution, ship a finished recommendation, ratify or override a prior conclusion, or postmortem a failed run. The pickup playbook ends here. The routed playbook owns the rest.
5. Verify the inherited claims against the original goal on the real artifact (the **principle-prove-it-works** skill). A passing prior self-report is not the proof. **Reply:** where the prior agent stopped, what you inherited vs redid (ideally nothing redone), the resume point, and the outcome. --- file: playbooks/shipping.md ---
### Shipping **You own what lands. Verify each PR independently, land only the verified run from the root, then keep your hands off the stack.** 1. **Resolve the forge, then verify each PR independently before it lands.** GitHub CLI (`gh`) is the default. If `command -v origin` succeeds and Origin can resolve the repository, use `origin pr` for every PR operation. Otherwise stay on `gh` and record the fallback. Never require Graphite (`gt`). One verifier per PR, each a Cursor cloud agent, runs the change the way a user would with the matching control skill (such as `control-ui` or `control-cli` from `cursor-team-kit`), parent against head, and posts `PASS`, `PASS+NOTES`, or `FAIL` on that PR. Only a verdict from an agent that did not write the code counts, because an author checks what it meant to build. Green CI and an approving bot review are not verdicts, because neither runs the change as a user would.
2. **Land only the contiguous verified run rooted at the bottom.** Walk up from the lowest unmerged PR and stop at the first one without `PASS` or `PASS+NOTES`. The PRs below it are the run, and the top one is the ceiling. A verified PR above an unverified one waits, because it cannot land without the code below it. One whose branch neither holds nor needs that code can move onto trunk and land on its own. It needs a fresh verdict first, because its old one ran with that code beneath it and trunk does not have it.
3. **Re-check that the verdicts still describe the code.** A verdict covers a patch, and a chain rebase moves every PR above it to a new SHA without failing any check. Compare `git patch-id` at the verdict SHA with the current head before trusting an older verdict. When the patches differ only in tests, docs, or lint config, a lane's result stands if what it ran builds the same at both SHAs apart from noise. Noise is a difference that also shows up between two builds of the verdict SHA, or an embedded commit SHA. Report each kind of noise with its files, so a reader can check the call. The change itself still gets fresh checks and a review, because the old verdict never saw it. A lane with no build output, such as a dev server, cannot show this, so rerun it, and re-verify anything else that drifted.
4. **Land bottom-up, one PR at a time.** Always merge the run's lowest unmerged PR, with `origin pr merge <pr>` or `gh pr merge <pr> --squash`. On Origin the plain command also merges every PR below the one you name, and on GitHub a PR whose base is still its parent's branch merges into that branch, not trunk. Read the PR back for the result (`origin pr view <pr>` or `gh pr view <pr> --json state,mergedAt,baseRefName`), because a merge command can report success when a merge queue only queued the PR, and a requested auto-merge is not a merge. A landed PR reads merged with trunk as its base, not its parent's branch. Arm `--auto` (Origin merge-when-ready or GitHub auto-merge) only on a PR whose verdict covers its current head, because it lands whatever head is ready. After a merge lands, retarget the PR whose base was the merged branch to trunk (`origin pr edit <pr> --base <trunk>` or `gh pr edit <pr> --base <trunk>`), move its patch onto the merge result, and push with `--force-with-lease`. The verdict covers the patch, not its commits, so step 3's patch-id rule decides whether the verdict survives. Merge it once its checks pass and its verdict survives.
5. **Leave the stack alone while it lands.** Step 4's move of the next PR is the only change to a branch or base, because a merge lands whatever its branch and base hold at that moment, verdict or not. On GitHub, watch the run with the queued watcher from `playbooks/babysit.md` (`scripts/watch-pr/watch-pr --queued-stack --stack-prs <bottom-to-top>`) under `/loop` until it reports `COMPLETE` at the ceiling. On Origin, re-read the current PR with `origin pr view <pr> --checks` each time `origin pr checks <pr> --watch` returns, until the ceiling reads merged. A base that moves to trunk when its parent merges is expected, not damage to repair. If a merge stalls, find out why before you change anything.
6. **Stop at the ceiling.** Extending the run takes new verdicts, so it is a new pass through step 1. **Reply:** the verified run and its ceiling, each PR's verdict and who produced it, what landed and how you confirmed it, and what the next gap needs. --- file: playbooks/trace-forensics.md ---
### Trace forensics **You own the diagnosis from the artifact.** Distinct from **Runtime forensics**, which instruments the live process. Here the capture already exists. The artifact is a fixed dataset, read it, don't re-run it. Keep tooling generic: a DevTools or trace parser for cpuprofile and `.json.gz`, a text editor for a spindump, your heap tooling for a heapsnapshot. 1. Identify the format and load it with the right tool. Parse large artifacts in a subagent (the **principle-guard-the-context-window** skill) and keep the reduced finding in the main thread. Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section.
2. Transform the raw artifact into a form you can query. Dump the trace or heap snapshot into sqlite, one row per sample, frame, or node. Reach the queryable shape before you read.
3. Narrow to the cause. Query for the frames that hold the most time and walk the call tree to the hot path. For a leak, follow the retainer chain from the leaked object to a GC root. For a spindump, find the thread stuck on-CPU or blocked and its wait reason.
4. Attribute to source. Map the hot frame to file, symbol, and line via the artifact's own symbols. A frame with no source mapping is not yet a diagnosis. Resolve the symbols, or say plainly the artifact does not carry them.
5. If you have a paired capture, diff the before and after artifacts to confirm. Otherwise, mark the finding as the strongest hypothesis the artifact supports, not a confirmed cause.
6. Hand back a cited diagnosis, no fix unless asked. Route to Bug fix or Perf issue once the cause is known. Throughput checkpoint stays one line: `throughput checkpoint: n/a, read-only forensics`. **Reply:** the artifact and format, the reduced finding, the source location, the artifact paths, and whether a paired capture confirmed it. --- file: playbooks/visual-parity.md ---
### Visual parity **You own pixel-exact equivalence. The baseline is the spec. You do not touch it.** Equivalence is verified by image diff, not by eye. 1. Establish the baseline first, before any migration: a visual regression harness that screenshots the current component across its states, plus the target when matching two implementations. No baseline, no parity claim. A blocking prerequisite, not a follow-up.
2. Anti-shortcut clauses, stated and held: no harness modifications, no baseline tampering, no component restructuring to make a diff pass. If the baseline looks wrong, stop and ask, don't edit it.
3. Migrate one component at a time. Parallelize across worktrees, one owner per component (the **separate-before-serializing-shared-state** principle skill). Shared primitives migrate first as a blocking phase.
4. Verify each component against its baseline via image diff on the matching surface via the control skill. A nonzero diff is a fail. Investigate the pixel delta. `/loop` per component until the diff is zero.
5. Run **Opening a PR** per component or per safe batch. **Reply:** components migrated, the diff result for each, the baseline harness location, what's left. --- file: playbooks/worktree-cleanup.md ---
### Worktree and simulator cleanup 1. Snapshot and audit. Record `df -h /`, then run `scripts/worktree-audit.sh [-b <pr-base-ref>] [repo-path]` (principle-build-the-lever). Without `-b` it checks `MERGED` against `origin/HEAD`, so pass `-b origin/<branch>` when PRs target another branch. It reads paths from `git worktree list`, never hand-typed, since a hand-typed `myrepo-worktrees/x` misses one that lives at `.cursor/worktrees/myrepo/x` (principle-encode-lessons-in-structure). It classifies each worktree by size, age, merge state, uncommitted work, PR state, and the newest chat that touched it, then suggests a bucket. The transcript scan is slow, so background it.
2. The bucket is advice, not permission. The pinned and active chats are the real artifact (principle-prove-it-works). Get that set from the user or sidebar and cross-check every candidate. The lever has marked `safe` a worktree the user had pinned, so the pinned set wins.
3. Verify usage before deleting. For every `verify-recent-chat` row, or anything you doubt, fan subagents out to read the transcripts and report whether the chat is pinned or ongoing and which worktrees it touches (principle-guard-the-context-window, transcripts are bulk). A pinned chat spawns arena and repro trees into sibling worktrees via background subagents, and those are in use even when their names never hit the sidebar. Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section.
4. Pause on irreversible loss. `wip:N` is N tracked uncommitted edits. Show the diff and get a decision first, since removing a clean worktree is recoverable from its branch but uncommitted work is gone. `scratch:N` is untracked throwaway, safe to drop, but name the files. Per Autonomy, clean and merged and not-in-use proceeds. `wip` and in-use pause.
5. Prune the confirmed set. Per path, `git worktree remove --force <path>`. If the dir survives on ignored build artifacts, `rm -rf` it, then `git worktree prune`. Branch refs survive, so no commits are lost. Confirm with `df -h /` and re-list.
6. Simulators and other reclaimers. Simulators are usually the next-biggest win. `xcrun simctl --set testing delete all` (XCTestDevices clones), `xcrun simctl delete unavailable`, and `xcrun simctl runtime list` then `runtime delete <id>` for old runtimes. More when needed: Xcode `DerivedData` and `iOS DeviceSupport`, `~/Library/Application Support/Cursor` (`state.vscdb.backup`, and `snapshots/roots/<root>` where a `<root>` named for a folder you opened as a workspace balloons), package caches (pnpm, uv, brew, yarn). Clear only caches the user has not said to keep. This is the one playbook that deletes user state with no code review to catch a slip, so the gates above are the review. **Reply:** `df -h /` before and after with space reclaimed, the worktrees pruned, and a one-line reason for each held back (in-use by which chat, or uncommitted work). --- file: references/bugbot-triage.md ---
# Bugbot triage Use this reference when the Babysit playbook (`../playbooks/babysit.md`) handles Bugbot or review-automation comments. The goal is not to ignore Bugbot by default. The goal is to stop treating every comment as a required code change. ## Decision rubric Classify each Bugbot thread before acting: - `fix`: The comment identifies a plausible correctness, security, privacy, data loss, auth, billing, migration, idempotency, race, or shipped-behavior issue. Fix it in the lowest owning PR, then reply with the commit SHA and resolve the thread.
- `dismiss`: The comment matches a documented low-risk noisy pattern, and the current code/context proves the concern does not need a code change. Reply with a short reason and resolve the thread.
- `ask`: The comment is novel, high-severity, security/privacy/data-related, or ambiguous. Ask the user instead of guessing. When in doubt, ask. Skipping a noisy code-quality comment is cheap; skipping a real data or security bug is not. ## Learned pattern format Add future patterns in this shape: ```markdown
### <short pattern name> - Confidence: candidate | recurring | strong
- Skip when: <conditions that must be true>
- Do not skip when: <risk boundaries>
- Example signal: <phrases or code context that identify the pattern>
- Source: <PR/comment URL or short historical note>
``` Use `candidate` for one or two examples. Use `recurring` after multiple real dismissals. Use `strong` only when the pattern is narrow, repeatedly verified, and low-risk. ## Recurring skip candidates ### Intentional UI or design-system visual changes - Confidence: candidate
- Skip when: The PR description, screenshots, design review, or nearby code makes the visual change explicit, and the Bugbot comment is only restating that a shared visual default changed.
- Do not skip when: The comment points to accessibility, focus visibility, keyboard navigation, color contrast, or a component API contract that the PR did not intentionally change.
- Example signal: Comments about focus outlines, button sizes, spacing, or shared component visual defaults where the owner replies "intentional" or "intended". ### Upstack or stack-local usage Bugbot cannot see - Confidence: candidate
- Skip when: Bugbot flags an export, component, helper, or file as unused, and the active forge's PR list and diffs, upper-stack diffs, or PR context show it is used by a later PR in the stack.
- Do not skip when: The current PR is not part of a stack, the symbol is public API, or the supposed upstack use cannot be verified.
- Example signal: "Exported component is never used" with a human reply like "used upstack". ### Temporary duplication during parallel implementation - Confidence: candidate
- Skip when: The PR intentionally duplicates a small amount of code to keep a new path parallel to an old path that is being deleted, replaced, or proven out.
- Do not skip when: The duplicated code changes security, billing, data access, API behavior, or a long-lived shared abstraction would clearly reduce risk.
- Example signal: "Significant duplication" or "duplicated validation logic" where the owner explains the old path will be deleted or the duplicate logic is intentionally local. ### Existing framework or component invariant covers the warning - Confidence: candidate
- Skip when: The concern is already guaranteed by a shared component, framework contract, type invariant, or single source of truth visible in the current diff or nearby code.
- Do not skip when: The invariant is assumed but not enforced, depends on timing, or crosses async/state boundaries where values can diverge.
- Example signal: Comments about missing max-height on an inner popover when the shared popover enforces viewport bounds, or nullable values where the local checked value and passed value share the same source. ### Owner-declared follow-up or deferred cleanup - Confidence: candidate
- Skip when: The PR owner explicitly says the issue is a known follow-up, the behavior is not made worse by the current PR, and the comment is not about a high-risk area.
- Do not skip when: The agent is acting without owner input, the issue is medium/high severity product behavior, or deferring would merge a new regression.
- Example signal: "I'll worry about that later" or "we'll delete this eventually". ### Self-withdrawn or explicit false-positive rule comments - Confidence: recurring
- Skip when: The comment body or a later Bugbot reply explicitly says the finding is withdrawn, compliant, or a false positive, and the agent can verify the relevant rule locally.
- Do not skip when: The only evidence is a human saying "false positive" on a high-risk issue without explanation.
- Example signal: A file-naming rule comment whose body says the file is already compliant. ## Ask by default Do not auto-skip these categories, even if a previous PR dismissed something similar: - Security, privacy, auth, billing, data retention, training-data, and permission-boundary findings.
- High-severity findings.
- Migration, schema, idempotency, concurrency, and cross-system behavior findings.
- Comments where the suggested fix is small and clearly reduces risk without changing product intent. Historical data showed humans sometimes dismiss security/data-flow comments. Treat those as owner judgment calls, not team-wide skip rules. ## Candidate learnings from recent babysits Append new candidate learnings here during or after babysitting when they look team-useful but not yet mature. Prefer promoting recurring candidates into the section above once several PRs confirm the pattern. ### Manual reimplementations of native browser behavior - Confidence: candidate
- Skip when: Practically never. When a diff replaces native browser behavior with a manual equivalent (native sticky → JS-positioned clones, native scroll targeting → forwarded wheel/touch events, paint-order occlusion → masks/clip-path), Bugbot's logic-bug findings against that code have been consistently legitimate.
- Do not skip when: The finding concerns event-forwarding gaps (wheel deltaMode, touch pans, scroll-chaining at edges, tap slop), mask/clip hit-testing divergence, or observer-vs-React state timing races in such code. Default to fix.
- Example signal: "masks do not affect hit-testing", "overlay blocks wheel scroll", "ignores deltaMode", "runs in the IntersectionObserver callback before React applies state".
- Source: one sticky-occlusion PR: six Bugbot passes, roughly eighteen findings, every one fixed rather than dismissed. ### Contract-test drift claims are cheaply verifiable - run the test first - Confidence: candidate
- Skip when: Never skip the verification itself; it costs one command. When a PR ships a contract test that pins protocol or documentation prose (regexes over a SKILL.md, snapshot of doc wording), and Bugbot claims "the test no longer matches the doc" (or vice versa), run that test on the PR tip before classifying. A red run confirms the claim empirically; a green run is a concrete disproof for the dismissal reply.
- Do not skip when: n/a - this is a verification shortcut, not a dismissal pattern. Note that repeat-pass lean-dismiss heuristics would misfire here: prose-pinning tests drift precisely BECAUSE earlier fix rounds edit the prose.
- Example signal: "Contract test omits the pre-fix wait" on a PR whose earlier fix commits reworded the pinned passage; the test run on the tip failed on exactly the cited assertion.
- Source: one prose-pinning PR with eight Bugbot passes; the claim was real on pass 7 despite every earlier pass being fixed-and-resolved. ### Stale security-review finding already fixed later in the same PR - Confidence: candidate
- Skip when: An agentic security review (or similar) claims a missing authz/validation call, and the current PR tip clearly includes that exact gate (with tests), typically added in a later hardening commit after the review ran.
- Do not skip when: The cited helper is a no-op for the principal under discussion, the check runs after the side effect it guards, or coverage for the claimed principal is missing.
- Example signal: A HIGH "missing authorization check" finding while the exact guard is already called before the side effect on the tip.
- Source: one webhook-endpoint PR whose hardening commit postdated the review run. ### Widening a deliberately narrow error condition would mask the real error - Confidence: candidate
- Skip when: The finding asks to broaden a narrow error condition (a specific `errno`, error code, or status class) into a catch-all, and that narrowness encodes a real distinction. The canonical shape is a dependency fallback gated on `ENOENT`: "binary is not installed" is a different situation from "the command ran and failed". Retrying on any non-zero exit would re-run a legitimate failure (not found, expired auth, network) against the fallback and then report the fallback's error, hiding the true one.
- Do not skip when: The narrow condition misses a case in the SAME category (another "binary unusable" errno such as `EACCES`, another transport-level failure), the unhandled path loses data or leaves partial state, or the retry is idempotent AND the original error is still surfaced.
- Example signal: "only retries when X fails with ENOENT … never tries the fallback even when a working Y exists", pointing at code whose fallback exists for a missing dependency rather than a failed operation.
- Source: one CLI-rename PR whose fallback existed for a missing binary rather than a failed command. --- file: scripts/bootstrap.ts ---

skills.name: pre-draft-check
skills.description: Use before showing the user any draft text, email, or message to a real person (lead, client, parent, vendor), or before booking anyone. Verify the recipient, plan term, recent calls and texts, times, and facts live first.
skills.instructions:
# Pre-draft check The user approves what they are shown, so the draft itself must be right before it reaches them. ## Step 0: run the script first 1. Make a fresh folder for this run: `/workspace/predraft-test/--/`. Never reuse another bot's folder. 2. Save the draft there, and use your own connectors to export: the contact/prospect Sheet rows; Gmail and Quo messages with this person (sent or received only, no unsent drafts; Quo plain text is fine). Main Quo inbox is PNBNkklRXP. Include recent calls and texts yourself from Quo and Gmail (and Numa notification emails in work Gmail if texts still route there); never ask the user whether someone called or texted. Also export busy blocks from ALL calendars (Achieve, where evals live, plus Personal and Work) for every offered day. 3. Run: `python3 /home/box/agent-data/shared/scripts/chief/pre_draft_check.py --contacts --touches --busy --kind email|text|ad [--mode confirm] --workdir ` [REDACTED paragraph: parent_child_or_family_with_person] ## Judgment checks the script can't make 1. **Gmail signature (create_draft).** Connector-made Gmail drafts do **not** get the signature added automatically. Every email draft saved to Drafts must end with "Thanks," then the full signature block typed in, matching his sent mail: "Ryne Gioviano, MSEd, CSCS / Owner, Achieve Sports Performance & Personal Training / www.achievesportsperformance.com / (blank line) / For scheduling or account questions: / contact@achieve-personaltraining.com | Text: 630.340.4114". Pass both a plain-text body with blank lines between paragraphs and an htmlBody in Gmail style: each paragraph in a `
`, then `

` after the greeting, between paragraphs, after "Thanks," and before "For scheduling..."; each signature line in its own `
`. Never use bare `

` tags for spacing (they collapse in Gmail). 2. **Client status and plan term.** State whether the person is a current client, a former client, or a lead, how often they come in now (or used to), and their plan term when it matters (annual, 12-month, month-to-month, or none). Read status and plan term from Mindbody, the prospect/contact Sheet, recent messages, or the live contract yourself; never ask the user and never guess. Write the draft for that status (a former client is a win-back, not a stranger). 3. **Last channel.** Find how they last reached the user (text or email) and draft in that channel unless the user said otherwise. Name it when you show the draft. 4. **Recipient.** Partial names ("Holly L.") or anything the script couldn't match. 5. **Recent touches (calls and texts).** Look up Quo and Gmail yourself. If there is a message to or from this person in the last 48 hours or since the draft was written, decide whether to drop or rewrite. Never ask the user "did they call?" or "did they text?" 6. **Times.** Offered times must fit real coaching hours and still be open right now. Re-read the calendar; don't reuse times from an older draft. Check by hand any time the script marks NOT CHECKED (no day or no am/pm). 7. **Who they are.** Never call someone a parent (or say "your son/daughter") unless the sheet, its Comments, or one of their messages confirms it. Otherwise write to the person neutrally. 8. **Prices.** No price, fee, or package amount unless it was read from the live source today; name that source. Standing rule: no prices in first-touch or inbound replies (Achieve lead emails may include one "Pricing starts at $X/mo" line when that policy applies). 9. **Age.** A draft older than 48 hours is re-checked or dropped. 10. **Facts and tone** are right for this person. Only state what was confirmed; never credit a source with more than it said (see Cite or label). When you show the draft, put one line above it: status (current/former/lead, how often, plan term if known), last channel, and that the signature block is included for Gmail drafts. ## Relayed approvals When Chief or Dr. Eggbot relays an approval that quotes the user's words, treat it as the user's yes. Do not ask the user to reconfirm that same approval. ## Bookings (any scheduling system) - Do not book until the user confirms the named person and slot. - After booking, re-open the roster or schedule and confirm name, date, and time; report what you read back. ## Stop condition If the script or any check fails, do not present the draft as ready. Show it as **HELD** with the one-line reason (for example "phone does not match sheet", "she replied 10/17", "offered time passed", "client status unknown", "plan term unknown").

skills.name: pri-breathing-exercise-selection
skills.description: Use when choosing Achieve breathing, PRI repositioning, or warm-up/tertiary exercises from Left AIC / Right BC / PEC findings, especially for swimmers and overhead athletes. Open the PRI course and handout skills linked below for expert-depth theory, tests, decision trees, and hierarchies.
skills.instructions:
# PRI breathing exercise selection Full source: `/home/box/agent-data/shared/sc-reference/pri-breathing-exercise-selection.txt` (Ryne Gioviano, *PRI Foundations for the Strength Coach*). ## Core idea
Humans are asymmetrical. Fix pelvis/ribcage position **before** loading. Breathing/PRI sits early in the warm-up so we don't squat a flared, extended frame. ## Patterns to recognize
- **Left AIC:** left hemi-pelvis anterior/forward, mass on right; hard to shift into left AF IR. Look for right foot turn-out, right-biased stance, limited left adduction drop.
- **Right BC:** right lat / apical restriction; limited left trunk rotation/sidebend; common in swimmers with overworked lats.
- **PEC:** bilateral extension bias; limited trunk rotation both ways; hard toe-touch / SLR. Red flags (inform warm-up/tertiary, don't diagnose): can't toe-touch, heels-up squat, SLR <90°, limited shoulder IR, limited trunk rotation, left adduction drop fail, obvious right weight shift. ## Repositioning menu (coach these)
| Exercise | Objective |
|---|---|
| 90/90 Hip Lift w/ Balloon | Inhibit Left AIC, restore ZOA, inhibit Right BC/lat |
| Left Sidelying Left Flexed Adduction | Left IC adductor + right abductor (frontal plane) |
| Retro Stairs | Left glute med / Left AF IR |
| Standing Resisted Wall Reach | Serratus, thoracic flexion, lat inhibition | Still generally **one** athlete-specific technique at warm-up and end of session (same drill). Very patterned or in-pain athletes may get a second warm-up-only drill. ### Standing Serratus Squat vs Standing Wall Press with L PME
Pick from Postural Respiration lists - do not paraphrase as "stiff mid-back." - **Standing Serratus Squat** (Anterior Neck Inhibition list, p.76; also filed under L LT/L Serratus and L PME): forward head, neck that won't relax on reaches, limited horizontal abduction or cervical rotation. Script (appendix p.18): face wall, elbows at shoulder height bent 90°, press elbows into wall, round/tuck, squat until knees touch the wall, heels down, 4-5 breaths filling the upper back ×5.
- Platt rule of thumb (appendix p.52): right intercostal work ≈ frontal plane; left posterior mediastinum ≈ transverse plane. ## Squat breathing variations
1. Partial exhale down, full exhale up - weaker abs / heavier loads
2. Exhale down, hold 1-3 breaths at bottom, exhale up - extension breathers / PEC-Right BC
3. Inhale down, exhale up - earned; established ZOA only Detail and Left AIC/PEC rationale: open [PRI The Squat and Respiration](sand-workflow:pri-squat-and-respiration). ## Programming link
- Pair extension-heavy strength with a flexion/reach or breathing check (e.g. trap-bar + serratus/child's-pose breathing).
- Swimmers: every program needs some squat-and-reach / wall-reach work, lat inhibition, serratus + subscap focus - not cuff isolation alone.
- Success isn't only bar weight; can they keep neutrality (toe-touch / SLR) after training?
- Lift order after restoration gates: [Fitness and Movement](sand-workflow:fitness-and-movement). ## Deep PRI course references (open when …) Use this skill for day-of Achieve breathing/tertiary picks. Open the matching skill when you need expert-level discussion, test interpretation, inhibit/facilitate tables, hierarchies, or decision trees: | Open | When |
|---|---|
| [PRI Pelvis Restoration](sand-workflow:pri-pelvis-restoration) | Pelvic inlet/outlet, pelvic diaphragm, PADT/PART, PEC vs Patho PEC, IS instability, hemibridge/adductor pull-back/wall-reach course selection. Gate: **− ADT / + PADT** (or bilateral −/+ ) → Pelvis. |
| [PRI Postural Respiration](sand-workflow:pri-postural-respiration) | ZOA, Right BC, PEC thorax, apical expansion, lat/intercostal/paraspinal inhibition, neuromotor order overview. |
| [PRI Right BC Treatment Guidelines](sand-workflow:pri-right-bc-treatment-guidelines) | Right BC **test cluster + decision tree**: when to progress R low trap/tricep vs L low trap/serratus vs R serratus vs R subscap; Superior T4 / Subclavius / Infraclavicular clinician paths; ZOA NM entry list. |
| [PRI The Squat and Respiration](sand-workflow:pri-squat-and-respiration) | Squat descent/ascent breathing variants; when inhale-on-descent is earned; Left AIC / PEC pelvic-rib setup under load. |
| [PRI Swimming An In-Depth Look](sand-workflow:pri-swimming-in-depth) | PRI swim pattern (PEC + L AIC/R BC), stroke pathomechanics, dryland implications (freestyle/fly/back/breast). Not pool ISO angles. |
| [PRI Primary Non-Manual Techniques Workshop](sand-workflow:pri-non-manual-techniques-workshop) | Technique selection, reference/referent cueing, position ladders, workshop technique cards. |
| [PRI Impingement and Instability](sand-workflow:pri-impingement-instability) | Positional vs primary impingement; multi-directional instability grading; calcaneal/knee/FA/HG/scapular-thoracic tables; subscapularis vs lat IR; secondary course after intros. |
| [Swim turn and start ISO angles](sand-workflow:swim-turn-and-start-iso-angles) | Pool-transfer ISO joint angles for flip/open turn or start (separate from PRI swim dryland skill). | **Course chain:** Myokinematic (AF/FA) → Pelvis (inlet/outlet hold) → Postural Respiration (ZOA/thorax) → Right BC guidelines (thorax decision tree) → Impingement & Instability (joints that still impinge or go unstable). # PRI Impingement & Instability (course skill) **Source (full text):** `/home/box/agent-data/shared/sc-reference/pri-impingement-instability.txt` *(OCR from scanned PDF - Prefer cross-checking exercise titles against Postural Respiration clean appendix when OCR is noisy. Host copy notes Achieve / James Anderson June 2019.)* **Manual:** *Impingement & Instability* (PRI, © 2007-2019). **Course level:** Secondary / advanced relative to Myokinematic, Pelvis, and Postural Respiration intros. --- ## 1. Core theory / asymmetry model (this course) ### Positional impingement ≠ primary (shape) impingement
PRI definitions (manual "PRI Concepts of Impingement and Instability"):
- Impingement here is **not** attributed primarily to abnormalities of the shape of long bones/articulating surfaces. - It reflects **occult dynamic instability** from **malaligned structural position/orientation**. - It reflects **Left AIC and Right BC patterns of compensation**. - Assessed/addressed with PRI approaches. Symptoms can mimic primary impingement, but **positional impingement** is different. Traditional conservative/operative approaches aimed at assumed primary impingement often failed until the **patterned instability** (Left AIC/Right BC unilateral dominance, habit, consistent hand/foot usage) was addressed first - then impingement resolved secondarily. ### Instability framing (Position vs Primary table)
**Frequency**
- Acute - maintain neutral position - Recurrent - reposition and immediately address joint internal rotation - Chronic - after repositioning, maximize with **Right AIC / Left BC** tri-planar neuromotor strength and skills **Etiology:** atraumatic positional patterns → retrain opposition muscles of Left AIC/Right BC after repositioning (PRI non-manual or manual). Distinguish microtraumatic/repetitive, voluntary/involuntary, traumatic macro, congenital (primary column). **Direction**
- Unidirectional - see PRI pathology table; **1 PRI test per girdle joint is negative** - Bidirectional - **2 PRI tests negative** per girdle joint in different planes - Multidirectional - **2+ PRI tests negative** per girdle joint in **2+ planes** **Degree:** subluxation refers to FA, HG, MT joints (vs dislocation on primary side). Patient volition: involuntary as produced by PRI examiner vs voluntary. ### Biomechanical treatment considerations of impingement (Position vs Primary)
Position column examples: capsular malalignment; proximal aligned control; compensatory bony impact secondary to unorganized triplanar unilateral overactivity; poor strength secondary to improper muscle attachment position; generated force from inappropriate muscle (dyssynchrony). Primary column: capsular stiffness; joint degeneration; malformation of arthrokinetic surfaces; weakness of antagonistic/agonistic force couples; poor timing (asynchrony). ### Pitfalls to stabilization rehabilitation (manual list)
Failure to address pain/hypomobility; failure to follow progression steps; failure to ensure proper patterns of movement; failure to ensure proper muscle firing sequences; allowing incorrect movement patterns; failure to understand mechanics of selected movements; failure to understand demands of patient's functional activities; failure to involve the whole (pattern), etc. ### Overview table - possible I&I associated with Left AIC / Right BC
Examples (RIGHT vs LEFT columns in manual):
- Hallux limitus (active R / passive L) - Ankle inversion sprains (R) vs talocalcaneal instability (L) - Anterior medial knee instability (R; ↑ valgum → lateral knee strain) vs lateral knee instability (L; ↑ varum → medial knee strain) - Anteromedial FA impingement (R) vs anterosuperior AF impingement (L) - Laterosuperior FA impingement / AF multidirectional instability themes - Ilio-sacral mechanical vs pathomechanic instability - Superior posterior humeral glenoid impingement; HG multidirectional instability; humeral acromial impingement - Thoracic-sternal instability; SLAP lesions (especially if full HG IR exists) - L4/L5/S1 instability notes Unilateral idiopathic indicators listed early: hip (AF or FA) impingement / iliosacral pain; posterior superior ilio-lateral (QL) "tightness"; ear fullness or preference. --- ## 2. Patterns to recognize (I&I lens) ### Left AIC / Right BC remains the patterned engine
I&I assumes the intro patterns. When neutrality is intermittent or tests go negative in multiple planes, joints express **impingement on the compressed side** and **instability on the unsupported side** of the same patterned system. ### Foot / ankle / calcaneal
Agenda: Left AIC foot and ankle pattern; PEC foot and ankle; calcaneal instability; frontal-plane calcaneal stability. Calcaneal eversion programs appear in snapping-hip / FA instability hierarchies when frontal-plane FA instability couples to calcaneus. ### Knee
Genu hyperextension instability; anterior medial vs lateral knee instability paired to Right vs Left pattern columns. ### Hip / groin / FA-AF
Hip and groin impingement lab; anteromedial FA vs anterosuperior AF; multidirectional FA instability; snapping hip syndrome (lateral FA instability secondary to long/weak glute med/min - femoral head migrates; often left; clicks with FA IR/ER more than AF). ### Ilio-sacral
Ilium stability depends on position/efficiency of iliacus, glute med/min, biceps femoris, adductor brevis, pectineus - stabilize ilium during contralateral swing; sagittal/frontal force closure for acetabulum-on-femur. Poor iliacus/pectineus-adductor position → reduced ilium stability; ground forces facilitate superior-posterior sacral advancement (ilio-sacral internal rotation) → unilateral lordosis themes (cross-ref Pelvis Restoration). ### Scapular-thoracic / HG
Scapula-thoracic instability; Hruska classification of scapular resting position; superior posterior HG impingement when patterned IR is forced (links to Postural Respiration Right BC humeral test position warning); multidirectional HG instability; need **subscapularis** for true HG IR after lat/pec pathways are inhibited. ### Right AIC / Left BC frontal-plane view
Manual includes Right AIC / Left BC posterior frontal-plane figures (left thoracic abduction / right thoracic adduction language) - the flip side after successful inhibition of Left AIC/Right BC, used when maximizing chronic instability rehab. --- ## 3. Assessment themes I&I uses intro PRI tests as the language of "how many tests are negative per girdle joint / how many planes" to grade unidirectional vs multi-directional instability. **Examples of clinical clusters (OCR treatment pages):**
- + Left ADT; decreased/limited Left FA IR; medial tibial plateau pain with medial footwear issues → orthotic/footwear notes; achieve bilateral Adduction and Abduction Lift scores ≥3; maximize Right AF ER; balance hamstrings with left medial hamstring focus; standing supported Left AF IR with right FA abduction integration. - Snapping hip test results themes: ↑ passive FA abduction; limited active FA abduction strength; ipsilateral Adduction Lift >3 / Abduction Lift findings → hierarchy below. **Hruska Classification of Scapular Resting Position & Testing** - appendix item on Day 2 agenda; use when scapular-thoracic instability is the complaint after thorax neutrality attempts. --- ## 4. Inhibit vs facilitate (how I&I uses intro tables) Same composite facilitate/inhibit tables as intros. I&I-specific emphasis:
- After repositioning, **facilitate opposition muscles of Left AIC / Right BC** - Chronic: build **Right AIC / Left BC** tri-planar capacity - HG IR: facilitate **right subscapularis**, **not** right latissimus or pec major (explicit treatment guideline language) - Scapular-thoracic: Right low trap/tricep → Left low trap/serratus → Right serratus → Right subscapularis (same neuromotor order as Postural Respiration; I&I applies it when instability/impingement persist) --- ## 5. Repositioning / treatment hierarchies (selected) ### General order philosophy
1. Reposition (intro non-manual/manual as needed) 2. Ensure PRI tests support neutrality 3. Address joint IR and opposition strength 4. Progress plane-by-plane; do not skip firing-sequence steps 5. Integrate upright reciprocal alternating activity only when tests stay negative ### Snapping hip hierarchy (manual)
1. Reposition 2. Ipsilateral Adduction and Abduction Lift scores of 3 or better with contralateral obturator foramen / ischium sense; consider sidelying supported left medial and posterior expansion with ipsilateral hip flexor inhibition; sidelying lateral thoracic expansion with balloon / intercostal inhibition to allow glute med shortening 3. For left frontal/transverse FA instability maximize left calcaneal eversion; for right, right calcaneal eversion (Calcaneal Eversion Programs) 5. Left stance upright integration / right stance upright integration activities ### Knee / medial tibial / Left FA IR cluster hierarchy themes
Achieve bilateral lift tests ≥3; maximize Right AF ER strength/control; balance hamstrings (left medial hamstring appendix); Standing Supported Left AF IR with Right FA Abduction (Integration). ### Ilio-sacral instability
Restore iliacus / glute med-min / biceps femoris / adductor brevis / pectineus positional efficiency; do not chase sacral symptoms without swing-phase ilium force closure. ### Right BC PRI treatment guidelines (I&I application)
- Right apical expansion family (including Mermaid variant with left arm reach + left adductor) - Seated resisted alternating tricep pull-downs - Seated right scapular pull-back with right HG - If tests return + after upright alternating → regress ### Right BC position progression (overview page - mirrors Postural)
Right low trap & right tricep → Left low trap & left serratus → Right serratus → Right subscapularis, with supine/sidelying/seated/standing/all-four/prone position ladders. ### Right subscapularis program themes
Supine resisted right HG IR; supine resisted right tricep extension with right HG IR; sidelying trunk lift variants; seated resisted pull-downs with right HG IR and left HG ER. Explicit rule: **facilitate right HG IR with right subscapularis, not lat or pec major.** ### Example upright integration titles appearing in I&I
- Standing Resisted Right Diagonal Flexion - Left Stance in Left AF IR from Left AIC pattern (right arm reach, head slightly right, inhale nose / exhale reach) - Right medial hamstring program (left sidelying supported right glute max with right hip extension and right FA IR; TFL inhibition variants; standing wall-supported Left AF IR with knee flexion and right trunk rotation; prone right hip extension with FA IR/ER) --- ## 6. What NOT to do / common errors - Do **not** treat positional impingement as primary bony "spurs first" without clearing Left AIC/Right BC patterning. - Do **not** strengthen into the patterned IR with lat-dominated HG IR - that feeds superior posterior HG impingement mechanics. - Do **not** skip progression steps or allow incorrect firing sequences (listed pitfalls). - Do **not** call multidirectional instability "core weakness" without counting **how many PRI tests are negative across planes**. - Do **not** jump to chronic Right AIC/Left BC max strength before acute/recurrent repositioning + IR restoration. - Do **not** ignore foot/calcaneal frontal-plane pieces when FA frontal-plane instability keeps returning. - Do **not** use I&I as a first course - intros first (Myokinematic / Pelvis / Postural). --- ## 7. How courses link | Stage | Course |
|---|---|
| Unlock AF/FA & Left AIC LE tests | [Myokinematic Restoration](sand-workflow:pri-myokinematic-restoration) |
| Inlet/outlet & pelvic diaphragm hold | [Pelvis Restoration](sand-workflow:pri-pelvis-restoration) |
| ZOA / Right BC / PEC thorax | [Postural Respiration](sand-workflow:pri-postural-respiration) |
| When neutrality exists intermittently but joints impinge or go multi-directionally unstable; scapular-thoracic & HG IR details; calcaneal/knee/FA/IS tables | **This course** | Postural Respiration treatment guidelines explicitly route "all BC tests − but insufficient right scapular-thoracic function" toward BC manuals (Infraclavicular Pump, Sibson, Intercostal) and right serratus - that is the doorway into I&I thinking for the upper quarter. --- ## 8. Achieve programming translation - Overhead/swim athletes with lat-dominant IR and scapular winging after breathing work → subscapularis + serratus + low trap order; inhibit lat. - Recurrent groin/hip "impingement" language from athletes → screen ADT/FA IR/AF IR and pattern before loading deep flexion IR under load. - Medial knee / footwear complaints with Left AIC → lift-test gates + Left AF IR integration; don't only strengthen VMO. - Keep I&I as the "why the joint keeps yelling after intros" reference, not the first warm-up picker - start with [PRI breathing exercise selection](sand-workflow:pri-breathing-exercise-selection) then the matching intro skill. Open the full OCR reference for complete pathology tables, calcaneal programs, and appendix exercise numbers.
