- Lumbar/thoracic flexion with abs + breathing (e.g. Standing Wall Supported Reach) - Glute control in that flexed position - Reciprocal trunk rotation once sagittal flexion holds (e.g. All Four Belly Lift Reach - serratus as goal exercise) - Subscap without lat dominance for HG control - Lateral chest wall / lat / hip flexor flexibility ### Butterfly
Strongest **PEC** demand (no rotation; head/trunk extension for breath + dolphin). Painful shoulders: wider hand entry, ↓ serratus at entry, ↓ subscap/teres minor; lat/pec unchanged but serratus down throughout. [REDACTED paragraph: custom_skill_person_names_unsure] ### Backstroke
Face out (less respiratory hold demand) but **subscap + teres minor** become power muscles (~30% less lat EMG than those). Main risk: anterior instability / impingement if inadequate body roll at entry → humeral hyperextension. Limited cervical axial rotation (R BC/PEC) limits thoracic roll under a still head. [REDACTED paragraph: custom_skill_person_names_unsure] ### Breaststroke
Least shoulder complaints (hands stay forward; less hyper-extension/rotation demand). Unique issue: **breaststroker's knee** (MCL / PF / pes) - correlated with more hip abduction / less FA IR in whip kick. Freestyle mileage predisposes anterior pelvis / limited FA IR-adduction → compensatory ER/abd → medial knee stress. [REDACTED paragraph: custom_skill_person_names_unsure] --- ## 5. Starts, turns, streamline (dryland implications) | Demand | PRI lens | Dryland note |
|---|---|---|
| Start | Needs full thoracic/lumbar flexion without losing glute/leg power | If uncomfortable → paraspinal release / flexion family first |
| Flip turn | Like Full Functional Squat tuck | Can't Functional Squat → slow/loose flip + weak push |
| Touch turn (fly/breast) | Same tucked squat + turn direction | Train Reverse / Full Functional Squat family |
| Streamline | Full HG flexion, arms by head, neutral head | Extension + poor scap position = impingement risk; restricted lat limits streamline → Latissimus Hang Stretch + pelvic position | For **ISO angles** on wall/block transfer, use swim-turn-and-start-iso-angles. For **exercise banks / volume by stroke / starts power menu**, use swim-dryland-programming. --- ## 6. What NOT to do - Band pull-aparts / cuff isolation as the only "swim shoulder" fix while thorax is PEC/Right BC. - Feed more lat pull volume on dryland without serratus / subscap / flexion opposition. - Ignore unilateral breath preference as "just preference" - check trunk/cervical rotation. - Treat breaststroker's knee with only local knee care - check FA IR / pelvic position. - Confuse this skill with pool ISO angle selection or the Achieve dryland stroke playbook. --- ## 7. Achieve programming translation Every swim program needs some combination of:
- Flexion / wall-supported reach / squat-reach (ZOA + PEC opposition) - Lat / intercostal / paraspinal inhibition - Serratus + subscap progressions after neutrality language - Glute + hamstring opposition to kick-driven hip flexors - Stroke-biased extras: fly → more PEC inhibition + LT squat; back → LT/tricep rotation + HG IR without lat; breast → FA IR / adductor-glute med Warm-up early; pair extension-heavy land lifts with reach/exhale checks. Open Right BC guidelines when L horiz abd / R apical / R HG IR drive exercise choice; open I&I when neutrality exists but ST/IR still fail. Open [Swim dryland programming](sand-workflow:swim-dryland-programming) for starts/turns/UW loading and in-season constraints.

skills.name: pri-techniques-by-pattern
skills.description: Use when choosing a PRI restoration technique. Pick the pattern first (Patho PEC, PEC, Left AIC, Right BC), then the earliest position that pattern has earned. Not for Fitness and Movement lifts.
skills.instructions:
# PRI techniques by pattern and position Full step scripts live in the source file this skill was built from. Open the pattern section, then the earliest position. Pattern pick: Patho PEC if they can toe-touch or deep-squat and bilateral ADT and PADT are positive. PEC if bilateral extension and they cannot toe-touch (opening drills stay in the PEC skill). Left AIC uses supine then sidelying, and the non-responder block here only if 90-90 does not change them. Right BC subscap sheets only after a left zone of apposition, and only if apical expansion is not still asymmetric (left low trap and serratus first when it is). Core opening scripts (90-90 hemibridge, 90-90 balloon, right sidelying left adductor, left sidelying right glute max, hemi 90-90, standing wall reach, modified all-four belly lift, wall squat with balloon) stay in Left AIC, PEC, Patho PEC, and Right BC. Injury gates, not new protocols: shoulder impingement or instability keeps left IO/TA and uses subscapularis not lat, and only after the thorax gate. Hip pain on a patho screen starts in Patho PEC, not glute med. Hip OA can muddy ADT, PART, and PADT. SI pain still uses the toe-touch gate. Low back has no dedicated ladder. Do not invent one. Neck and thoracic outlet manual branches stay out of the gym. Knee and ankle are not their own menu. Swim and overhead IR is subscap after the thorax is neutral. [REDACTED paragraph: custom_skill_person_names_unsure] The numbered steps below are the 2012 technique sheets, wording kept. ## Left AIC non-responder order
All four posterior mediastinum, then wall squat with right apical expansion, then short-seated left arm reach (balloon, then no balloon), then kneeling bar reach, then standing resisted alternating reach, then forward walking reach, then late left stance with right arm reach. Not the first block of a normal Left AIC session. 1. Hands and knees, 1-inch towel under the left knee.
2. Round the spine and roll the pelvis so the bottom tucks.
3. Inhale through the nose and gently press down with both arms, filling the left upper back.
4. Exhale and hold.
5. 4-5 breaths, fill the left upper back on each inhale.
6. Relax and repeat 4 more times. Heels 7-10 inches from the wall. 4-6 inch ball between the knees. Bottom on the wall, slight knee bend, pelvic tilt, low back flat. Squeeze the ball, inhale. Exhale and reach both arms forward. Then exhale and reach only the right arm, inhale into the back of the chest, exhale and reach the right arm further, one more breath. Then inhale and reach the left arm, exhale and hold. Inhale and reach the left arm further and slightly right so the nose is over the right knee, weight on the left, left outside hip on. Repeat that once. Stand up still shifted left. Relax and repeat the whole sequence 4 more times. Reference: left abs, left heel, right arch. ### Short seated: Wall Short Seated Left Arm Reach with Balloon
1. Sit, mid to low back flat on the wall, legs straight.
2. Balloon in the right hand.
3. Knees to the chest, one leg at a time.
4. Inhale and reach the left hand forward. Right mid back stays on the wall. Left mid back may come forward.
5. Exhale into the balloon.
6. Pause 3 seconds, tongue on the roof of the mouth.
7. Do not pinch the balloon. Inhale and reach the left hand further, filling the back of the chest.
8. Exhale into the balloon again.
9. 4-5 breaths, further left reach on each inhale.
10. Relax and repeat 4 more times.
Reference: left abs, left sit bone, left heel, right arch. ### Short seated: Wall Short Seated Left Arm Reach (no balloon)
Same wall sit. Knees to the chest, knees together, feet slightly apart, no outward rotation. Inhale. Exhale and reach both arms, back on the wall from bra-line to belt-line, pause 3 seconds. Then inhale and reach only the left hand, right mid back flat, left mid back may come forward. Exhale and hold 3 seconds. Further left reach on the next inhale. 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Kneeling: Kneeling Bar Reach
1. On the knees, bar in front, pillows under the bottom if needed.
2. Roll the pelvis back, back rounds.
3. Hold 4-5 breaths, fill the upper back on the inhale.
4. Relax and repeat 4 more times. ### Standing: Standing Resisted Alternating Respiratory Reach
Tubing anchored behind, both hands, arms at shoulder level. Left hip back, weight on the left midfoot and heel, left outside hip on. Inhale and reach the left arm, fill the left upper back. Exhale and reach the right arm. Repeat 4-5 breaths. Then the same with the right hip back and the right arch down. Repeat 4 more times. Tubing in each hand, resistance behind. Look straight ahead. Left hip back, inhale, left arm and right leg forward, fill the left upper back. Exhale, right foot down, right hip back. Inhale, right arm and left leg forward, fill the right upper back. Exhale, left foot down. Walk 10 steps. Repeat 2 more times. ### Standing: Late Left AIC Stance with Right Arm Reach
Left foot on a 1-inch block, right leg behind. Round the back, look ahead. Right hip forward or left hip back, weight on the left midfoot and heel, right heel down, left knee slightly bent, chin and zipper over the left foot. Left thigh and left outside hip on. Right arm up, left arm down, sidebend left, left abs on, stretch in the right chest. Inhale and exhale while reaching the right arm forward and up, 4-5 breaths, fill the right chest on the inhale. Repeat 4 more times. ## Patho PEC step 2
After 90-90 Hip Lift in Passive FA IR with Balloon. Standing, then all four, then seated. Before Left AIC facilitation. ### Standing: Wall Supported Passive FA IR with Balloon
Ball between the knees, feet 7-10 inches from the wall and wider than the hips. Pelvic tilt, low back flat, upper back off the wall. Inhale, blow into the balloon, pause 3 seconds, tongue up. Inhale again without pinching, upper back expands. Blow again. No neck or cheek strain. After the fourth inhale, pinch the balloon and let the air out. On the last exhale, stand through the heels with the low back flat. Repeat 4 more times. ### Standing: Wall and Chair Supported IO/TA
Same wall and ball, hands on a chair, look ahead. Low back and mid back flat, upper back off. Inhale. Exhale and press the hands into the chair. Front of thighs and outer abs on. Inhale and relax the hands but keep the abs on. Upper back expands. 4-5 breaths. Stand through the heels on the last exhale. Repeat 4 more times. ### Standing squat: Squatting Bar Reverse Reach
Wooden pole across a door frame. Best squat with heels down and knees inside the elbows, bottom of the pelvis toward the heel cords. Inhale through the nose into the back of the chest, eyes level. Exhale and lean back until the air is out. 3 to 4 more breaths. Heel cords, front of thighs, and back muscles stay soft. After the fourth inhale, exhale and stand, pushing through the heels, back rounded, pole slides up the frame. Repeat 4 more times. Goal is the pole at the ankle, elbows straight, knees in the chest, pelvis on the heel cords (PRI squat level four or five). Once that is honest, after the fourth inhale reach forward on the exhale so the pole leaves the frame, and stand while still reaching. A 1 inch by 4 foot pole, pipe insulation for cushion. ### All four: All Four Belly Lift (non-modified)
Hands and knees, back rounded. Knees off the mat so they are straight. Weight forward, nose over the fingertips, outer abs on. Shift left and lift the right hand slightly, left abs on, 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. The sheet also allows the other side: shift right and lift the left hand. ### Seated: Seated Bar Reach
Chair, feet flat, knees at or slightly above the hips. Bar on the outside of a door frame, hands slightly below shoulder level. Inhale, exhale, round the back, take up slack, pelvis rolled back. Stretch across the back. Hold 4-5 breaths, fill the back of the chest. Repeat 4 more times. ## Right BC after the thorax gate
Position order when the cluster is clear: supine, sidelying, seated, prone, standing. Do not start these while apical expansion is still asymmetric. Three Point Stance is unsided. The QL stretch is not a low-back protocol. ### Supine: Supine Resisted Right HG IR
Back, knees bent, arms at shoulder level on bolsters, elbows 90. Tubing from above the right hand into both hands. Left thumb toward the body. Right palm toward the body. Shoulder blades down and together. Straighten the right elbow against the tubing. Then turn the right hand down toward the mat. Front of the right shoulder on. Hold 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Supine: Supine Resisted Right HG IR with Weighted Left HG ER
Tubing above the right arm, weight in the left hand, arms on bolsters, elbows 90. Left hand on the mat, right hand toward the ceiling. Blades down, elbows into the bolsters. Turn the right hand down and lift the left hand until they match. Front of right shoulder and back of left shoulder. Hold 4-5 breaths. Lower back to start. Repeat 4 more times. ### Supine: Supine Resisted Right Tricep Extension with Right HG IR
Same bolster setup. Tubing knotted above the right hand, both hands in the loop. Blades down, palms toward the feet. Left hand stable. Straighten the right elbow. Then turn the right hand toward the mat. Back of the right shoulder blade and arm, then front of the right shoulder. Hold 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Supine: Supine Resisted Right HG IR with Left HG ER
Tubing above the right arm and below the left. Arms on bolsters, elbows 90. Blades down, elbows into the bolsters. Right hand down, left hand up. Front of right shoulder, back of left shoulder. Hold 4-5 breaths. Return. Repeat 4 more times. ### Sidelying: Left Sidelying Weighted Right HG IR with Left FA IR
Left side, knees bent, head on pillows. Bolster under the left side and the right elbow. Weight in the right hand, elbow 90. Push the left hip down so the left abs leave the towel. Right blade down and back, right arm to shoulder level. Right knee ahead and turned up, right outside hip on. Right hand turns up, back of the right shoulder blade on. Left knee turns up toward the right, left inner thigh on. Inhale, then exhale and turn the right hand down. Inhale up, exhale down, 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Sidelying: Left Sidelying Resisted Right HG IR
Left side, back on the wall, knees bent. Tubing above the head. Bolster under the left side, pillows under the head. Right arm at shoulder level in the tubing. Left hip down, left abs off the towel. Right knee ahead and up, right outside hip on. Left knee up toward the right, left inner thigh on. Right elbow into the wall, blade down and back. Turn the right hand toward the feet. Front of the shoulder on. Hold 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Sidelying: Sidelying Trunk Lift
Left side first: hips and knees 90, prop on the left forearm, elbow under the shoulder. Abs on, right knee down into the left. Left blade down and back, lift the hip. Left abs, back of the left shoulder, right inner thigh. Right hand overhead, 5 breaths. Lower. Repeat 4 more times. Then the right side, mirrored: prop on the right forearm, left knee into the right, right blade down, left hand overhead. ### Sidelying: Three Point Stance (side not named)
Two setups. Do not assign a left or right.
Top leg in front, bottom leg behind. Prop on the bottom hand, elbow straight, hand and trunk between the legs. Tighten lower abs and the upper inner thigh by arching up. Top hand behind the head, blades down and together. Lift the hip and waist. Back of the shoulder blades, lower abs, top inner thigh. 4-5 breaths. Lower. Repeat 4 more times.
Other setup: bottom leg in front, top leg behind. Same prop. Tighten lower abs and the lower outside hip. Same blade cue and lift. Feel lower outside hip instead of the top inner thigh. 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Sidelying: Modified Three Point Stance (side not named)
Top leg forward, bottom leg back. Prop on the bottom forearm. Arch up and press both ankles into the mat. Top hand at the side, blades down and together. Lift the hip and waist. Back of the shoulder blades and lower abs. 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Seated: Seated Resisted Pull Downs with Right HG IR and Left HG ER
Chair, feet flat, knees at hip level. Tubing from above, ends at shoulder level in front of the face. Palms toward each other. Round the back, find the sit bones. Straighten the arms toward the hips. Right elbow stays straight, right palm turns away, thumb in. Left elbow 90, left hand turns out. Front of right shoulder and back of left shoulder blade. Hold 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Seated: Seated Resisted Right HG IR
Tubing from above into the right hand, right elbow at shoulder level. Round the back, sit bones. Right blade down and back, elbow into the wall. Turn the right hand down and reach the left hand toward the floor, sidebend left. Front of the right shoulder blade and left outer abs. Hold 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Prone: Prone Weighted Right Abducted HG ER with HG IR
Stomach, right arm can hang. Pillows under the stomach, towel under the forehead. Right arm at shoulder level with a weight, bolster under the right shoulder, left hand on the mat. Blades down and together. Turn the right hand up toward the head (back of the right shoulder blade). Then lower and turn the hand down toward the feet (front of the right shoulder). Hold 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. ### Prone: Prone Resisted Weighted Abducted Right HG IR
Same prone setup. Tubing from a door in front and to the right, plus a weight, in the right hand. Bolster under the upper arm. Blades together. Turn the right hand down toward the feet against the tubing. Front of the shoulder. Hold 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times. Four tubing directions, each with the right elbow at 90, right foot off the ground, 4-5 breaths.
1. Tubing behind: slight forward reach.
2. Tubing on the right: slight turn in.
3. Tubing in front: slight pull back.
4. Tubing on the left: slight turn out.
Reference: left abs, left heel. The sheet prints "right right arm" on the front-tubing line. Keep it as a right-arm drill. ### Standing: Standing Quadratus Lumborum and Intercostal Stretch
Face a doorway. Right hand inside the frame, palm out. Feet shoulder width, right foot behind. Round the back, turn the trunk right, left arm hangs. Shift toward the right hip and take up slack in the right arm. Stretch in the right chest. Rotate the hips right. Stretch just above the right hip bone. Hold 4-5 breaths. Repeat 4 more times.

skills.name: principle-attack-the-premise
skills.description: Apply when two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate. Write the premise down and test it directly before you write another fix that assumes it.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-attack-the-premise
description: "Apply when two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate. Write the premise down and test it directly before you write another fix that assumes it."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Attack the Premise When two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate, suspect the premise, not the fixes. **Why:** Each failed fix is evidence against the belief it assumed. A third fix on the same premise spends effort where the evidence already says the cause is not. **Pattern:**
- **Write the premise down.** The premise is the one sentence that every failed fix assumed.
- **Test the premise before the next fix.** Find an observation that would come out differently if the premise were false, and make it. Look at how the failures are distributed, not only at how large they are. Make the check rerunnable per [Build the Lever](../principle-build-the-lever/SKILL.md).
- **Follow the evidence.** If it contradicts the premise, the cause is elsewhere. Look for what the failures have in common that the premise did not predict. If it confirms the premise, ask the next "why" per [Fix Root Causes](../principle-fix-root-causes/SKILL.md). The earlier fixes may have treated a consequence instead of the cause.
- **Remove the condition instead of compensating for it**, per the [Laziness Protocol](../principle-laziness-protocol/SKILL.md). If the evidence shows that one part always lands on the losing side, change what puts it there. A mechanism that cleans up after it leaves the cause in place and adds work on every run. **Stop:** Do not start the next fix before the premise is written down and tested. This principle is distinct from [Redesign from First Principles](../principle-redesign-from-first-principles/SKILL.md), which rebuilds a design around a new requirement. It questions a fact the current design assumes.

skills.name: principle-boundary-discipline
skills.description: Apply when wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters. Concentrate guards at system boundaries (CLI, config, network, external APIs); trust internal types and keep business logic in pure functions.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-boundary-discipline
description: "Apply when wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters. Concentrate guards at system boundaries (CLI, config, network, external APIs); trust internal types and keep business logic in pure functions."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Boundary Discipline Place validation, type narrowing, and error handling at system boundaries. Trust internal code unconditionally. Business logic lives in pure functions. The shell is thin and mechanical. **Why:** Scattered validation is noisy, redundant, and gives a false sense of safety. Keep logic out of framework wiring so it can be tested without the framework. **The pattern:**
- **At boundaries** (CLI args, config files, external APIs, network protocols): validate, return errors, handle defensively.
- **Inside the system:** typed data, error propagation, no re-validation. Trust the types.
- **Across the boundary.** Expose domain concepts, not the boundary's private representation. Keep general-purpose mechanism inside and special-purpose policy at the edge. **Applications:** Validation and error handling:
- Validate config at parse time (the boundary), not inside business logic
- Parse raw data into domain types at the boundary
- Do not re-export transport, storage, framework, or wire types through the public surface
- No redundant nil checks deep in call chains if the boundary already validated Code organization:
- Business logic in pure functions with no framework dependencies
- Parse functions: pure transforms from raw bytes to typed state
- Prompt construction: structured state in, string out
- Scoring and assessment: pure transforms from state to results **The tests:**
- "Is this data crossing a system boundary right now?" If not, validation is redundant.
- "Can this be a pure function that the shell just calls?" If yes, extract it.

skills.name: principle-build-the-lever
skills.description: Apply to any non-trivial work, not just bulk work: edits, migrations, analyses, checks. Build the tool that does it or proves it (codemod, script, generator, or a skill your subagents follow) instead of working by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-build-the-lever
description: "Apply to any non-trivial work, not just bulk work: edits, migrations, analyses, checks. Build the tool that does it or proves it (codemod, script, generator, or a skill your subagents follow) instead of working by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun."
disable-model-invocation: true
---
# Build the Lever When the work isn't trivial, build the tool that does it instead of doing it by hand. A codemod, generator, or script does the work the same way every time and reruns for free. The tool is one artifact a reviewer can read and rerun to check the work. Hand-done changes can only be re-verified by redoing them. A deterministic script turns "trust me" into "run this". Default to building the lever. Skip it only when the task is trivial, a couple of obvious edits you can see at a glance. - Do the first unit by hand to learn the recipe, then build the tool. Prove it by rerunning it on that unit and diffing against your hand-done version. Make the lever safe to rerun.
- Codemod or script for edits, generator for repetitive files, a dump-to-sqlite query for analysis, a rerunnable check for verification.
- A deterministic lever beats fan-out. If the tool can process every unit in one pass, run it yourself. Don't fan out delegates to hand-apply what a script can do.
- When you fan work out to subagents, write the lever as a skill they all read: the recipe, the verification contract, and the do-not-touch fences in one artifact. Keep it outside the delegates' write scope so they can't quietly edit the contract.
- Applying this principle produces a file. If you cited it and there is no codemod, script, generator, or delegate skill in the diff, you didn't apply it.
- Commit the lever when the work outlives the session. The bar is triviality, not repetition. A one-off still earns a lever when the lever is what makes the work checkable. Per the [Laziness Protocol](../principle-laziness-protocol/SKILL.md), build the smallest script that does or proves the job, never a framework. Distinct from [Encode Lessons in Structure](../principle-encode-lessons-in-structure/SKILL.md), which makes a recurring instruction a durable guardrail. This is throughput and reviewability on the work in front of you. For scripting the verification itself, see [Prove It Works](../principle-prove-it-works/SKILL.md).

skills.name: principle-encode-lessons-in-structure
skills.description: Apply when you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time, or notice a recurring correction. Encode the rule as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-encode-lessons-in-structure
description: "Apply when you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time, or notice a recurring correction. Encode the rule as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Encode Lessons in Structure If the lesson needs judgment and cannot be encoded, make the instruction more prominent and add an example of the failure mode. **Corollary:** If the fix is structural, only use the structural fix. The instruction is the symptom.

skills.name: principle-experience-first
skills.description: Apply when product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs come up. Choose user delight over implementation convenience; ship fewer polished features over more rough ones.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-experience-first
description: "Apply when product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs come up. Choose user delight over implementation convenience; ship fewer polished features over more rough ones."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Experience First When implementation convenience conflicts with user delight, choose delight. - Every feature, control, and option must be justified
- Ship less, ship better (polished experience with three features beats rough one with ten)
- Prototype before committing (design decisions are cheaper in throwaway HTML than production code)
- Get the details right (transitions, alignment, spacing, feedback, error states)
- Tighten the core loop (every feature should serve the central workflow or get out of the way) The user is whoever consumes the work. For a UI that is the end user. For a library or an internal API it is the colleague who imports it. The engineer who maintains the code next is a user too. Weigh their experience the same way, and explain impact from their perspective. Foundations should serve the experience. Foundational thinking governs the *sequence* of work. This principle governs the *target*.

skills.name: principle-explain-the-number
skills.description: Apply before you measure, and before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured: a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result. Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-explain-the-number
description: "Apply before you measure, and before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured: a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result. Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Explain the Number - **Write the decision before you run.** Name the result that would change a decision, and the noise floor. Stop when the run-to-run spread is larger than the effect.
- **Ask "why not double?"** Name the resource or code path that bounds the result, such as a core, a lock, the disk, the network, or the load generator itself. Get it from a profile or from system counters taken during a run, then map it to source. A guess from reading the code is not a limiter. If you cannot say why the number is not twice as good, you do not know what you measured.
- **List what else the number could be measuring, and rule out each one with evidence.** The usual suspects are errors, skipped or cached work, code that never ran, an untuned side (one left on default settings), noise, and a piece too small to matter end to end.
- **Keep the evidence with the number.** Put the run count, the spread, and the limiter in the notes or a linked artifact. For a performance number, run the full procedure with the [benchmark-checklist](../benchmark-checklist/SKILL.md) skill. For an eval result, ask the same of the trials: did every run do the task, does the gap hold across trials and models, and does the scenario matter. You skipped this when a run started without the result that would change a decision, when the evidence behind a number has no run count, no spread, or no named limiter, or when the time saved is larger than the time the changed piece took. Distinct from [Prove It Works](../principle-prove-it-works/SKILL.md), which checks that an output is real.

skills.name: principle-fix-root-causes
skills.description: Apply when debugging. Trace each symptom back to the first place the system went wrong and fix it there. A guard is a fix only when the state it handles is legitimate.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-fix-root-causes
description: "Apply when debugging. Trace each symptom back to the first place the system went wrong and fix it there. A guard is a fix only when the state it handles is legitimate."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Fix Root Causes When debugging, fix the fault, not the place where it surfaced. The symptom is where a wrong state became visible. The root cause is the first place the system did something it should not do, or failed to handle a state it should handle. **Why:** A symptom fix hides the evidence and leaves the fault free to surface somewhere else. Each one makes the system harder to reason about, because the code now carries a workaround for a bug that nobody named. **Pattern:**
- Reproduce first.
- Ask "why" at each step until the answer is a wrong decision in the code, not a consequence of an earlier one.
- When stuck, instrument. Read the actual error and the actual state. Do not guess.
- Ask whether the state that triggered the symptom is legitimate. If the system may be in that state, the code that broke on it is the root cause, and handling the state there is the fix. If the state should never exist, a check where it broke hides the bug. Find what produced the state. Guards, retries, swallowed errors, clamped values, and discarded state are the usual ways to hide a bug.
- When something fails only after a restart, suspect persisted state first: config files, caches, lock files, serialized state.
- Check for the pattern, not just the instance. Find every place with the same fault and fix them all.
- If a workaround needs a paragraph-long comment to justify it, the code is wrong. Fix the code, not the comment.
- If the deciding fact took a deep dig to find, propose the cheap, always-on signal that would have shown it at first look.

skills.name: principle-foundational-thinking
skills.description: Apply before writing logic: choosing core types and data structures, sequencing scaffold-vs-feature work, asking what concurrent actors share. Get the data structures right so downstream code becomes obvious.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-foundational-thinking
description: "Apply before writing logic: choosing core types and data structures, sequencing scaffold-vs-feature work, asking what concurrent actors share. Get the data structures right so downstream code becomes obvious."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Foundational Thinking **Structural decisions** protect option value. **Code-level decisions** protect simplicity. **Data structures first.** Get the data shape right before writing logic. Define core types early, trace every access pattern, and choose structures that match the dominant paths. At code level, DRY the structure, not every line. Types and data models should converge. Three similar statements still beat a premature abstraction. Prefer explicit over clever. Test behavior and edge cases, not line counts. **Concurrency corollary.** Before sharing state between actors, ask "what happens if another actor modifies this concurrently?" If not "nothing", isolate. **Scaffold first.** If something helps every later phase, do it first. Ask "does every subsequent phase benefit from this existing?" CI, linting, test infrastructure, and shared types are scaffold. Sequence for option value: setup before features, tests before fixes. Keep commits small and single-purpose. Each increment should land a coherent abstraction or deepen one that exists. Do not spread a new capability across callers as special-case coordination. Subtraction comes before scaffolding. Remove dead code first, then lay foundations.

skills.name: principle-guard-the-context-window
skills.description: Apply when context is filling up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents; keep summaries in the main thread, not raw payloads.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-guard-the-context-window
description: "Apply when context is filling up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents; keep summaries in the main thread, not raw payloads."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Guard the Context Window **Why:** Context overflow degrades reasoning quality, creates compression artifacts, and halts progress. **Pattern:**
- **Size phases and cap scope.** Limit files per phase, set turn budgets, account for mechanism costs.

skills.name: principle-laziness-protocol
skills.description: Apply when refactoring, evaluating diff size, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Bias toward deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-laziness-protocol
description: "Apply when refactoring, evaluating diff size, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Bias toward deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Laziness Protocol - **Consolidate decisions.** Do not repeat the same choice in several places. Put it behind one source of truth and pass the result as a simple flag.
- **Minimize the diff.** Make the smallest change that solves the problem. Fewer lines beat "elegant" boilerplate.

skills.name: principle-make-operations-idempotent
skills.description: Apply when designing commands, lifecycle steps, or processing loops that run amid crashes, restarts, and retries. Converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-make-operations-idempotent
description: "Apply when designing commands, lifecycle steps, or processing loops that run amid crashes, restarts, and retries. Converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Make Operations Idempotent Design operations so they converge to the correct state regardless of how many times they run or where the previous run stopped. Every state-mutating operation should answer: "What happens if this runs twice? What happens if the previous run crashed halfway?" **Why:** Commands, lifecycle operations, and processing loops run where crashes, restarts, and retries are normal. If partial state changes the next run's outcome, every restart becomes a debugging session. **The idea:** derive each step from the state that exists, not from what the previous run meant to do. Read the current state, compare it to the goal, and apply only the difference. A step written this way is safe to repeat, because a repeat finds nothing left to do. Anything a run leaves behind, such as a lock, a temporary file, a half-written record, or a claimed job, must be recognizable as stale by the next run. Judge staleness by evidence that stays true wherever the previous run could have stopped, not only in the common case. A marker that the next run cannot judge turns every crash into manual cleanup. For example, write to a temporary path and rename it into place, or compare artifacts by content instead of by creation order. **The test:**
1. What happens if this runs twice in a row?
2. What happens if the previous run crashed at every possible point?
3. Does re-execution converge to the same end state? If any answer is "it depends on what state was left behind," the operation needs a reconciliation step.

skills.name: principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis
skills.description: Apply when introducing a new internal API while old callers still exist. Migrate callers and delete the old API in the same wave instead of preserving compatibility layers.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis
description: "Apply when introducing a new internal API while old callers still exist. Migrate callers and delete the old API in the same wave instead of preserving compatibility layers."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs - Update tests to assert the new contract, and delete tests that only protect pre-refactor implementation details **When this applies:**
- No external users depend on backward compatibility
- The project can absorb coordinated breaking changes
- The new API is part of a simplification or refactor initiative

skills.name: principle-minimize-reader-load
skills.description: Apply when reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers between question and answer, and hidden state in the reader's head; collapse one-caller wrappers and shrink mutable scope.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-minimize-reader-load
description: "Apply when reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers between question and answer, and hidden state in the reader's head; collapse one-caller wrappers and shrink mutable scope."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Minimize Reader Load Maintainability is the work a reader must do to understand code. Track two axes: **layers to trace** (indirections between the question and the answer) and **state to hold** (hidden or mutable context the reader must keep in their head). LOC, cyclomatic complexity, and "clean architecture" are proxies. Reader load is the thing that matters. The two axes are independent. A flat file with 50 globals can be as hard to reason about as a 6-layer adapter stack. Guard both. This is the human analog of [Guard the Context Window](../principle-guard-the-context-window/SKILL.md). Working memory is finite for readers too. - **Collapse layers** that cost more than they save: wrappers with one caller, adapters with no second implementation, speculative indirection that was never needed. Inline them.
- **Make adjacent layers change the abstraction.** A layer that repeats the same methods and arguments adds reader load without compression. Collapse pass-through layers.
- **Demand interface compression.** A broad interface that hides little complexity makes readers learn both the surface and the implementation. Prefer boundaries that hide meaningful decisions.
- **Shrink state scope:** prefer pure functions (returns over mutations), locals over fields, fields over module state, and module state over globals. Derive instead of sync.
- **Name the invariant at the boundary,** not in every consumer, so the reader learns it once.
- Before adding a layer or a piece of state, ask: does it reduce reader load elsewhere by at least as much? **The test:** can a new reader answer "where does X come from?" and "what can change X?" in under 30 seconds? If not, cut layers or cut state.

skills.name: principle-model-the-domain
skills.description: Apply when writing stateful logic, or when code branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-model-the-domain
description: "Apply when writing stateful logic, or when code branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Model the Domain Encode the real domain in a data structure instead of scattering it across conditionals. A structure that matches the domain makes invalid states unrepresentable and deletes branches. Choosing it at write time is cheap. Recovering it later reads as a refactor and gets deferred. Reach for: - A state machine instead of scattered booleans, phases, or lifecycle checks.
- A typed model instead of loose parameters or repeated shape assumptions.
- A map, registry, lookup table, or discriminated union instead of branching spread across files.
- A reducer or command/event model instead of ad hoc state mutations.
- A module organized around one body of domain knowledge instead of a sequence such as load, validate, transform, and save. Execution order is not ownership.
- A small module boundary that gathers repeated behavior, ownership, or invariants.
- A queue, cache, index, graph, tree, or normalized collection where the access pattern calls for it.
- Any other structure that fits. When none fits, work out what the code must never allow and how the data gets read, then find the structure that encodes exactly that. Do not force an abstraction. Prefer boring code if the current shape is already clear, local, and unlikely to grow. Be skeptical of an abstraction that adds indirection without removing branches, duplicated rules, invalid states, or lifecycle risk. The sign that you skipped this is a new feature that grows an existing if/else chain by one more branch, or a second boolean that must stay in sync with the first. Temporal decomposition is another sign. Phase-named modules repeat the same domain rules across steps.

skills.name: principle-never-block-on-the-human
skills.description: Apply when tempted to ask 'should I do X?' on reversible work.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-never-block-on-the-human
description: "Apply when tempted to ask 'should I do X?' on reversible work."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Never Block on the Human The human supervises asynchronously. Agents must stay unblocked. Make reasonable decisions, proceed, and let the human course-correct after the fact. Since code changes are reversible and reviewable, a wrong decision usually costs less than blocking. - Proceed, then present. Do the work, show the result. Don't ask "should I do X?" Do X, explain why.
- Make the system self-healing. When you notice a problem, log it and fix it in the next round.
- Irreversible actions (force-push, delete production data, send external messages) still require confirmation.
- Reversible actions (write code, edit notes, split tasks) should proceed without blocking.
- Product direction comes from the human. Execution should not block.

skills.name: principle-outcome-oriented-execution
skills.description: Apply during planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture; don't preserve smooth intermediate states with throwaway compatibility code.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-outcome-oriented-execution
description: "Apply during planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture; don't preserve smooth intermediate states with throwaway compatibility code."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Outcome-Oriented Execution Optimize for the intended, verifiable end state rather than preserving smooth intermediate states. **Why:** Keeping every intermediate step fully stable often creates temporary compatibility code that becomes long-lived debt. Converge on the target architecture and prove correctness at explicit verification boundaries. **Core rule:**
- Prioritize end-state integrity over transitional stability
- Intermediate breakage is acceptable when it is planned, scoped, and reversible **Guardrails:**
- Use this for planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries
- Declare where temporary breakage is acceptable
- Keep high-signal checks for actively touched areas while migrating
- Require full static and runtime verification at plan completion

skills.name: principle-prove-it-works
skills.description: Apply after completing a task, before declaring done. Verify against the real artifact (run the feature, read the actual value, inspect the diff), not a proxy, self-report, or 'it compiles.'
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-prove-it-works
description: "Apply after completing a task, before declaring done. Verify against the real artifact (run the feature, read the actual value, inspect the diff), not a proxy, self-report, or 'it compiles.'"
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Prove It Works Verify every task output by checking the real thing directly. Do not infer from proxies, self-reports, or "it compiles." **Why:** Unverified work has unknown correctness. Indirect verification (file mtimes, output freshness, agent self-reports, cached screenshots) feels cheaper than direct observation. Acting on a wrong inference costs far more than checking the source. Check the real thing, not a proxy:
- Check process liveness directly, not indirectly through derived state
- Read the actual value, not a cached or derived representation
- When verification fails, suspect the observation method before suspecting the system ## Script the check when you can The strongest proof is a deterministic script that re-runs the same comparison, not a one-time eyeball. Write the script, run it, and keep its output as an artifact a reviewer can re-run instead of trusting your word. Keep the artifact visible for the human. Commit it only for large or complex work where the trail has to be auditable later, like a big port or migration (the **show-me-your-work** skill).

skills.name: principle-redesign-from-first-principles
skills.description: Apply when integrating a new requirement into an existing design.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-redesign-from-first-principles
description: "Apply when integrating a new requirement into an existing design."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Redesign From First Principles When integrating a change, don't bolt it onto the existing design. Redesign as if the requirement had been a foundational assumption from the start. - Read all affected files and understand the current design
- Ask: "if we were writing this from scratch with this new requirement, what would we build?"
- Propagate the change through every reference: types, docs, examples, rationale sections
- Think about the whole redesign, then deliver it incrementally This is the method for preserving option value when integrating changes into an existing design.

skills.name: principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state
skills.description: Apply when concurrent actors might write to the same file, branch, key, or state object. Eliminate the sharing first; serialize structurally only when one shared writer is a real invariant.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state
description: "Apply when concurrent actors might write to the same file, branch, key, or state object. Eliminate the sharing first; serialize structurally only when one shared writer is a real invariant."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Separate Before Serializing Shared State When concurrent actors might share mutable state, first ask whether they need the same mutable object. If not, eliminate the sharing. When sharing is real, enforce serialization structurally: lockfiles, sequential phases, exclusive ownership. Instructions and conventions are not concurrency control. **Why:** Concurrent writes to shared state create race conditions that are intermittent, hard to reproduce, and expensive to debug. **Pattern:**
1. **Identify shared mutable state** (files both read and write, branches both push to, APIs both define and consume).
2. **Default: eliminate the shared write target.** Ask: do these actors need one canonical object, or are they publishing independent facts? Give each actor its own owned file, key, branch, or state directory, and merge only at the read/reporting boundary. Two workers writing their own `lastX` field into one `state.json` is still shared mutation. `indexer-state.json` + `metrics-state.json` is not.
3. **Only when one shared write target is a real invariant, serialize access structurally** (lockfiles, sequential phases, single-writer actor, or atomic compare-and-swap). Treat "we need a lock" as a design smell to check, not as the default answer.

skills.name: principle-sequence-verifiable-units
skills.description: Apply to multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and to how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a verifiable state, check each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself to a reviewer.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-sequence-verifiable-units
description: "Apply to multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and to how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a verifiable state, check each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself to a reviewer."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Sequence work into verifiable units Order work as a sequence of small units, each ending in a state you can check, and don't advance until the current one is green. **Why:** A break caught at the unit that caused it is cheap to localize. A break caught after a batch is buried, and you have already built further on a broken base. Sequencing those same units into a delivery a reviewer can replay turns "trust me" into "watch it go red, then green." **Execution.** In a sweep, migration, or any run of similar edits, verify each change before starting the next. Each unit is a before/after bracket: known-good state, one change, run the check, then proceed. Rebase onto clean trunk first so every check measures against the real baseline. When a lever does the edits, the per-unit check is nearly free. Run it anyway. **Delivery.** Stack commits and PRs in the order that proves the work. The canonical shape is the failing test first, then the fix on top. Other story orders are a subtraction before the reshape, a baseline capture before the treatment, the scaffold before the feature. Each commit lands on its own and the sequence reads as an argument. The sequencing complement to the **prove-it-works** principle skill, which keeps each check real, and the **build-the-lever** principle skill, which makes the per-unit check cheap.

skills.name: principle-subtract-before-you-add
skills.description: Apply when sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite. Remove dead code, redundant validators, and stub references first, then build on the simpler base.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-subtract-before-you-add
description: "Apply when sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite. Remove dead code, redundant validators, and stub references first, then build on the simpler base."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Subtract Before You Add When evolving a system, remove complexity first, then build. Default to subtraction. Make simplification a continual investment. Leave the design slightly simpler and more capable behind the same or smaller surface than you found it. - Sequence removal before construction
- Cut before you polish (get to the minimum before investing in quality)
- Design for observed usage, not speculative edge cases
- No speculative validators, parsers, or guards beyond what the spec demands
- Simplify prompts (remove redundant instructions, excessive templates)
- When a reference has no novel content, delete it rather than leaving a stub

skills.name: principle-test-behavior-not-implementation
skills.description: Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-test-behavior-not-implementation
description: "Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Test Behavior, Not Implementation A test is a claim about what the code does for its users: a caller, an end user, or another service. Behavior is what those users can observe through the interface they use. That includes return values, errors, state they can read back, and effects on systems outside the code, such as a request sent, a row written, or a message emitted. Implementation is what they cannot observe: private helpers, internal call order, intermediate data, and which internal collaborator did the work. Judge each test against two imagined edits: - **Break the behavior.** Make the code return a wrong value, skip an effect, or do the effect twice. If the test still passes, it proves nothing. The usual causes are an assertion looser than the contract, an expected value computed by the code under test, a restated constant or prompt string that never runs the code that reads it, and an assertion on data that the test built itself.
- **Change the internals.** Keep every observable result the same and restructure the code underneath. If the test now fails, it is pinned to the implementation. It will need a rewrite on every refactor and still catches no bug. Keep a test that catches the first edit and survives the second. Rewrite or delete the rest. To write a test that does both, drive the code through its users' interface with a concrete input. Derive the expected value from the requirement, not from a run of the code. Assert what the contract promises, no less and no more. The contract decides, not the shape of the assertion. When "an empty cart never charges" is the promise, an assertion that the payment client got no call is behavior. Pair it with a case where the charge happens, so that the test shows it can see a call. The payload that a mocked external service receives is behavior, because that service observes it. A call to an internal helper is implementation, because no user can see it. An empty list is the exact answer when no record matches, and a hollow check when the test only needs some result. An exact error message pins wording that no caller reads. The error type that callers branch on is the contract. A test can pin an invariant instead of a call, such as a key that must exist in two tables or a compile-time type check. The invariant is the behavior.

skills.name: principle-type-system-discipline
skills.description: Apply when designing types, reviewing a function signature, or writing code in any statically-typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand semantic primitives, parse external data at boundaries, exhaust variants, derive from authoritative schemas.
skills.instructions:
---
name: principle-type-system-discipline
description: "Apply when designing types, reviewing a function signature, or writing code in any statically-typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand semantic primitives, parse external data at boundaries, exhaust variants, derive from authoritative schemas."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Type System Discipline Make the compiler reject impossible states, mismatched primitives, and unhandled variants. Prefer defining errors and special cases out of existence over proliferating handlers. For TypeScript syntax, see the `typescript-best-practices` skill. - **Brand semantic primitives.** `UserId` and `OrderId` are strings underneath but should not be interchangeable. Give each its own type, such as a branded intersection in TypeScript or a newtype elsewhere. Validate once at creation, trust the type downstream. If two arguments share a primitive type but mean different things, brand them.
- **External data is untyped until parsed.** RPC payloads, JSON, IPC messages, CLI args, config files, environment variables, database rows. Have a parse function at every boundary that turns unstructured input into the typed model. The **boundary-discipline** principle skill says where to put validation.
- **Derive types from authoritative schemas.** When a protocol buffer, OpenAPI spec, GraphQL schema, database migration, design-token file, or another file owns a shape, derive from it instead of hand-rolling a parallel type. See the **encode-lessons-in-structure** principle skill.

skills.name: program-design-basics
skills.description: Use this when writing or checking an Achieve session structure - order, pairings, 1-4x/week layout, sets/reps defaults, deload, and cook-vs-chef house rules from Ryne’s Program Design Basics.
skills.instructions:
# Program Design Basics Source (Ryne Gioviano): `/home/box/agent-data/shared/sc-reference/program-design-basics.txt` PDF: `/home/box/agent-data/agents/0c56f311-56b5-4ded-ae36-22f03da7a160/memory/reference/program-design-basics.pdf` Cook vs chef: new coaches follow this recipe until told otherwise. ~1-hour sessions. Deviate only when earned / instructed. ## Session order (fatigue high → low)
1. Self-myofascial release 2. Breathing / PRI 3. Warm-up 4. Speed 5. Agility 6. Upper/lower body power 7. Knee-dominant (bilateral then unilateral as programmed) 8. Hip-dominant 9. Horizontal push / pull 10. Vertical push / pull 11. Anti-extension → anti-lateral flexion → anti-rotation → hip flexion w/ neutral spine 12. Accessory / scapular stability / rotator cuff (tertiary) ## Speed & agility
- Fresh only: after warm-up, before power/strength. Max intent every rep. Long rest.
- Categories: linear, lateral, COD, deceleration.
- Swimmers: land speed for RFD / reaction; sport speed mostly in water. ## Power
- After speed, before strength. Non-competing pairs (usually LB + UB). High intent, full recovery.
- LB vertical / horizontal / lateral; UB overhead / rotational / horizontal.
- Swimmers: bias lower-body **horizontal** power. Land athletes: include lateral when sport needs it. ## Strength pairings (2-day house)
**Day 1:** B1 bilateral knee-dom + B2 pull; C1 unilateral hip-dom + C2 push. **Day 2:** B1 bilateral hip-dom + B2 push; C1 unilateral knee-dom + C2 pull. Rules:
- Knee-dom with pulls; hip-dom with pushes (lats stabilize hinges).
- Prefer unilateral over stacking two bilaterals. Day 2 is the inverse of Day 1 (if Day 1 had bilateral UB push, Day 2 is unilateral UB push).
- **Overhead athletes: no true vertical press.** Closest = landmine / DB incline / overhead holds. Limited shoulder mobility → same rule. ## Core (non-competing)
Categories: anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral flexion, hip flexion w/ neutral spine. Good pairs: AE + ALF or AR; ALF + AE or hip-flexion. Avoid: AE right after hard push-ups; AR right after unilateral presses (already anti-rotational). ## Tertiary / accessory
Knee flexion, plantarflexion, ankle eversion/inversion, late PRI, cuff, scap work, needs-based fillers. ## Example 2-day swim template
| Day 1 | Day 2 |
|---|---|
| A1 Box Jump | A1 Standing Broad Jump |
| A2 Standing MB Slam | A2 Supine MB Vertical Throw |
| B1 BB Front Squat | B1 Trap Bar Deadlift |
| B2 Neutral Grip Pull-Up | B2 ½ Kneeling 1-Arm Landmine Press |
| C1 Landmine SL RDL | C1 DB Goblet Reverse Lunge |
| C2 Standing 1-Arm Cable Chest Press | C2 2-Point DB Row |
| D1 Standing TRX Fallout | D1 Dead Bug w/ Cross Reach |
| D3 Prone 1-Arm Y On Table | D3 Sidelying 1-Arm DB ER | ## Weekly frequency
- **1-3x/week:** full body every session (power → strength → core → tertiary).
- **4x/week:** upper/lower split (consecutive days need recovery). ## Structure counts
- Breathing: 1-2. Warm-up / movement prep: 6-8 (eval-driven).
- Athletes ~8-9 total training exercises; adults ~6-7. Mostly supersets/tri-sets. ~1 hour. ## Sets / reps (defaults)
- Sets: **3** standard. Advanced sometimes 4-5 only when sport stress is low (off-season / early season / break). Taper: 1-2 main sets (~40-60% volume cut).
- Reps: **8** standard. Accessories up to 12. Strength meso for intermediate/advanced: 3-6 after pattern is owned.
- By slot: B1/B2 often 6-8 (adv strength 3-6); C1/C2 8-10 (sometimes 12); core D1/D2 time 20-45s or 10-15 reps; tertiary D3 10-12 (to 15). ## Deload & progression
- Blocks 4+ weeks: last week deload - drop anything >3 sets down to 3; keep intensity.
- Non-loaded / timed work: +5 seconds per week.
- Start conservative. Assessment, training age, injuries, sport, and season override defaults. ## Logistics
Start on younger athletes (11-14) and master this format before nuanced cases. Check eval results. Collaborate with other coaches. ## Related skills
- [Athlete program design guidelines](sand-workflow:athlete-program-design-guidelines)
- [Adult program design guidelines](sand-workflow:adult-program-design-guidelines)
- [S&C prescriptions by 1RM](sand-workflow:s-c-prescriptions-by-1rm)
- [Exercise progressions and selections](sand-workflow:exercise-progressions-and-selections)
- [PRI breathing exercise selection](sand-workflow:pri-breathing-exercise-selection)
- [Guide to tapering](sand-workflow:guide-to-tapering)

# Programming direction only ## Default (1:1 Coach flow; Programming room gone 2026-11-05) **Owner: Coach** (`5d64c948-3315-41b3-b9a6-196b4d1e2072`) with Ryne in chat. Strength Coach is deleted; do not wait on it or hand work to it. ### Flow when Ryne names an athlete
1. **Context** - Asana (or Ryne) supplies sport, stroke/position, days/week, constraints, tags, last block notes if known.
2. **Specialists** - each sends **ONE private note to Coach** in order when needed: **Hawkin → PRI → S&C Research** (Research only if needed; may stay silent). Do not wait on a shared room.
3. **Coach**: wait for those notes (and Asana), then post **exactly one** final wrap using [Strength Coach program output](sand-workflow:strength-coach-program-output). Incorporate their notes plus dose, exercises, and direction. No duplicate wraps. ### Coach post shape
Use sections: Force Plates → S&C research (omit if silent) → PRI (omit if not in loop) → Strength Coach. Flex bullet counts; omit empty sections. No full Day 1/2 unless Ryne asks. Details live in strength-coach-program-output. No hang / SSC / propulsion-speak. Spectators quiet unless @-mentioned.
