skills.name: strength-coach-program-output
skills.description: Use when Coach posts a program wrap - wait for Hawkin/PRI/Research specialist notes, then one final wrap; Force Plates higher/lower/plateau; SC section is the final call.
skills.instructions:
# Strength Coach program output ## Default (locked 2026-10-02 by Ryne; room-flow update same day via Achieve) Coach owns the wrap with Ryne. On a normal athlete ask you post the **final** prescription in chat after specialists have sent their notes. **Public room flow (normal asks):**
1. Wait for Achieve’s Asana room post.
2. Wait for **one public room message each** from specialists in order: **Hawkin → PRI → S&C Research** (Research only if needed; they may stay silent).
3. Then post **exactly one** final wrap incorporating those room posts plus your expertise (dose, exercises, direction). No private-only loop for normal asks. Do not wrap from DMs alone when the room posts are the source of truth. No duplicate wraps. **ONE message per athlete ask** from you. If you revise, **one** revise post only - not a duplicate of the original plus a revise. **Do not write full Day 1 / Day 2 programs in chat** unless Ryne asks for a full draft. He writes TrainHeroic. Talk like a coach. Plain English. No gymspeak pile-on. ```
{Name} Force Plates
- Main finding
- Main finding
- Main finding (as many as the plates warrant)
- Programming recommendations based on findings: S&C research (when applicable)
- Article - Why it's relevant
- Article - Why it's relevant
- Recommendation based on findings PRI
- Warm-up technique based on client information - Why
- Possible other technique to be used near the end of the program along with core and tertiary exercises Strength Coach
- Specific programming recommendation
- Specific programming recommendation
- Specific programming recommendation
- Specific programming recommendation (count flexes)
``` ### Force Plates language (locked 2026-10-02)
- Never say **soft** (or soft day) for plate output. Use **higher / lower / plateau** with dates.
- Lead with **trend** when Hawkin gives one.
- **Swimmers:** put **SJ next to CMJ** (SJ often primary); mirror Hawkin’s trend line.
- Keep curve/mechanics findings in plain words; numbers and dates fine. ### Strength Coach section = the final call (not a recap)
Specialist sections can keep plate/PRI/research findings and their own recs. **Strength Coach must synthesize into your prescription**, not restate what they said. Include as relevant:
- Programming direction for this block (what wins this week/month)
- Training volume / density (days/week, jump contacts, how hard to push)
- Specific exercise ideas (names he uses) driven by plates + PRI + Asana + research
- Session shape hints (e.g. warm-up → jump quality → strength pairs → serratus/core) without a full A-H writeup unless asked
- Hard stops / gates folded into the call ### Rules
- Force Plates / PRI / Research content comes from their **room posts** - synthesize into the sections; do not invent plates, papers, or PRI techniques.
- Omit **S&C research** entirely when Research was silent.
- Omit **PRI** if they were not in the loop / nothing PRI-relevant.
- No keep/swap/drop. No NEW/KEEP tags. No walls of text.
- Number of bullets depends on the athlete and what you have to share. ## Full draft (only if he asks) Only then use a scannable Day 1 / Day 2 layout with sheet names, sets/reps, and start loads.

skills.name: subscription-management
skills.description: When the user asks to cancel a subscription they named, to read the price and renewal date on a service they named, to start a free trial and leave before it bills, to find paid subscriptions they no longer use or pay for twice, to watch a subscription price for a change, or to ask a service to refund a subscription charge, read this before you open the billing or signup page, or their receipt mail, even when you could answer from memory, because the price, the date, and proof of cancellation have to come from a page or email opened this turn.
skills.instructions:
---
name: subscription-management
description: >- When the user asks to cancel a subscription they named, to read the price and renewal date on a service they named, to start a free trial and leave before it bills, to find paid subscriptions they no longer use or pay for twice, to watch a subscription price for a change, or to ask a service to refund a subscription charge, read this before you open the billing or signup page, or their receipt mail, even when you could answer from memory, because the price, the date, and proof of cancellation have to come from a page or email opened this turn.
---
# Subscriptions You cancel a subscription the user named, or you read its price and renewal date. Later sections add other jobs. A job that does not have its own section below is not specified yet. Say that, and do not invent the missing steps. ## Shared rules These rules apply to every job in this skill. - The service and the plan come from the user. Ask only when they named neither.
- Run SearchPlugins for the service, and for the user's email. Use a connector when one is installed. Install a missing connector with InstallPlugin without asking; its connect card is the ask. Ask in one widget first only when the user named no service and several plugins fit (Gmail or Outlook, Google or Outlook Calendar), or the plugin has no connector. Say in the user's words why it helps, without saying plugin, MCP, or plugin id, and never paste a connect link. An email connector finds the signup confirmation and the cancellation message.
- When the site wants a sign-in, a one-time code, or a verify-you-are-human check, follow the Cursor-managed `sign-in` skill in its order, which ends with the Secure Form (`RequestUserForm`) and then handing over the screen with `request_box_help` and one instruction ("Sign in to your <service> account"). Never send a question widget before these; the tool is the ask. After a receipt or a hand-back, dispatch the subagent again; the session persists across turns.
- Every price, date, and status comes from a page or email opened for this task. When you cannot open one, say so instead of guessing.
- A signup, a plan change, or a cancellation starts with one question widget that states the service, the plan, the price, and the date. A dismissed widget is a no. A yes opens that page. It does not answer a retention offer, and it does not answer a final confirm. Each later submit is its own `computerUse` dispatch, and it is not read-only.
- A retention offer, such as a cheaper plan, a pause, extra free time, or a discount, stops the job. Send its own question widget, with the renewal price and the end date, and end the turn. Do not click Continue, Confirm, or any control that leaves that page until the user answers that widget. The user's request to cancel is not that answer, and neither is a yes on the earlier question. Taking the offer stops the cancellation. Declining the offer, or dismissing that widget, is the only way to go on.
- The final confirm page stops the job again. Send a question widget that names the service, the plan, and the date access ends, and end the turn. Do not click the confirm control until that widget's yes. The user's request to cancel, a yes on the first question, and a decline of a retention offer are not that yes. A later section does not waive either stop.
- Report a subscription as cancelled only when a confirmation page or the service's email states that it is cancelled and names the date access ends. Send that page or email, with a screenshot. Save the service, the plan, the end date, and the link with UpdateMemory.
- When the page says the cancellation is requested, pending, or processing, use those words and say it is not confirmed yet.
- When no page confirms the cancellation, say that in the same message. Give the phone number, the hours, and the menu path the page shows. When place_phone_call is among your tools, offer to place that call, and place it only after the user says yes. Report it cancelled only after the call's result or a later page or email states the cancellation and the end date, and save that proof the same way.
- Show what you collected in the user's language, which is the language they write to you in unless they asked for another or the Memory section names one they prefer. When a page is in another language, translate the words you put in a card or a summary, such as titles, descriptions, specs and their labels, notes, review summaries, policies, delivery and status lines, and option names. Keep brand, store, seller, and venue names, model numbers, order numbers and other codes, prices with their currency, and links as the page shows them. Brief the browser subagent and type into the site in the site's own words, and match a choice the user makes in their language back to those words. ## Read or cancel a named subscription 1. Dispatch a `computerUse` subagent, read-only, to the service's billing page. Have it read the plan, the price, the next charge date, and whether a cancellation keeps access until that date. Screenshot the page.
2. When they asked for the price or the date, send those from the page and stop.
3. When they asked to cancel, send the first question widget and end the turn. On a no or a dismissal, stop, and do not open the cancel page. On a yes, open the cancel page and read it. Stop on that page when it shows a retention offer or a final confirm.
4. When it shows a retention offer, follow the retention stop before any other click. If the user takes the offer, stop. If the user declines it or dismisses the widget, go on, and stop again at the final confirm.
5. On the final confirm page, follow the final-confirm stop. Click the confirm control only after that widget's yes, then follow the proof rule. On a no or a dismissal, stop, and leave the subscription in place. The confirm dispatch is not read-only. ## Try it, don't pay for it You start a free trial the user named and keep the renewal from charging them. Read the trial terms on the service's own page, sign up only after they approve the renewal price and the date it starts, then either cancel while access still lasts or set a reminder before the charge. A stop after that signup that leaves the trial in place still sets the reminder. ### Entry points - "Start the free trial and make sure I never pay full price" is a signup plus a cancel or a reminder.
- "Try this for the trial month, then get me out" is the same job for a service they named.
- "Cancel this trial before it renews" is the cancel half, for a trial that already exists. Skip signup. When access lasts until the trial end, start at Cancel while access lasts. When cancelling now would end access immediately, start at Reminder before the charge. That start reads the terms and stops when a minimum term would still bill them after cancel. ### Read the terms 1. Dispatch a `computerUse` subagent, read-only, to the service's signup or plan page. Have it read the trial length, the date the trial ends, the price charged on that date, whether cancelling now keeps access until that date or ends access immediately, and any minimum term. Screenshot the terms.
2. Take the renewal price, the end date, and any minimum term from that page. When the price or the end date is missing, stop and tell the user which one the page left out. Leave the signup unsubmitted. When the page shows a minimum term that still bills them after a cancellation during the trial, stop and say that. Leave the signup unsubmitted. That lock-in is not a trial they can leave before it bills. ### Approve, then sign up - Send one question widget that states the service, the plan, the trial length, the end date, the renewal price, whether cancelling now keeps access until the end date, and the minimum term. When the page shows no minimum term, the widget says that. A dismissed widget is a no. The widget ends the turn. Do not sign up before they answer.
- On a yes, sign up for that plan only. The signup keeps a card on file for the charge on the end date, so it is not a purchase due today. Use a card already saved on the service's account when it has one. Otherwise follow the `purchases` skill for the user's own card. A one-time card cannot stand in for a card the service will charge later, so leave it out.
- Read the confirmation page for the account, the plan, and the end date. Screenshot it and send it. When the confirmation disagrees with the widget, say so and stop before any cancel step. A yes on this widget approves the signup only. It does not approve a cancellation. ### Cancel while access lasts When the terms say access lasts until the trial end after a cancellation, and no minimum term would still bill them, cancel in the same session, before you tell the user the trial is set up. For a trial that already exists, this is the whole job. Read the terms first, including any minimum term. When a minimum term would still bill them after cancel, stop and say that. Do not open the cancel page. 1. Send the first question widget from Shared rules, naming the service, the plan, the renewal price, and the date access ends, and end the turn. On a no or a dismissal, do not open the cancel page. When this cancel follows a signup in this session, fall back to Reminder before the charge. Otherwise stop. A yes on the signup widget is not this yes. An existing trial has had no signup widget, so this is the first ask.
2. On a yes, open the cancellation page and read the date access ends. Then follow the retention stop and the final-confirm stop in Shared rules before any confirm click. The confirm dispatch is not read-only. Then follow the proof rule in Shared rules.
3. A finished cancellation, with proof, gets no reminder. When the user takes a retention offer, or says no or dismisses the final confirm, the subscription is still in place. When this cancel follows a signup in this session, fall back to Reminder before the charge. Use the charge date the page shows after that stop, including the end date of an offer they took. ### Reminder before the charge Use this when cancelling now would end access immediately, when the trial has no cancel control yet, or when a cancel after this session's signup stopped with the subscription still in place. When the user asked to cancel a trial that already exists, and cancelling now would end access immediately, read the terms first, including any minimum term. When a minimum term would still bill them after cancel, stop and say that. Do not open the cancel page, and do not set the reminder. Otherwise ask before you remind. Send a question widget that names the service, the plan, the renewal price, the end date, the minimum term, and that access ends immediately, and end the turn. When the page shows no minimum term, the widget says that. On a yes, open the cancellation page and follow the retention stop and the final-confirm stop. A yes on an earlier widget is not this yes. On a no or a dismissal, continue to the routine below. - Offer a routine that messages the user before the renewal, with time to cancel. Read the Cursor-managed `routines` skill before you create it. Write the service, the plan, the renewal price, the end date, and the cancel page link into its instructions. Schedule it two days before the end date, and tell the user that day. When two days before that date has already passed, do not create the routine. Say the charge is too soon for a two-day warning. If this session's signup is what left the subscription in place, send a question widget that names the service, the plan, the renewal price, the end date, and that cancelling now is the only way to stop the charge, and end the turn. On a yes, open the cancellation page and follow the retention stop and the final-confirm stop. On a no or a dismissal, stop.
- The routine reminds. Cancelling then follows Cancel while access lasts, including the first question widget, the retention stop, and the final-confirm stop. When cancelling would end access immediately, cancelling then follows the question above, including the minimum-term stop. ## Find subscriptions you no longer use You list paid subscriptions the user may not want, and you cancel one only after they pick it. - For this job the services come from their mail and card activity. Do not ask which service before you read them. Ask only when neither has a repeating charge.
- This job is paid subscriptions. A newsletter or other mailing list is a different job. Leave those out of this list.
- Read receipt and billing mail opened for this task. When the Finance connector is connected, also read its card and bank transactions for the same months. The user linked those accounts, so reading them needs no other ask, and nothing there is changed. Without it, read mail only. Each charge is one row: the merchant as the receipt or the statement names it, the amount with its currency, the date, and where it came from, the email's sender and subject or the account and its last four digits. A receipt and the card transaction for it are one row with both sources. Two transactions, or two receipts with different order or invoice numbers, are two rows, even for the same amount on the same day. Leave out a row that its source does not show whole, and never fill in a merchant, an amount, or a date yourself. A charge that repeats, names a service, and shows an amount is a subscription row. A one-time order is not.
- Show the service, the amount, the date of the latest charge, and where it came from. When a row is missing any of those, leave that row out.
- Mark a row duplicate when the same service bills twice for the same period, such as on two accounts, two emails, or two cards. Mark two rows overlapping only when a plan page, opened read-only for this task, shows that one plan already includes the other, such as a family plan that covers the user beside their own plan. Similar names are not an overlap. Put duplicate and overlapping rows first, each with the reason and the page or charges that show it.
- Ask which rows they no longer use. A dismissed widget is a no. The widget ends the turn. Do not open a billing page before they answer. Quiet mail is not a reason to mark a row unused, and a duplicate or overlap flag is not their answer.
- For a duplicate charge they want back, follow Ask for a refund for the extra charge.
- For each row they mark unused, dispatch a `computerUse` subagent, read-only, to that service's billing page, the same read as Read or cancel a named subscription. Then follow that section from its cancel step. The plan, the price, and the date access ends come from that page. The receipt is not that page. One row at a time. A yes on the unused-row widget is not the cancel yes. ## Watch a renewal price You compare the price the user pays with the public price of the same plan, and you can check again before the renewal. - The service comes from the user, or from a subscription already saved with UpdateMemory for this skill. Ask when they named neither and none is saved.
- Dispatch a `computerUse` subagent, read-only, to the billing page and the public plan page. Have it read the price they pay, the date of the next charge, and the current public price of the same plan. Screenshot both pages.
- Tell them those three numbers and which page each came from. When the price they pay is higher than the last price saved for that service, or higher than the public price, say that in the same message.
- Save the service, the price they pay, the public price, the renewal date, and the links with UpdateMemory.
- Offer a routine that checks again. Read the Cursor-managed `routines` skill before you create it. Write the service, the last price, the renewal date, and the page links into its instructions. Schedule it two days before the renewal date, and tell the user that day. When two days before that date has already passed, do not create the routine. Say the renewal is too soon for a two-day check. The routine messages only when the price or the date changed. A plan change waits for a question widget under Shared rules. ## Ask for a refund You ask a service to refund a subscription charge the user did not want, such as a renewal they forgot to cancel or the same plan billed twice. A refund does not cancel the plan. - The charge comes from the user, or from a row they picked in Find subscriptions you no longer use. Take the service, the amount, the date, and the account it billed from a receipt or a billing page opened for this task.
- Dispatch a `computerUse` subagent, read-only, to the service's billing or help page. Have it read whether the service refunds that charge, any refund window, and each way to ask: a refund form or button, a support email address, or a phone number with its hours. Screenshot the page. When the page says that charge is not refunded, tell the user, and go on only when they still want to ask.
- Send one question widget that names the service, the charge with its amount and date, and each way to ask as its own option. A dismissed widget is a no. The widget ends the turn.
- A refund request goes out only after the user approves it. Draft an email with DraftExternalMessage, as the `send-on-behalf` skill says, to the support address the page shows. Never send it with a connector's send tool before the user has seen that card, even when they asked you to send it. When place_phone_call is among your tools, place a call only after their yes on the question that offered it; its approval card shows the script, and they can edit it. Fill a refund form on the service's or store's own page, screenshot it, and send a question widget that shows what it says and the amount. Submit it only after that widget's yes. The submit is not read-only.
- The request names the service, the account, the charge with its amount and date, and the reason the user gave. It says they did not use the plan only when they said so.
- Report a refund only when a page, an email, or the call's result states it with the amount. When it says the refund is requested, pending, or processing, use those words. Save the service, the amount, the date, and the link or the call's result with UpdateMemory.
- When the user also wants the plan cancelled, follow Read or cancel a named subscription. A yes on the refund question is not the cancel yes.

skills.name: superpower-narrow-vs-wide-programming
skills.description: Use when classifying or programming Narrow/elastic vs Wide/muscle-driven athletes (ISA, CMJ/four-jump strategy, Superpower vs Kryptonite phases and dose by training age).
skills.instructions:
# Superpower: Narrow/elastic vs Wide/muscle programming **Source:** Hunter Eisenhower, SimpliFaster (2024-04-15) - *How to Train Narrow & Elastic-Driven Athletes vs. Wide & Muscle-Driven*. Full clip: `/home/box/agent-data/shared/sc-reference/superpower-narrow-elastic-vs-wide-muscle.md` **Cross-links:** [CMJ force-time curve shape classification](sand-workflow:cmj-force-time-curve-shape-classification) · Hawkin Dynamics for plates · [Isometrics programming guide](sand-workflow:isometrics-programming-guide) when rigidity/iso is the elastic base · house order [Athlete program design guidelines](sand-workflow:athlete-program-design-guidelines) Eisenhower’s frame: structure (ISA) biases **Superpowers** vs **Kryptonites**. Dose kryptonite early (raise the floor), flip to superpower closer to season (raise the ceiling). Spectrum, not binary - place the athlete, then dose by **timing + training age**. --- ## 1. Classify the athlete ### Infrasternal angle (structure)
Cited via Conor Harris:
- **Wide** ISA ≈ **>110°**
- **Narrow** ISA ≈ **<100°**
- In between = spectrum; extreme examples often readable without a goniometer (rib-cage width). | | **Narrow** | **Wide** |
|---|---|---|
| Typical bias | External rotation; feet more **supination**; more A-P space, less frontal | Internal rotation / compression; feet more **pronation**; more frontal space, less A-P |
| Stance preference | Staggered / **split**; avoid grinding bilateral IR | **Bilateral**; less space for split |
| Movement strategy | **Elastic** - muscle more isometric; tendons stretch/recoil (“free energy”) | **Muscular** - classic ecc→con; high force, slower / costlier |
| Sport fit (examples) | Guards, springy skill - short GCT | Linemen / “force over time” tasks |
| Coach bias risk | Overdosed all year on powerlifting = kryptonite | Feels natural to most S&C coaches | ### Force-plate strategy (how > jump height alone) **CMJ (hands-on-hips):**
- **Muscular / Wide-leaning:** deeper countermovement; slower time to takeoff; **bimodal** F-T curve (peaks at end of braking + start of propulsion). Continuum: bimodal **secondary** (most muscular) → bimodal **primary** (mid) → **unimodal** (most elastic).
- **Elastic / Narrow-leaning:** shallower CM; faster TTT; **unimodal** sharp peak. **Four-jump / multi-rebound** (prefer over single drop jump for rhythm/coordination):
- Similar RSI can hide strategy: Wides often **longer GCT + higher jump**; Narrows **shorter GCT**.
- Measures efficiency of the elastic system under repeated contacts. Do not classify from jump height alone. Pair ISA + CMJ shape + four-jump strategy. Hand full Hawkin pulls to Hawkin Dynamics; use this skill for programming bias once classified. --- ## 2. Annual logic: Kryptonite → Superpower | Phase | When | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| **Kryptonite** | Earlier off-season (time before competition) | Build the other archetype’s qualities; raise the **floor**. Short-term KPI dips OK. |
| **Superpower** | Later off-season → into preseason | Dose native strengths hard; raise the **ceiling**. Concurrent sport-volume resiliency. | **Training-age dosage (example 8-week off-season):**
- Young Narrow: kryptonite ~**6**/8 weeks (foundation)
- Veteran Narrow: kryptonite ~**2**/8 weeks (then maximize elastic ceiling)
- Maintain small doses of the “other” means year-round so the floor doesn’t collapse
- Never “peak” everyone with bilateral 1RM PR week right before season - outdated for elastic types Speed: still progress max velocity + repeat sprint (e.g. 10×10 Hansen) **regardless** of bucket; later individualize speed by archetype. --- ## 3. Kryptonite menus ### Narrow / elastic - kryptonite (train more like a Wide)
- Highest yearly dose of **traditional bilateral** loading + rising intensity
- Deadlifts, bilateral press/pull, deep bilateral squat patterns as appropriate
- Expect: CMJ JH may drop from training stress, but *how* shifts - greater CM depth, slightly slower TTT, unimodal → **slightly more bimodal**; four-jump: ↑ GCT and ↑ JH (RSI maybe flat) = more muscular strategy
- Still not *only* these weeks in the year - just the peak dose ### Wide / muscular - kryptonite (train more like a Narrow)
- Strip bilateral high-intensity; challenge **force in short time / short ROM / light loads**
- Progress **extensive plyo** volume; unilateral lower + upper; rotation (crawl, roll, gymnastic-type)
- Expect: JH may fall faster (OK) if **TTT ↓** and CM **shallower**; four-jump: **↓ GCT** even if JH flat **Phase goal:** Narrows behave more Wide-like and Wides more Narrow-like before the flip. --- ## 4. Superpower menus ### Narrow / elastic - superpower
- Avoid high-intensity bilateral that forces prolonged IR + heavy compression (bilateral U+L)
- Prefer **staggered / split** lower body
- **Speed of movement > load intensity**
- Upper body: rotation + freedom
- Plyos: more elastic variation (e.g. SL approach jumps) vs standstill vertical only
- Keep **some** muscular means; majority elastic **Plate targets:** ↑ JH, ↓ TTT, shallower CM, sharp unimodal. Four-jump RSI ↑ mainly via **↓ GCT**, secondarily ↑ JH. ### Wide / muscular - superpower
- Return to **higher intensity bilateral** lower + upper
- Faster movements: allow more time to produce force; load **slightly heavier** than Narrow superpower group
- “Peak” feel: 1-3RM near season OK for this archetype (physio + psych)
- Still build plyo volume for sport resiliency even if not their native love **Plate targets:** ↑ JH, ↓ TTT, **deeper** CM (ideally: fast load + hard brake so TTT still improves with more depth). Curve: bimodal secondary → primary, or primary → unimodal as elastic qualities catch up. Four-jump RSI ↑ mainly via **↑ JH**, GCT steady or slightly better. --- ## 5. Achieve translation 1. **Classify** with ISA (when known) + Hawkin CMJ shape + multi-rebound if available - ask Hawkin; don’t invent curves.
2. **Early block / young training age:** bias kryptonite (raise floor). **Late block / veteran elastic:** bias superpower (raise ceiling).
3. In Programming drafts: name the bias in Direction (“Narrow/elastic superpower: split stance, speed, elastic plyos; maintain floor with light bilateral”) rather than dumping both menus equally.
4. Swimmers / overhead: still honor overhead rules and [Swim dryland programming](sand-workflow:swim-dryland-programming); ISA bias modulates stance, plyo type, and bilateral dose - it does not override scap/PRI constraints.
5. Force-time continuum language matches Achieve CMJ guide: secondary bimodal ↔ primary bimodal ↔ unimodal. Use both skills together. ## Anti-patterns
- Year-round powerlifting peak for Narrow/elastic athletes
- Calling skill athletes “soft” for avoiding heavy bilateral IR/compression
- Programming only from absolute JH without strategy metrics
- Treating every athlete as Wide because that’s what most coaches prefer to train

skills.name: swarm
skills.description: Fan out N parallel workers, drain them, and return one report. Use for /swarm, 'swarm this', or parallel coverage, races, gauntlets, and exploration.
skills.instructions:
---
name: swarm
description: "Fan out N parallel workers, drain them, and return one report. Use for /swarm, 'swarm this', or parallel coverage, races, gauntlets, and exploration."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Swarm ## Start Open a todolist with one entry per phase before launching anything. 1. Frame
2. Fan out
3. Aggregate
4. Report ## Phase A: Frame 1. State the done predicate and the artifact or report the swarm must return.
2. Choose the shape. Partition into slices, race N workers on identical briefs, or mix both. For a race or mixed shape, declare `first pass`, `rank all`, or `best-of` before spawning.
3. Pick the worker model from the `swarm workers` line in `~/.cursor/rules/pstack-models.mdc`. If the rule or that line is missing, use `grok-4.7-xhigh-fast`. For `auto` or `inherit-parent`, omit `model` so the workers run on the parent model. If the Task tool rejects a slug, use the default and say so. If it rejects the default, use the closest valid slug of the same family from its error message. For a model race, name each arm's model up front. Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section of the **poteto-mode** skill.
4. Give each worker its own writable output when it writes. When workers verify or measure commits, each brief names the exact SHAs. A measurement brief also names the method (sample count, what one sample is, order). The worker records both in its result. ## Phase B: Fan out Spawn all N workers in one message with `subagent_type: generalPurpose`, `environment: "cloud"`, `run_in_background: true`, and the step 3 model, left unset for `auto` or `inherit-parent`. Use `environment: "local"` only when the worker needs access to something on the user's computer. When a worker must start from a non-default pushed branch, pass `cloud_base_branch`. Every brief stands alone. Include the goal, scope, exact slice or race arm, how to verify, and what to report. Reports use `PASS`, `ISSUES`, or `BLOCKED` with evidence. A worker that can prove a defect reports `ISSUES` and lists every issue it can prove, not only the first. If a worker drops out, proceed with N-1 and note it. ## Phase C: Aggregate Read the terminal results. Drop a result that does not record the SHAs and method its brief names, and respawn that worker once. After a second miss, record a gap. A gap does not count as a pass. For coverage, every required slice needs a result. For a race, apply the selection rule declared up front. Use first pass, rank all, or best-of. Do not paste raw worker dumps. ## Phase D: Report Return one consolidated in-chat report with a result table, issue one-liners, gaps or dropouts, and the race rule when used.

skills.name: swim-dryland-programming
skills.description: Use when designing or reviewing Achieve dryland for swimmers by stroke (fly, back, breast, free sprint/distance), starts/turns/underwaters, scapular and shoulder-pain rules, in-season constraints, or dryland performance screens.
skills.instructions:
# Swim dryland programming Full notes: `/home/box/agent-data/agents/0c56f311-56b5-4ded-ae36-22f03da7a160/memory/reference/strength-conditioning-programming-for-swimmers.txt` **Separate skills (do not merge):**
- [PRI Swimming An In-Depth Look](sand-workflow:pri-swimming-in-depth) - PRI pathomechanics / PEC-AIC-BC
- [PRI shoulder pain prescription](sand-workflow:pri-shoulder-pain-prescription) - Advanced Integration bicipital vs impingement technique menus
- [Swim turn and start ISO angles](sand-workflow:swim-turn-and-start-iso-angles) - pool-transfer isometric angles
- [FRC progressions and prescriptions](sand-workflow:frc-progressions-and-prescriptions) - CARs / PAILs / swimmer hovers / ERR
- House session order: [Athlete program design guidelines](sand-workflow:athlete-program-design-guidelines) This skill owns **stroke-specific dryland bias, starts/turns/UW, scapular rules, shoulder pain fixes, and in-season constraints**. --- ## Always-on swimmer rules 1. **Scapulae / neck** - R scapula → R lower trap + R triceps - L scapula → L serratus (depression / protraction / rib-cage retraction) - Every program needs a **squat-and-reach** somehow (seat scapulae on rib cage, quiet neck). Cue **reach forward, not shrug**. - Wall supported reach → band-resisted wall reach → squatting bar reach → squatting bar reverse reach - UT / neck inhibition: rib-cage IR, SCM balance 2. **Streamline triad** (fly, breast, sprint free, UW): full **shoulder flexion + hip extension + plantar flexion**. Normal PF ROM **40-50°**. Much "toe point" = **midfoot flexion**. 3. **Catch pain** = over-active lat + under-active subscap. Impingement theme: better **R triceps + L ZOA**, lat inhibition, rib expansion, **R HG IR** (R scap retraction). 4. **Straight-arm press down** = key for fly + free. Straight-elbow shoulder extension helps all strokes. 5. **Rolling + rotation:** MSR (and lumbar-locked rotation / ISA as needed). **Prone↔supine rolling** is a primary corrective for free + back body roll. Back needs ~**30°** roll relative to water. 6. **Core:** ~**2** core exercises per workout across the 4 categories; progress toward stability **with moving limbs**. 7. **In-season / within 2 weeks of a key meet:** minimize slideboard/glider + eccentrics; favor concentric; **no new exercises** (soreness). 8. **Season shoulder math:** IR strength rises more than ER over a season → IR:ER drifts. Bias ER / scap control and don't only feed IR. (JSR: high-school swimmers over a competitive season.) --- ## Volume bias by stroke / event | Population | Loading / volume bias |
|---|---|
| Fly | Less bilateral; **upper > lower** volume likely; still train legs for kick/starts/turns |
| Back | More bilateral; **upper > lower** likely; slightly more leg than free (kick volume) |
| Breast | Less bilateral; **upper ≈ lower** (kick-driven but multi-event athletes) |
| Free sprint | More bilateral; **legs + jumps priority**; more RT volume than distance |
| Free distance | More bilateral; **upper > lower** likely; endurance / circuits; connecting U+L | --- ## By stroke (prescription lens) ### Butterfly
- PF/DF screen; glutes + leave bilateral extension (sagittal / QL / lat inhibition) if dolphin LBP
- Straight-arm press down; prone HA via **swimmer hovers**, HA ball drops, functional squat w/ low trap ### Backstroke
- Trunk rotation for deep catch (palm down); R HA (L if needed) via: - L sidelying resisted serratus punch + R trunk rotation - L sidelying L flexed FA adduction + R glute max + R trunk rotation
- Rib integration / sidelying Swiss ball + R apical expansion for roll
- Watch pull-phase hyperextension / anterior glide / impingement ### Breaststroke
- Tall kneeling core (OH reach, anti-rotation, MB OH throws) for straight-hip + stability
- **PADT negative bilaterally** required for breast kick - else ipsilateral LBP / knee / groin
- Knee flexion **with straight hips**: Swiss ball / slideboard / TRX curls, Nordics, GHD, SHELC
- Breaststroker’s knee often **missing hip IR** → IR-bias SL squat etc.
- Assess: hip IR/ER, extension + adduction drop, prone hip ext, PF/DF ### Freestyle
- Full hip ext without lumbar cheat (prone table); PRI all-4 SL R glute max; leave extension posture
- Trunk rotation for DPS / early catch / high elbow; R HA (same L-sidelying pair as back)
- Neck rotation for bilateral breath (L abs + R chest wall themes) **Sprint free:** kick + vertical/horizontal jump culture (starts/turns ~leg-driven); less shoulder roll than distance; own top speed in first 2 strokes (straight-arm extension); higher RT volume; streamline. **Distance free:** more shoulder roll / stroke length; endurance over max strength; lower volume; TGU / contralateral offset connectors; triceps may matter for reach-glide rhythm. --- ## Starts - Spinal flexion to grab block: toe touch; PEC / paraspinal inhibition (often pairs with limited OH for streamline)
- PF + **first ray** strength matter
- Horizontal / split-stance power bank: staggered broad jump (± band); weighted squat jump (± bands); split-stance weight slides (arm drive); GHD; DB step-up jump; staggered trap-bar DL; staggered BB hip thrust; KB swing as horizontal option
- Explosive split-stance: sandbag hang clean → step/box; trap-bar high pull; 1-arm DB snatch ± step; SL RDL → hang clean; rotational reverse lunge → hang clean; sled 1-push / multi / jump from split
- Backstroke start: MB OH scoop toss or scoop behind
- FFE split stance broad / box jump; box jump with front foot on DC blocks ## Turns - Push-off knee **110-120°** (SSC): mid-pause squats, paused box jumps, heavy partials in that range, hurdle / depth jumps, bands/chains
- Compact flip = spinal flexion (same PEC/toe-touch theme as starts)
- Season: full-depth early → bias **½ squat / 110-120°** closer to championship meets ## Underwater / kick - +10° PF ≈ +16 N on dolphin downsweep (~66% peak force at feet)
- UW breath-hold often limiting; deep pre-race breathing may help 50/100 free
- Strong up-kick = glutes + hammies; GHD useful for starts + kick --- ## Shoulder pain menus (PRI-named) Full Advanced Integration banks: [PRI shoulder pain prescription](sand-workflow:pri-shoulder-pain-prescription). Short Achieve list below. **General shoulder pain**
1. Lat hang (standing lat inhibition 1)
2. L sidelying weighted R HG HA + R FA ER (R low trap / R triceps 4) - R scap retraction + L IO → R HG IR theme
3. Supine resisted R HG IR + L HG ER (R low trap / R triceps 16) - R towel wedge, towel under L elbow; keep L ZOA/PME/IO
4. L SL resisted R HG IR (R subscap 2) - L ZOA + L trunk rotation + R HG IR **Impingement:** abs exhale + stay contracted on inhale (rib expansion); lat inhibition; R low trap + R triceps. **Biceps tendonitis:** R upper trunk rotation; R apical expansion; R subscap + lat inhibition. Same L sidelying serratus punch + R trunk rotation as HA driver. **L shoulder pain (often MDI):** treat as bilateral / longer course. After repositioning → L posterior mediastinum expansion (reach + L abs); may need L pec inhibition. AF belly lift reach; modified AFBL pad under L hand; long seated alternating crossovers; AF belly lift. **Long seated supported press downs** (R iliacus/psoas **or** abs) - useful when UT / FHP / bicipital / rounded shoulders / flat back / tight calves / anterior scalenes themes stack. --- ## Dryland performance screens (optional standards) Candidate weakness map: front squat velocity, **1RM pull-up**, trap-bar DL, **non-CMJ**, standing broad jump. Published protocol notes: pull-up 1RM; back squat velocity @ **½ BW** to hip-crease-below-knee (rope depth), Tendo average concentric m/s; non-CMJ with **1s pause** at depth. Use as **screens**, not automatic auto-gates - individualize to training age and season. --- ## Quick decision tree 1. Stroke / event + season → volume bias + in-season constraints 2. Pain? → shoulder menu / PADT (breast) / extension posture before loading more pull 3. Starts/turns/UW priorities this block? → horizontal/split power + 110-120° + PF/first ray 4. Always include squat-and-reach + 2 core; add rolling/rotation for free/back 5. Pair FRC swimmer hovers / HA when end-range ownership is the limiter; pair PRI breathing when ZOA / roll / neck is the limiter

skills.name: swim-turn-and-start-iso-angles
skills.description: Use when picking isometric joint angles for swimmers for pool transfer (flip turn, open turn, or start) instead of defaulting to a land jump quarter squat. Also use when separating CMJ-plate ISO from swim-transfer ISO.
skills.instructions:
# Swim turn and start ISO angles Locked 2026-09-14 from S&C Research (Araujo 2010; Maglischo; Slawson 2012 OSB11; breast open-turn means). Swimmers need **turn or start** angles for pool transfer - not a typical land-sport jump depth. ## Two tools (do not mix them up)
1. **CMJ / land plates** → put the ISO where force dips on *their* curve (often ~quarter squat for early bimodal hang).
2. **Pool transfer** → use the turn or start angles below. Do **not** default every swim ISO to a land quarter squat when the goal is the wall or the block. ## Flip turn (wall push)
- Knee at plant: about **100-120°** (Araujo 2010; Takahashi peak ~120°)
- Hips: about **90°** flexed (Maglischo)
- Too tucked → long wall contact; too straight → weak push ## Open turn (breast / fly)
- Thinner data
- Breast open turns often about **108-112°** knee mean
- Coaching target about **90-120°** knee ## Start (kick / track block)
- Rear knee about **80-90°** for peak vertical force
- Rear knee about **100-110°** for peak horizontal (Slawson 2012 OSB11)
- Many fast starts near about **80°** rear knee
- Keep hips relatively open ## Achieve use
- Breaststroker open-turn ISO ≈ **100-120°** knee
- Freestyle/back flip-turn ISO ≈ **100-120°** knee, hips ~90°
- Start ISO → pick rear-knee band from the intent (more vertical vs more horizontal)
- Name the tool in Direction: plate-dip ISO vs turn/start ISO Breaststroker example (2026-09-14): plate dip still = quarter-squat `Split Squat ISO Push`; swim-transfer ISO later ≈ 100-120° knee for breast open turn.

skills.name: tasks-build
skills.description: Build a task from a Notion page URL. Fetches task details, marks it in progress, implements the work, and updates status in Notion.
skills.instructions:
---
name: tasks-build
description: Build a task from a Notion page URL. Fetches task details, marks it in progress, implements the work, and updates status in Notion.
--- # Build Task from Notion Build a task that is tracked in Notion. The user may be watching the Notion board, so all feedback should be sent through Notion. ## Input The user provides a Notion task URL. ## Workflow ### 1. Fetch the task details Use the Notion MCP tools to:
- Get the page content including title, description, and any relevant properties
- Look for acceptance criteria, requirements, or specifications
- Read any linked pages or references if needed ### 2. Mark in progress - Change the status of the task to "In progress"
- Update the "Agent status" field (if present) to contain a short description: an emoji followed by a word like "Starting..." or "Working..." ### 3. Build it - Work on the task per the specification. If this is a codebase, implement the code changes.
- At each step, update the "Agent status" field to explain what's currently happening, so the user can see progress. Keep it brief: a relevant emoji followed by a few words. Examples: "Searching relevant files...", "Updating color scheme...", "Running tests..."
- If you need user input to clarify the spec or answer questions, add a comment to the task prefixed with "Message from AI:" and set any "Agent blocked" field to true. ### 4. Update the task status Once complete:
- Update the task status in Notion to "Done"
- If you made a code change, consider using the `tasks-explain-diff` skill to generate documentation
- Add a final comment summarizing the results ## Notes - If the URL is invalid or inaccessible, ask the user to verify the URL and their Notion connection
- If requirements are unclear, ask clarifying questions before implementing

skills.name: tasks-explain-diff
skills.description: Generate a rich Notion document explaining code changes. Creates comprehensive documentation with background, intuition, code walkthrough, and verification steps.
skills.instructions:
---
name: tasks-explain-diff
description: Generate a rich Notion document explaining code changes. Creates comprehensive documentation with background, intuition, code walkthrough, and verification steps.
--- # Explain Code Changes Create a rich explanation of code changes as a new Notion page. ## Input The user will point to code changes to explain. If not explicitly specified, explain the most recent batch of changes made in the conversation. ## Document Sections ### Background Explain the existing system relevant to this change:
- Broadly explore surrounding code for context
- Include deep background for beginners (can be skipped by familiar readers)
- Provide narrow background directly relevant to the change ### Intuition Explain the core intuition for the code change:
- Focus on the essence, not full details
- Use concrete examples with toy data
- Use figures and mermaid diagrams liberally ### Code High-level walkthrough of the changes:
- Group and order changes in an understandable way
- Explain the purpose of each significant change
- Link to specific files and line numbers ### Verification Explain how the code change was verified:
- Unit tests, integration tests, etc.
- Step-by-step guide for manual QA ### Alternatives Describe 1-2 alternative approaches (if identifiable):
- Each alternative includes pros and cons
- Layout pros/cons in 2 columns
- Only include if it represents an orthogonal approach
- Omit this section if no meaningful alternatives exist ### Quiz 5 questions testing reader's knowledge:
- Medium difficulty - requires understanding the substance
- Multiple choice with explanations
- Use toggle blocks for answers: ```markdown
1. Question > Option 1 - Explanation for why incorrect > Option 2 - Explanation for why correct
``` ## Formatting Guidelines - Use the Notion MCP to create the page and return its URL
- Write with clarity and flow - engaging, classic style
- Smooth transitions between sections
- Use consistent diagram families throughout
- Include callouts for key concepts, definitions, and edge cases

skills.name: tasks-plan
skills.description: Create an implementation plan from a Notion task or specification. Breaks down requirements into actionable steps with estimates and dependencies.
skills.instructions:
---
name: tasks-plan
description: Create an implementation plan from a Notion task or specification. Breaks down requirements into actionable steps with estimates and dependencies.
--- # Plan Task Implementation Create a detailed implementation plan from a Notion task or specification page. ## Input The user provides a Notion page URL containing a task or specification. ## Workflow ### 1. Fetch the specification Use the Notion MCP tools to:
- Get the page content including requirements, acceptance criteria, and constraints
- Read any linked pages or references for additional context
- Identify dependencies and blockers ### 2. Analyze requirements Extract and categorize:
- Functional requirements (what the system should do)
- Non-functional requirements (performance, security, etc.)
- Acceptance criteria (how to verify completion)
- Dependencies (what needs to happen first) ### 3. Break down into tasks Create a structured implementation plan:
- Group work into logical phases or milestones
- Break each phase into specific, actionable tasks
- Identify the technical approach for each task
- Note any risks or uncertainties ### 4. Create the plan in Notion Use the Notion MCP to create a new page with:
- Title: "Implementation Plan: [Feature Name]"
- Overview section summarizing the approach
- Phases with task checklists
- Dependencies and risks sections
- Link back to the original specification ### 5. Optionally create tasks If the user has a task database, offer to create individual task items for each step in the plan. ## Output Format The plan should include:
- **Overview**: Brief summary of what will be built
- **Specification Link**: Reference to the source document
- **Technical Approach**: High-level architecture decisions
- **Phases**: Numbered phases with task checklists
- **Dependencies**: What needs to be in place first
- **Risks**: Potential issues and mitigations

---
name: tasks-setup
description: Set up a Notion task board for tracking tasks. Guides users through using a template or connecting an existing board.
--- # Notion Task Board Setup Help the user set up their Notion workspace to work with the task skills in this plugin. ## Setup Options ### Option 1: Use a Template If the user wants to start fresh: 1. Point them to duplicate this template: https://notion.notion.site/code-with-notion-board
2. Instruct them to duplicate the template to their workspace by opening the link and clicking the duplicate button in the top bar (icon is two squares).
3. Once duplicated, have them share the URL of their new board - tell them to click the share button in the top-right and then Copy Link. ### Option 2: Use an Existing Board If the user already has a Notion board they want to use: 1. Ask them to provide the URL to their existing board
2. Use the Notion MCP tools to inspect the board structure
3. Verify it has the necessary properties for task management (e.g., Status, Title, etc.)
4. If properties are missing, suggest what they should add ## After Setup Once the user has a board configured: 1. Confirm you can access it via the Notion MCP
2. Let them know they can now use other skills: - `tasks-build` to build a specific task - `tasks-explain-diff` to generate documentation for code changes Remember: Be conversational and helpful. This is a setup wizard, not a one-shot command.

skills.name: tdd
skills.description: Use only when the user explicitly asks for TDD, a failing test, or a regression test, OR when the bug has an obvious cheap local test target. Skip when the test path is unclear, expensive, integration-heavy, or not requested.
skills.instructions:
---
name: tdd
description: "Use only when the user explicitly asks for TDD, a failing test, or a regression test, OR when the bug has an obvious cheap local test target. Skip when the test path is unclear, expensive, integration-heavy, or not requested."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # TDD Bug Fix When fixing a bug with a clear, cheap test path, make the broken behavior executable before changing production code. The goal is a focused regression test that fails before the fix and passes after it. Do not force a test when it would be impractical. If the available test would require broad harness setup, brittle mocks, slow end-to-end infrastructure, production-only state, vague reproduction steps, or large unrelated fixture churn, skip adding a new test and use the closest useful verification instead. ## Workflow 1. **Understand the bug.** Identify the intended behavior, current behavior, affected path, and smallest observable reproduction.
2. **Choose the narrowest executable check.** Prefer the closest unit, component, integration, or regression test already used for that codepath. If no practical test path is obvious, do not create one from scratch just to satisfy the workflow.
3. **Write the failing test first.** Add the smallest focused test that would have caught the bug. The test should encode intended behavior, not mirror the current implementation.
4. **Run the new test before fixing.** Confirm it fails for the intended reason. If it passes or fails for an unrelated reason, correct the test or reproduction before editing the implementation.
5. **Fix the bug.** Make the smallest production change that satisfies the intended behavior while preserving nearby contracts.
6. **Rerun the regression test.** Confirm the test now passes. ## If a Failing Test Is Impractical Use the closest executable regression check instead: a targeted script, manual reproduction command, browser automation, snapshot comparison, log assertion, or focused integration check. Prefer no new test over a bad test. A bad test is one that mostly tests mocks, encodes current implementation details, depends on timing or unrelated global state, needs expensive infrastructure for a small fix, or would be deleted immediately after proving the fix. ## Guardrails - Do not change tests merely to match a wrong implementation.
- Do not weaken existing assertions unless the expected behavior has genuinely changed and the reason is clear.
- Keep the regression test focused on the bug. Avoid broad fixture churn or unrelated coverage expansion.
- If the bug is flaky, make the test deterministic where possible and document the signal being locked down.
- If the bug exposes a broader class of failures, first land the focused regression path, then consider additional sibling coverage. ## Final Response Report the evidence, not just the outcome: - Name the failing-before test or executable check and the failure it produced.
- Name the passing-after test run and any nearby validation performed.
- If failing-before evidence could not be demonstrated, state why and describe the closest regression check used instead.

skills.name: teach
skills.description: Explain a body of work plainly so a person actually understands it. Runs the `how` and `why` skills and weaves what they find into one clear explanation. Use for 'teach me this', 'help me really understand X', 'explain this change or subsystem to me'.
skills.instructions:
---
name: teach
description: "Explain a body of work plainly so a person actually understands it. Runs the `how` and `why` skills and weaves what they find into one clear explanation. Use for 'teach me this', 'help me really understand X', 'explain this change or subsystem to me'."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Teach **You explain what a thing is, how it works, and why it's built that way, in one plain account at the person's pace. The goal is that they understand it, not that you change anything.** Teach sits on top of `how` and `why`. Get your bearings on what the work is and what it touches, then run `how` for how it works and `why` for why it's that way. Those are real skill invocations that do their own digging. Blend what they find into one plain explanation, lead with what matters to the person, and go deeper when they ask. Reword freely for teaching, with one exception. Keep `why`'s confidence language intact (its hedges are findings, not style). 1. Decide the few things they should walk away understanding. Choose them from why they're asking (about to change it, reviewing it, debugging it, new to it) and what they already know, both read from the conversation, not quizzed out of them. Skip what they plainly already know. Put the depth where their question is.
2. Let `how` and `why` do the work, don't redo it. Read the code yourself to get oriented, then run `how` for how it works and `why` for why. Run them in parallel and combine the results. Match the size to the question. Run both for a subsystem, maybe one is enough for a small change. Keep `why` narrow by default since its full sweep is slow. Put the narrowing in the ask itself (a scoped question, git plus a source or two) so `why` records the skipped categories per its own contract, and widen it only when the reasons are the point.
3. Start with a plain definition. Name the thing and say what it is in general terms, the way a senior engineer would say it out loud, with its common name if it has one. Then tie it to the case in front of you ("in X, we use this to ...") and build from there: how it works, the deeper reasons, the edge cases. For each part, explain the idea so it clicks: the problem it solves and how it actually works. Walk through what happens as the person does the thing (opens a long chat, scrolls up) when that is what makes it land. Listing functions and constants is reference, not teaching. Don't print framing labels ("the one idea to hold onto", "the thing to walk away with", "the key insight", "at its core", "TL;DR"). Give the smallest complete answer first, a sentence or two, not a dense paragraph, then stop. Add layers when they ask. Never a wall of text.
4. Keep it a conversation, not a lecture or a performance. Offer to go deeper or move on, and follow their lead. No quizzes. No pacing theater. Don't print "Pause", don't ask them to say it back, don't announce "the sentence to nail", and don't flag a part as important or hard ("here is the part worth slowing down on", "this is the tricky part", "here is where it gets interesting"). Just say it. When you would pause, stop and let them respond. Running one-shot with no live human, deliver it cleanly and put any offer to go deeper at the end.
5. Show, don't only tell, and build the picture up diagram by diagram. Open the diff, the code, or the debugger when that is the fastest way to land it. Draw when a picture lands faster than words. For anything with three or more moving parts, do not draw one diagram with all of them at once. Draw a short series instead, where each diagram redraws the last and adds a single part, so the reader watches the system assemble. A single all-at-once diagram, especially one saved for the end, is a reference, not teaching. Concretely, to teach a flow from A to B to C, draw it three times. First A to B. Then redraw and add C. Then redraw and add the return edge or the next piece. Match the medium to the idea, and use both kinds when both help. A mermaid diagram fits a flow or structure where the labels carry the meaning. When the idea is spatial, like layout, overlap, scroll position, or a before and after, reach for the image-generation tool and draw it marker-on-whiteboard style with a few short labels, since image models garble long text. Generate that picture, don't settle for describing it in words. The build-up rule holds for generated images too. A single simple point needs no figure. Write every response through the **unslop** skill, in plain spoken English, the way you'd explain it to a colleague. Be tight, not terse. Cut filler and hedging, keep the part that makes it click. State the concrete mechanism, not a metaphor, a framing, or a preview of what is coming. This is the target density: "Virtualization runs in two parts, one for rendering and one for loading from disk. When an item scrolls out past the buffer, both its DOM node and its in-memory data are evicted." Normal sentence case, not all-lowercase. No em dashes. Prefer periods over commas. Keep each sentence to one or two commas. If clauses pile up, split them into separate sentences. Give each concept one name and keep it. Avoid mirror sentences ("A without B, or B without A") and tidy closers ("the rest follows", "it all falls out"). The words in these steps are directions to you, not labels to print. Don't echo the structure as headers or stock phrases. **Reply:** the explanation itself, never a report about what you did or delivered. Lead with the main point, then the plain account of what it is, how it works, and why, and the threads worth chasing with `how` or `why`.

skills.name: team-bot-links
skills.description: When your user's request is clearly a job for a shared Bot they haven't added yet (found with SearchTeamBots, or marked not added in your teammates list), and you're about to recommend it.
skills.instructions:
---
name: team-bot-links
description: >- When your user's request is clearly a job for a shared Bot they haven't added yet (found with SearchTeamBots, or marked not added in your teammates list), and you're about to recommend it.
---
# Recommending a shared Bot to your user Some shared Bots on your user's team are ones they haven't added yet. SearchTeamBots finds them by what they do and marks each result added or not added. You can hand your user a link that opens the bot's chat with a message ready for them to send. ## The link Write [<name>](grokbot://app/v1/prompt?id=<id>&text=<message encoded with encodeURIComponent, so spaces are %20>). Use the bot's id and real name as SearchTeamBots or your teammates list gives them. The text is the message your user would send, in their own voice, as a request to that bot ("How many signups did we get this week?"), not a note about them. Keep it to one or two sentences. Encode it with encodeURIComponent so spaces become %20 and characters such as &, ?, and # don't break the link. ## Recommending one Recommend a bot only when the request is clearly its job going by its name and description, such as a data bot for a metrics question. If the ask is quick enough to just answer, answer it. Describe the bot only by what its name and description say, and don't claim it has data or tools they don't mention. Link one bot, not a list. Say in one sentence why it fits, give the link, and offer to do it yourself instead if they'd rather stay here. Once your user passes on the bot or asks you to do it, do the work yourself and don't recommend that bot again in this conversation. In a routine run, do the routine. Link a bot there only when the routine's instruction asks for it. Don't link a bot your user has added: it takes a SendToAgent message or a teammate link instead. Message a bot they haven't added only when they ask you to, in a message typed to you here. ## What your user sees The link shows as a pill with the bot's icon. Clicking it opens the bot's chat with your text in the message box, and nothing is sent until your user sends it. If they already have a draft in that chat, the draft stays and your text is not added.

skills.name: technical-writing
skills.description: Layered technical-writing standard: Diátaxis structure, Google developer style sentences, STE instruction rules, Global English syntax. Use for /technical-writing or when writing or reviewing docs, RFCs, readmes, PR descriptions, or commit messages.
skills.instructions:
---
name: technical-writing
description: "Layered technical-writing standard: Diátaxis structure, Google developer style sentences, STE instruction rules, Global English syntax. Use for /technical-writing or when writing or reviewing docs, RFCs, readmes, PR descriptions, or commit messages."
disable-model-invocation: true
--- # Technical writing Write so a tired engineer understands on the first read. Apply all four layers. Three rules sit above the layers: - **Cut every word that does no work.** If the sentence survives without a word, the word goes. "In order to" is "to". "It is important to note that" is nothing.
- **Use the short, everyday word.** "Use", not "utilize". "Help", not "facilitate". "Do", not "perform". A long word has to buy its length with precision.
- **When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.** A sentence that follows every rule and sounds like a machine wrote it has failed. The codebase is the word list. Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it. Don't invent jargon. Use the words a developer would say out loud: "move", "delete", "a budget that only decreases", not "evacuate", "ratchet", or "endgame". A named pattern is fine when the doc says what it means the first time. Propose a new offender and its replacement as an addition to `unslop`'s abstract-metaphor rule in your reply, with the diff. Don't edit that skill. ## Vary the rhythm A doc can obey every layer and still read machine-written: every sentence clipped short, no view anywhere, nothing specific. - Mix sentence lengths on purpose. Short sentences land a point. Longer ones carry a fact with its condition or consequence.
- One thought per sentence does not mean one length per sentence. Split the sentence that carries two thoughts. Keep the long sentence that carries one.
- Have a view where the mode allows it. Explanation weighs trade-offs, so say what you make of them instead of listing pros and cons. Reference stays dry.
- Be specific over sterile. Not "schema changes can cause issues" but "a column rename fails the build". ## Pick the mode first (Diátaxis) One document, one mode. Two questions pick it: does the content inform action (doing) or understanding (thinking), and does it serve learning or work? - Action + learning: **tutorial**.
- Action + work: **how-to**.
- Understanding + work: **reference**.
- Understanding + learning: **explanation**. Use the compass on a whole document or on one sentence. **Tutorial: learning by doing.** The learner's success is your job, not theirs. Open by saying what the learner will build, not what they will "learn". Every step produces a visible result, early and often. Tell them what they should see: the expected output, the prompt change, the log line. Cut explanation to one clause and a link. Stay concrete. Write as "we", in commands: "First, do x. Now, do y." **How-to: steps to a goal.** Solve a problem a person has, not an operation the machine can perform. Assume competence and skip teaching. Action only: no digressions, no background, no completeness for its own sake. Link those instead. Allow forks and judgment: "If you want x, do y." Name the guide by the task: "How to calibrate the radar array", not "Radar array calibration". **Reference: facts for lookup.** Only describe. No instruction, no persuasion, no opinion. Be dry, complete, and sure. State facts, options, limits, and errors with no hedging. Mirror the structure of the thing described, so code and docs can be navigated together. Put material where readers expect it. Generate from code where possible. **Explanation: understanding and why.** One bounded topic, readable away from the product. Each title should tolerate an implicit "About..." in front. Anchor on a real why question. Give context: design decisions, history, constraints, alternatives. Opinion is allowed here and nowhere else. Don't mix modes: no reference tables inside a tutorial, no tutorial hand-holding inside reference, no arguing inside a how-to. Split and link instead. ## Write sentences to the reader (Google developer style) - Talk to the reader as "you", in the present tense. "Will" only for things that genuinely happen later.
- Say who does what: "the compiler checks", not "is checked". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or beside the point.
- Write instructions as commands: "Click Submit." State facts plainly. Never "should be done".
- Put the condition before the instruction: "To delete the document, click Delete."
- Put the common case first. Exceptions after.
- Sound like a knowledgeable friend. No buzzwords, no figurative language, no "please" in instructions, and never "simply", "easy", or "quickly" in a procedure. If it were simple, the reader would not be here.
- Don't pre-announce ("we will soon support...") and don't start consecutive sentences with the same phrase.
- Link with words that say where the link goes: the page title or a short description. Never "click here". Prefer a sentence of context on the page over a link off it.
- Headings carry the point, not just the topic ("Pick the mode first", not "Modes"). Sentence case. A task heading is a bare verb phrase ("Create an instance"). A concept heading is a noun phrase. One h1 per page, no skipped levels.
- Numbered lists for sequences, bullets for everything else. Introduce a list with a complete sentence. Keep items parallel.
- Code goes in code font. UI elements go in bold. Use serial commas. Drop "etc." and say up front that a list is partial. ## Make statements load one at a time (STE rules) - One instruction per sentence. One thought per sentence everywhere else.
- Split instructions longer than about 20 words and other sentences longer than about 25.
- Put the warning or condition before the step it guards: "If hot oil touches your skin, injuries can occur."
- Keep "the" and "a": "Remove backup file" reads two ways. "Remove the backup file" reads one.
- Give each word one meaning and one job, then keep it. If "check" means inspect, don't also use it for restrain.
- Pick one word per action and stick to it: "start", not "start" here and "initiate" there.
- Write procedures as direct commands, never as narration and never in the passive: "Install the component", not "the component must be installed".
- Avoid "-ing" words where you can. ## Leave no sentence open to two readings (Global English) - Keep words like "only" and "not" next to the word they change: "only fails on growth" and "fails only on growth" say different things.
- Break up long noun strings: "the proto import budget check script" becomes "the script that checks the proto-import budget".
- Make every "it", "they", and "this" point at one obvious thing. Repeat the noun when in doubt. Never use "this" or "which" to point at a whole clause.
- Don't drop verbs: "Phase 1 moves the converters and Phase 2 the runtime" leaves Phase 2 without one. Give it one.
- Keep the small words that show structure, such as "that" in "Ensure that the switch is off". Never trade clarity for word count.
- Repeat the article in a series when it prevents a misread: "the client and the host", not "the client and host", when they are two things.
- Say which parts "and" or "or" joins when a sentence can group two ways. "Both...and", "either...or", and "if...then" are free disambiguators.
- Use periods, not semicolons. Replace an em dash with a new sentence.
- Make text in parentheses a full grammatical unit or its own sentence. Never form plurals with "(s)".
- No slashes: write "a, b, or both" instead of "a/b" or "and/or".
- Call each thing by one name, everywhere. A doc that says "the gate", "the ratchet", and "the budget check" for one thing teaches three things. Don't churn what didn't change.
- Skip idioms, colloquialisms, Latin abbreviations, and metaphors. ## Voice and repo specifics - Apply the **unslop** skill to every doc this skill touches. That skill owns the slop-pattern catalog: AI vocabulary, filler, hedging, formatting tells.
- PR descriptions and commit messages are writing too. Every layer except Diátaxis applies to them. A PR body is a briefing that a reviewer can read in under a minute. Do not paste swarm logs, SHA lists, or metric tables. Link them.
- Product UI strings are not documentation. Use your product's copy guidelines for those.
- Indent code snippets with tabs. Write real paths. Make every count or tree claim true at the commit that lands it, and include the command that regenerates it. ## Worked example Before: > Configuration of the proto import ratchet budget script parameters is performed via budget.json. Note that it's important to remember that running with --write, which updates the committed budget to reflect the current count, should only be done when lowering it. If exceeded, CI fails. After: > `budget.mjs` reads the committed budget from `budget.json` and counts the files that import protos. If the count exceeds the budget, CI fails. Run `budget.mjs --write` only to lower the budget.

skills.name: test-slack-app
skills.description: Use when a developer wants to test, try out, smoke-test, verify, or confirm that a Slack app built with the Slack CLI (or a plain Bolt app) actually works, by running it in a developer sandbox or a Free Team, never a workspace with real users, with `slack run` and exercising its real slash commands, shortcuts, events, actions, modals, App Home, and assistant surfaces. Also covers `slack doctor` and `slack manifest validate` health checks before hands-on testing.
skills.instructions:
---
name: test-slack-app
description: Use when a developer wants to test, try out, smoke-test, verify, or confirm that a Slack app built with the Slack CLI (or a plain Bolt app) actually works, by running it in a developer sandbox or a Free Team, never a workspace with real users, with `slack run` and exercising its real slash commands, shortcuts, events, actions, modals, App Home, and assistant surfaces. Also covers `slack doctor` and `slack manifest validate` health checks before hands-on testing.
--- # Test Slack App Help a developer confirm that a Slack app they already built actually works. This is the last step of the build loop, after the `slack:create-slack-app` skill scaffolds an app and the `slack:slack-cli` skill runs it. The approach is simple and safe: 1. **Run the app in a developer sandbox or a Free Team:** a sandbox for preference, or a Free Team the developer created for this. Never a workspace with real coworkers in it.
2. **Read the app's source** to learn what it actually listens for.
3. **Hand the developer concrete steps** to perform in Slack, then help them confirm the app responds. This is guided manual checking, not an automated test suite: you drive the setup and tell the developer what to type or click, and they confirm what they see. It works best for apps managed by the Slack CLI; there is a best-effort path for plain Bolt apps in Step 2. --- ## Step 1: Set Up a Safe Place to Test ### 1a. Detect the Slack CLI Use the `slack:slack-cli` skill (**Step 1: Detect the Slack CLI**) to check whether the public Slack CLI is installed and resolve its command name. The fingerprint check, alias fallback, and install instructions all live there; do not duplicate them here. Refer to the resolved command as `SLACK_CMD` throughout. If the CLI is not installed, guide the developer through that same step to install it, since running the app needs it. ### 1b. Make sure there is a safe workspace to test in Testing belongs in a workspace nobody is working in: a developer sandbox for preference, or a Free Team the developer created for this. Never a workspace with real coworkers in it. - **Explain it from the live docs, not from here.** Use the `slack:slack-docs` skill to fetch and summarize <https://docs.slack.dev/tools/developer-sandboxes.md>, so the recommendation always reflects the current docs rather than a copy that drifts out of date. Tell the developer that Slack recommends a sandbox for building and testing apps.
- **Find the current target.** Run `SLACK_CMD auth list` for the authenticated workspaces and their team IDs, and, from the project directory, `SLACK_CMD app list` for the apps already installed and their IDs.
- **Confirm the target is safe.** The CLI cannot tell a sandbox, a Free Team, and a workspace full of real users apart, so ask the developer which one they are pointed at. A sandbox or a Free Team they created for this is fine. A workspace with coworkers in it is not: stop and get them onto one of the other two.
- **If there is no safe target yet**, set one up with the `slack:create-slack-app` skill (**Step 3: Choose Where to Install the App**), which owns the ranked targets, the `sandbox list` / `sandbox create` flow, and the Developer Program links. Either path finishes in the browser, so have the developer come back here once the workspace exists and they have logged into it. ### 1c. Quick health check Catch obvious setup problems with the CLI's own validation before the slower hands-on checks: - `SLACK_CMD doctor`: checks the CLI, language runtime, and authentication.
- `SLACK_CMD manifest validate`: run from the project directory if the app has a manifest, to confirm the app configuration is well-formed. Surface anything these flag before moving on. --- ## Step 2: Run the App Whichever path you use below, first turn the app's log level up to debug so you have the most context while testing. Prefer a way that leaves the developer's code untouched: read the logger setup to see whether it reads a log-level environment variable (some templates wire one such as `SLACK_LOG_LEVEL` or `LOG_LEVEL`). If it does, set that variable instead of editing source. For a CLI-managed app, `SLACK_CMD env set <LOG_LEVEL_VAR> debug` stores it in the project `.env` that `slack run` reads; for a plain Bolt app, set it in the environment or `.env` the app already reads. Only when the logger reads no such variable should you edit the source, finding where the log level is set and switching it to debug for this run. ### CLI-managed apps (recommended) Follow **Step 6: Running an App Locally (`slack run`)** in the `slack:slack-cli` skill to start the local dev server in the background. This also installs the app into the target workspace, which matters for a fresh sandbox or Free Team where nothing is installed yet. Once it is running, file changes auto-reload. ### Plain Bolt apps without the CLI (best-effort) If the app is a plain Bolt app started with `node` or `python` rather than the Slack CLI, this skill can still help, but the run path is best-effort and not the primary flow: - Point the app at the test workspace: set its bot and app-level tokens (from that workspace's app settings) in the environment or the `.env` file the app reads.
- Prefer socket mode so the app needs no public URL. This works only if the app is coded for socket mode and the app-level token has `connections:write`; adding tokens to an app scaffolded for HTTP will not deliver events.
- Start the app with its own command (for example `npm start` or `python app.py`) and watch its logs. Say plainly that this path is best-effort, and that the smoothest experience comes from a CLI-managed app. --- ## Step 3: Try It Out in Slack and Confirm It Works This is the heart of the skill. Do not hand the developer a generic checklist. Ground every step in what _this_ app actually registers. ### 3a. Read the source to find what the app listens for Read the app's listener code and list the interactions it registers. Depending on the framework these look like: - **[Slash commands](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/implementing-slash-commands.md):** a registered command name such as `/ship`.
- **[Shortcuts](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/implementing-shortcuts.md):** global or message shortcuts with a callback ID.
- **[Events](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api.md):** subscribed events such as `app_mention`, `message`, or `reaction_added`.
- **[Actions](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/handling-user-interaction.md):** interactive components (buttons, selects) with an action ID.
- **[View submissions](https://docs.slack.dev/surfaces/modals.md):** modal submit handlers (`view_submission`).
- **[App Home](https://docs.slack.dev/surfaces/app-home.md):** an `app_home_opened` handler or a published Home tab.
- **[Assistant / agent](https://docs.slack.dev/ai.md):** an assistant or `assistant_thread_started` handler, common in the agent templates. Name the concrete identifiers you find (the actual command and callback names), not placeholders. ### 3b. Turn each into a "do this, expect that" step For every registered interaction, give the developer a concrete step and what a working app should do in response. A few spots are non-obvious, so spell them out: - **Slash command** → type the command (for example `/ship`) in a channel or DM in the test workspace → expect the response the handler sends.
